areas.title: General Security Concepts
areas.theme: Controls, CIA and Zero Trust, change management and cryptography: the vocabulary every other domain builds on.
story: Every defense starts with the basics.
Learn how controls are sorted, how trust is earned, and how secrets are kept.
canDo: Classify any security control by category and type
Explain CIA, AAA and Zero Trust
Pick the right cryptographic tool for a job

sections.title: Compare and contrast various types of security controls
Summarize fundamental security concepts
Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security
Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

items.back:
Definition: The first and smallest Security+ SY0-701 domain, about 12% of the exam. It covers the building blocks the rest of the exam relies on: security control categories and types, core concepts such as CIA, AAA and Zero Trust, change management, and cryptographic solutions.
Example: A question asking whether a door lock is a physical preventive control, or which PKI component checks certificate status in real time, comes from Domain 1.0.
Category: 1.0 General Security Concepts
Key Points: Four objectives: 1.1 security controls, 1.2 fundamental concepts, 1.3 change management, 1.4 cryptographic solutions; weighted 12%, the lowest of the five domains; its vocabulary is reused in every other domain

items.front: SY0-701 1.1: Compare and contrast various types of security controls
items.back:
Definition: Objective 1.1 asks you to classify any security control two ways: by category (how it is implemented: technical, managerial, operational, physical) and by type (what it is meant to do: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive).
Example: A security guard is a physical category control that can be preventive, deterrent and detective at the same time.
Category: 1.1 Security controls
Key Points: Category answers 'how is it implemented'; type answers 'what goal does it serve'; one control can have several types; read the scenario for the control's intent

Definition: The four ways SY0-701 groups controls by how they are implemented: technical (enforced by systems), managerial (policies and risk decisions), operational (carried out by people day to day) and physical (protect tangible spaces and assets).
Example: A firewall is technical, a security policy is managerial, security awareness training is operational, and a fence is physical.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Categories
Key Points: Technical, managerial, operational, physical; managerial is also called administrative; operational means people do it, technical means a system does it

Definition: A control implemented with technology such as hardware, software or firmware, so the system enforces it rather than a person. Also called a logical control.
Example: Operating system permissions, antivirus software, firewall rules and full-disk encryption.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Categories
Key Points: Enforced by a system; firewalls and antivirus are classic examples; contrast with operational, where a person performs the task

Definition: An administrative control focused on the design and oversight of security: policies, standards, risk assessments and procedures that guide how the organization manages security.
Example: A written information security policy, a risk assessment, or onboarding and offboarding policies approved by leadership.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Categories
Key Points: Also called administrative; documents and decisions, not technology; policies and risk assessments are the usual exam answers

Definition: A control carried out by people rather than by systems, as part of daily operations.
Example: Security guards checking IDs, security awareness training, and staff performing regular log reviews.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Categories
Key Points: Implemented by people; awareness training is the classic example; the trap is confusing it with managerial (managerial sets the policy, operational is people doing the work)

Definition: A control that limits physical access to buildings, rooms or equipment, or protects tangible assets.
Example: Fences, door locks, bollards, access badges and guard shacks.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Categories
Key Points: Protects the physical environment; locks, fences and badge readers; a guard can be counted as physical or operational depending on the question's framing

Definition: The six goals a control can serve: preventive (stop it), deterrent (discourage it), detective (identify it), corrective (fix it after), compensating (substitute when the primary control is not possible) and directive (tell people what to do).
Example: A lock prevents, a warning sign deters, a motion sensor detects, restoring from backup corrects, isolating an unpatchable server compensates, and a policy directs.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive; one control can serve several types; deterrent discourages but does not physically stop, preventive stops

Definition: A control that blocks an incident from happening in the first place by restricting access or actions.
Example: A firewall rule blocking inbound traffic, a door lock, or account lockout policies.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Stops the event before it occurs; deterrent only discourages, preventive actually blocks; firewalls and locks are the standard answers

Definition: A control that discourages an attacker or user from trying something, without physically or technically stopping them.
Example: A login banner warning that misuse will be prosecuted, a visible guard at reception, or threat of demotion for policy violations.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Psychological effect only; a determined attacker can ignore it; contrast with preventive, which actually blocks the action

Definition: A control that identifies and records an event while it happens or after, so it can be investigated, without stopping it.
Example: Reviewing system logs, an intrusion detection system raising an alert, or a motion sensor tripping an alarm.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Identifies and alerts, does not block; IDS is detective, IPS is preventive; logs and cameras that are reviewed are detective

Definition: A control applied after an event to limit damage and restore systems or operations to normal.
Example: Restoring data from backups after ransomware, or an incident response process that removes malware and patches the hole.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Acts after the event; backups and restoration are classic; contrast with compensating, which substitutes for a control that cannot be used

Definition: An alternative control used when the primary or required control cannot be implemented, providing similar protection by other means.
Example: A legacy system that cannot be patched is placed on an isolated network segment with strict firewall rules until it can be replaced.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: A substitute, often temporary, when the ideal control is not feasible; look for 'cannot', 'unable to' or 'legacy' in the scenario; not the same as corrective

Definition: A control that tells people what they should or should not do, relying on them to comply rather than enforcing it.
Example: A policy requiring sensitive files to be stored in a protected folder, or a sign reading 'Authorized personnel only'.
Category: 1.1 Security controls > Control types
Key Points: Instructs, does not enforce, so it is a relatively weak type; policies and instructional signage; a warning of consequences leans deterrent instead

Definition: Objective 1.2 covers the core ideas of security: the CIA triad, non-repudiation, AAA, gap analysis, Zero Trust architecture, physical security controls, and deception and disruption technology.
Example: A question asking which Zero Trust component makes the allow or deny decision, or what a honeytoken is, belongs to objective 1.2.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts
Key Points: Zero Trust components and physical sensors are frequently tested details; know honeypot vs honeynet vs honeyfile vs honeytoken

Definition: The three core goals of information security. Confidentiality keeps data secret from unauthorized parties, integrity keeps data accurate and unaltered, and availability keeps systems and data accessible to authorized users when needed.
Example: Encryption protects confidentiality, hashing detects changes to protect integrity, and redundant servers protect availability.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > CIA
Key Points: Confidentiality: encryption, access controls; integrity: hashing, digital signatures; availability: redundancy, patching, fault tolerance; a DDoS attack targets availability

Definition: Proof of the origin and integrity of data, so the sender cannot later credibly deny having sent or signed it.
Example: A contract is digitally signed with the signer's private key; anyone with the public key can verify that only that signer could have created the signature.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Non-repudiation
Key Points: Provided by digital signatures (hash plus private key); a hash alone gives integrity but not non-repudiation; symmetric keys cannot provide it because both parties share the key

Definition: A framework for controlling access. Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and accounting records what you did (logins, resources used, time spent).
Example: A VPN user logs in with credentials verified by a RADIUS server (authentication), is placed in a group allowed to reach file servers (authorization), and the session start, stop and data use are logged (accounting).
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > AAA
Key Points: Order: identification claim, authentication, authorization, accounting; logging and audit trails are accounting; RADIUS and TACACS+ are common AAA servers

Definition: Verifying a human user's claimed identity, usually with credentials such as a password, plus other factors like a token, a phone prompt or biometrics.
Example: An employee enters a username and password and then approves a push notification on a phone (multifactor authentication).
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > AAA
Key Points: Username is identification, password proves it; factors: something you know, have, are, plus somewhere you are; MFA combines different factor types, two passwords are not MFA

Definition: Verifying that a device or system is the trusted one it claims to be, since a device cannot type a password. Commonly done with digital certificates installed on the device and signed by the organization's certificate authority.
Example: A company laptop presents its device certificate when connecting to the corporate VPN, and the VPN concentrator only accepts devices with a certificate signed by the internal CA.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > AAA
Key Points: Device certificates signed by a trusted CA; used for VPN, Wi-Fi and network access control; answers 'how do we know this device is ours'

Definition: Frameworks that map users to permissions through an abstraction such as roles, groups, attributes or rules, instead of assigning rights to each user for each resource individually.
Example: Rather than granting 500 users access to 40 shares one by one, the admin grants access to a 'Shipping' role and adds staff to that role.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > AAA
Key Points: Abstraction scales and is easier to audit; examples: role-based, attribute-based, rule-based, discretionary, mandatory (detailed in 4.6); direct per-user permissions do not scale

Definition: A study comparing the current security posture with a desired state, often a framework or standard, to find the gaps and plan how to close them.
Example: A company compares its controls against NIST SP 800-171 requirements, finds no formal incident response plan, and builds a roadmap to add one.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Gap analysis
Key Points: Current state vs target baseline; produces a plan or roadmap; often uses a framework such as NIST or ISO/IEC 27001; can take weeks or months

Definition: A security model that trusts nothing by default, even inside the network: every subject and every request is authenticated, authorized and checked before access is granted. It is split into a control plane (decides) and a data plane (enforces and carries traffic).
Example: An employee already on the office network must still authenticate and have device posture checked before reaching the HR application.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust
Key Points: Never trust, always verify; no implicit trust based on network location; control plane decides, data plane enforces; based on NIST SP 800-207

Definition: The part of a Zero Trust architecture that manages and makes access decisions: it defines policy, evaluates requests and configures the enforcement points. It includes the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator.
Example: A central identity and policy service decides whether a contractor's request to a database is allowed and tells the gateway what to do.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: Decides and manages; contains Policy Engine and Policy Administrator; adaptive identity, threat scope reduction and policy-driven access control are its concepts; data plane does the forwarding

Definition: Evaluating identity using context, not only credentials: location, device, time, behavior and risk signals change how much verification is required.
Example: A login from a new country on an unknown device triggers an extra MFA prompt, while the usual office laptop does not.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: Context and risk based; can step up authentication; considers relationship to the organization, location, IP, device

Definition: Shrinking the possible attack surface by limiting the number of entry points and giving subjects only the access they need.
Example: Users reach only the specific applications they need through a gateway, instead of having full network access over a VPN.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: Fewer entry points, least privilege; reduces what an attacker can reach after compromise; ties to microsegmentation

Definition: Granting or denying access based on defined policies that combine identity, context and rules, rather than on network location.
Example: A policy says finance staff may reach the payroll system only from managed devices during business hours.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: Rules decide access, evaluated per request; works with adaptive identity; policies are evaluated by the Policy Engine

Definition: The control plane component that carries out the Policy Engine's decision: it communicates with the Policy Enforcement Point to establish or shut down the communication path, for example by issuing session tokens or credentials.
Example: After the Policy Engine approves a request, the Policy Administrator signals the gateway to open the session and hands it a session token.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: Executes decisions, does not make them; talks to the PEP; Policy Engine decides, Policy Administrator acts, PEP enforces

Definition: The control plane component that makes the actual access decision (grant, deny or revoke) by evaluating the request against policy and other inputs such as threat intelligence and identity data.
Example: The Policy Engine sees that a device fails its patch posture check and denies access to the source code repository.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Control plane
Key Points: The decision maker; uses policy plus external signals; the trap is choosing Policy Administrator or PEP when the question asks who decides

Definition: The part of a Zero Trust architecture where traffic actually flows and decisions are enforced. It includes the subject or system, the Policy Enforcement Point and the implicit trust zone behind it.
Example: A user's traffic passes through a gateway that allows the session only because the control plane approved it.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Data plane
Key Points: Carries and enforces, does not decide; contains subject/system, PEP, implicit trust zones; contrast with control plane

Definition: The area behind a Policy Enforcement Point where entities are trusted once they have passed through it. Zero Trust aims to keep these zones as small as possible.
Example: After the gateway admits a session, traffic between it and the specific application server is in the implicit trust zone.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Data plane
Key Points: Trust only after passing the PEP; keep zones small; a flat internal network is a large implicit trust zone, which Zero Trust avoids

Definition: The entity requesting access in a Zero Trust architecture: the subject is the user or process, and the system is the device or application it uses.
Example: A nurse (subject) on a hospital tablet (system) requests access to a patient records application.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Data plane
Key Points: The requester; both the user and the device are evaluated; sits on the untrusted side of the PEP

Definition: The data plane gatekeeper that sits between the subject and the resource; it passes requests to the control plane and then enables, monitors and terminates the connection as instructed.
Example: An application gateway that holds every connection until the Policy Administrator tells it to allow or drop the session.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Zero Trust > Data plane
Key Points: Enforces, does not decide; all traffic passes through it; Policy Engine decides, Policy Administrator relays, PEP enforces

Definition: Controls that protect buildings, equipment and people from physical access and harm, including barriers, entry controls, surveillance, guards, badges, lighting and sensors.
Example: A data center uses fencing, bollards, a badge reader, an access control vestibule, cameras and guards in layers.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Layered defense; many physical controls are both preventive and deterrent; sensors and cameras are detective

Definition: Short, sturdy posts placed to stop vehicles from reaching a building or area while still letting people on foot pass.
Example: Concrete bollards in front of a store entrance prevent a car from being driven through the glass doors.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Stop vehicles, not people; preventive physical control; also used to channel foot traffic

Definition: A small space with two doors where only one door can be open at a time, so each person can be checked and tailgating is prevented. Formerly called a mantrap.
Example: At a data center entrance, the inner door stays locked until the outer door closes and the person badges in again.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Two interlocking doors; stops tailgating and piggybacking; old name mantrap

Definition: A perimeter barrier that marks a boundary and keeps people out; it can be see-through or opaque and made harder to climb with height or razor wire.
Example: A tall fence with razor wire surrounds a power substation.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Preventive and deterrent; transparent fences allow visibility, opaque ones hide activity; first layer of perimeter defense

Definition: Cameras (CCTV) that monitor and record areas, often with features such as motion detection, object detection and facial recognition.
Example: Cameras with motion detection record the loading dock and alert security when someone appears after hours.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Mainly detective, also deterrent when visible; CCTV = closed-circuit television; recordings support investigations

Definition: A person who protects a facility by checking identities, monitoring access, responding to events and verifying visitors. Two-person integrity can require two guards for sensitive areas.
Example: A guard at reception checks each visitor's ID against the visitor list and issues a temporary badge.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Flexible: preventive, deterrent and detective; can make judgment calls machines cannot; two-person integrity or control reduces insider risk

Definition: An identification card, often with a photo and an RFID or NFC chip, used to unlock doors and show who someone is; badge use can be logged.
Example: Employees tap their badges on a reader to open the office door, and each entry is recorded.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Identification plus electronic entry; usage logs support accounting; risks are lost, shared or cloned badges

Definition: Illumination of outdoor and indoor areas to discourage intruders and help cameras and guards see clearly.
Example: Bright, even lighting around a parking lot removes shadows and lets cameras capture usable footage at night.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security
Key Points: Deterrent; improves camera image quality; avoid shadows and glare; infrared cameras can work in low light

Definition: Devices that detect a physical change such as heat, weight, movement or sound and trigger an alert. SY0-701 lists infrared, pressure, microwave and ultrasonic sensors.
Example: An alarm system uses infrared motion sensors in hallways and pressure mats at doorways.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security > Sensors
Key Points: Detective controls; infrared detects heat, pressure detects weight, microwave and ultrasonic detect movement by reflected waves

Definition: A sensor that detects changes in infrared radiation (heat), such as a warm body moving through its field of view.
Example: A passive infrared motion detector turns on an alarm when a person walks through a closed office at night.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security > Sensors
Key Points: Detects body heat; common in motion detectors; works in the dark

Definition: A sensor that detects force or weight applied to a surface.
Example: A pressure mat under the carpet at a server room door raises an alert when someone steps on it.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security > Sensors
Key Points: Detects weight or force; floor mats and pressure-sensitive surfaces; does not need line of sight

Definition: A motion sensor that sends out microwave pulses and detects movement from changes in the reflected signal; it covers larger areas than infrared and can sense through some materials.
Example: A warehouse uses microwave motion sensors to cover large open floor areas.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security > Sensors
Key Points: Active sensor using reflected microwaves; larger coverage than infrared; more prone to false alarms

Definition: A motion sensor that emits high-frequency sound beyond human hearing and detects movement from changes in the echoes.
Example: An ultrasonic sensor in a stockroom triggers an alarm when the echo pattern changes because someone entered.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Physical security > Sensors
Key Points: Uses sound waves, not light or heat; detects motion by echo changes; contrast with microwave, which uses radio waves

Definition: Decoy systems and data that lure attackers, waste their time and reveal their methods: honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles and honeytokens.
Example: A security team deploys a fake file server, fake documents and fake API keys, and watches for anyone who touches them.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Deception and disruption
Key Points: Any interaction with a decoy is suspicious by definition; used to learn attacker techniques and detect intrusions; distinguish pot (system), net (network), file (document), token (traceable data)

Definition: A single decoy system that looks like a real, valuable target, built to attract attackers so their activity can be watched and studied.
Example: A fake server exposing what looks like a vulnerable database is placed online to record attackers' tools and commands.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Deception and disruption
Key Points: One decoy system; honeynet is many decoys together; attackers may recognize a poor honeypot

Definition: A network of multiple honeypots and other decoy resources (servers, workstations, routers) that together imitate a real environment.
Example: A research team builds a fake small-business network with several servers and workstations to observe how attackers move laterally.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Deception and disruption
Key Points: More than one honeypot, a whole decoy network; more convincing and shows lateral movement; contrast with a single honeypot

Definition: A decoy file with an attractive name and fake contents; any access to it triggers an alert.
Example: A file named passwords.txt on a file share sends an alert to security whenever someone opens it.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Deception and disruption
Key Points: Bait file, alert on access; contrast with honeytoken, which is traceable data that may be copied elsewhere

Definition: A piece of fake but traceable data, such as a fake credential, API key or email address, that has no legitimate use, so seeing it used or appear somewhere reveals a breach and where data went.
Example: A fake AWS access key is planted in a code repository; when someone tries to use it, the alert shows the repository was compromised.
Category: 1.2 Fundamental security concepts > Deception and disruption
Key Points: Traceable data, not a whole file or system; detects exfiltration and tracks where data ends up; fake credentials, records or email addresses

items.front: SY0-701 1.3: Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security
items.back:
Definition: Objective 1.3 covers how organizations control changes to systems safely: the business process (approval, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, testing, backout plans, maintenance windows, SOPs), the technical side effects of changes, documentation and version control.
Example: Before patching a production firewall, the team files a change request, tests it, gets approval, schedules a maintenance window and prepares a backout plan.
Category: 1.3 Change management
Key Points: Unmanaged changes cause outages and security holes; know each step of the process; technical implications include downtime, restarts, dependencies and legacy apps

items.front: Business processes impacting security operation (change management)
items.back:
Definition: The formal steps that govern a change before it reaches production: approval, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, a backout plan, a maintenance window and standard operating procedures.
Example: A change advisory board reviews a request to upgrade the email server, checks its impact analysis and test results, and approves it for Saturday night.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: A clear, repeatable process; usually overseen by a change advisory board (CAB); every change needs a way back (backout plan)

Definition: The formal review and sign-off a change must get before it is made, often by a change advisory board, based on the request's purpose, scope, risk and schedule.
Example: A change request to open a new firewall port is submitted, reviewed for risk and approved by the CAB before implementation.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: No change without approval; CAB = change advisory board; emergency changes still get approval, sometimes after the fact

Definition: Assigning the person or group responsible for a change and the affected system; the owner requests and is accountable for the change but does not necessarily perform it.
Example: The shipping department manager owns the label printing application and requests its upgrade, while IT performs the work.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Owner is accountable and is kept informed; owner is not always the implementer; makes responsibility clear

Definition: The people and groups affected by a change, who should be identified and consulted because the change may impact their work.
Example: Upgrading the payroll system involves HR, finance, IT and the payroll vendor as stakeholders.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Anyone impacted; a small change can affect many departments; involve them in planning and communication

Definition: Assessing the risks of making a change and of not making it, including possible failures, side effects and the effect on business operations.
Example: Analysis shows a database patch could break a reporting tool, so the team plans extra testing; it also notes the unpatched flaw is actively exploited.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Risk of the change and risk of doing nothing; rated high, medium or low; identifies side effects before approval

Definition: Evidence from trying the change in a non-production environment (a sandbox or test lab) first, to confirm it works and has no harmful side effects before approval or rollout.
Example: A patch is applied to a cloned test server, and the results show the application still starts and passes its checks.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Test in a sandbox or staging environment, not production; results support approval; also test the backout plan

Definition: A documented way to undo a change and return to the previous working state if the change fails or causes problems.
Example: Before a server OS upgrade, the team takes a full backup and snapshot so they can roll back if the upgrade breaks the application.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Also called a rollback plan; always required; usually depends on good backups; not every change is easy to reverse

Definition: A scheduled period, usually of low business activity, set aside for making changes so disruption is minimized.
Example: A retailer applies server updates at 2 a.m. on Sundays, but freezes changes during the holiday shopping season.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Pre-scheduled, low-impact time; often overnight or weekends; change freezes at critical business periods

Definition: A documented, step-by-step description of how a routine task, including the change process itself, must be performed so it is done consistently.
Example: The change management SOP describes how to submit a request, who approves it and how to record the outcome.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Business processes
Key Points: Written, repeatable steps; must itself be updated when processes change; SOP = standard operating procedure

Definition: The technical side effects to plan for when making a change: allow and deny list updates, restricted activities, downtime, service and application restarts, legacy applications and dependencies.
Example: Updating an application requires adding its new executable hash to the allow list, a service restart and checking that a dependent service still works.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Every change can have hidden effects; plan restarts and downtime; check dependencies and legacy systems before approval

Definition: Lists that explicitly permit (allow list) or block (deny list) applications, addresses or traffic. A change may require updating them, or the change may be blocked or create an unintended opening.
Example: After an application update, the new version is blocked because its hash is not on the application allow list until the list is updated.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Allow list: only listed items run, everything else is denied; deny list: listed items are blocked, everything else runs; updates can break or open access

Definition: Limits on what may be done during a change: the implementer must stay within the approved scope and not make unapproved extra changes.
Example: A technician approved to update one router's firmware notices another misconfiguration but may not fix it without a separate approved change.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Stay inside the approved scope; scope expansion needs new approval; protects against untested side effects

Definition: The period when a service is unavailable because of a change. It should be planned, minimized and communicated, for example with a failover system or a maintenance page.
Example: An e-commerce site shows a maintenance page for 30 minutes while the database is upgraded, during a pre-announced window.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Affects availability; schedule in maintenance windows; use redundancy or failover to reduce it; notify users

Definition: Restarting a background service or daemon so a change takes effect, which can interrupt anything using it and may fail to come back cleanly.
Example: Changing a web server's TLS configuration requires restarting the web service, briefly dropping active connections.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Brief outage risk; a service may not restart correctly; plan and verify after the restart

Definition: Closing and reopening an application so an update or configuration change takes effect, which can interrupt users and lose unsaved work.
Example: A client accounting application must be closed and reopened on every workstation after its update.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Affects users directly; can lose unsaved data; differs from a service restart, which affects background services

Definition: Older applications that may be unsupported, poorly documented or fragile, so changes around them carry extra risk and may require special handling or compensating controls.
Example: An OS patch is held back on one server because the vendor of its 15-year-old manufacturing app no longer exists and cannot confirm compatibility.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: Often unsupported and fragile; document how they work; may need isolation or compensating controls

Definition: Relationships where one component relies on another, so changing one may require changing or restarting others, sometimes on different systems.
Example: Upgrading a database server requires first upgrading the client library used by three applications that connect to it.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Technical implications
Key Points: A change can cascade to other systems; map dependencies before approval; order the steps correctly

Definition: Keeping records current so they match the environment after every change, mainly by updating network diagrams and policies or procedures.
Example: After adding a new firewall, the team updates the network diagram and the firewall management procedure.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Documentation
Key Points: Changes happen often, documentation must follow; outdated documents mislead troubleshooting and incident response; include documentation updates in the change process itself

Definition: Revising network and system diagrams after a change so they show the current architecture.
Example: A new VLAN for IoT devices is added, so the network diagram is updated to show it and its firewall rules.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Documentation
Key Points: Diagrams must match reality; used in troubleshooting and incident response; easy to forget

Definition: Revising written policies and procedures after a change so staff follow steps that fit the new system or process.
Example: After moving to a new backup product, the backup and restore procedure is rewritten for the new tool.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Documentation
Key Points: New systems often need new procedures; stale procedures cause errors; part of closing a change

Definition: Tracking every change to code, configurations or documents over time, with who changed what and when, so earlier versions can be compared or restored.
Example: Router configurations are stored in a Git repository, so a bad change can be found with a diff and the previous version restored.
Category: 1.3 Change management > Version control
Key Points: History of changes with the ability to roll back; applies to code, configurations and documents; supports backout plans and audits

items.front: SY0-701 1.4: Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions
items.back:
Definition: Objective 1.4 covers PKI and keys, encryption levels and types, cryptographic hardware and tools, obfuscation, hashing, salting, digital signatures, key stretching, blockchain and digital certificates.
Example: Choosing full-disk encryption for laptops, an HSM for a CA's keys, or OCSP for real-time certificate checks are all objective 1.4 decisions.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions
Key Points: Largest objective in Domain 1 by item count; symmetric vs asymmetric and hashing vs encryption are core distinctions; know certificate status checking (CRL vs OCSP)

Definition: The policies, roles, hardware, software and procedures used to create, distribute, manage, store and revoke digital certificates that bind public keys to identities.
Example: A company runs an internal certificate authority that issues certificates to its servers, laptops and users.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > PKI
Key Points: Built on asymmetric (public/private) key pairs; certificate authorities vouch for identities; covers the whole certificate lifecycle including revocation

Definition: The half of an asymmetric key pair that is shared openly; it is used to encrypt data for the key owner and to verify the owner's digital signatures.
Example: A web server's certificate contains its public key, which browsers use during TLS to set up a secure session.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > PKI
Key Points: Shared with everyone; encrypt with the recipient's public key; verify signatures with the sender's public key; cannot be used to derive the private key

Definition: The half of an asymmetric key pair that only its owner holds and must be kept secret; it decrypts data encrypted with the matching public key and creates digital signatures.
Example: A user signs an email with their private key; recipients verify it with the user's public key.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > PKI
Key Points: Never shared; decrypts what the public key encrypted; signs data; if compromised, the certificate must be revoked

Definition: Storing a copy of encryption keys with a trusted third party or a protected internal store so data can be recovered if the key is lost or access is legally required.
Example: A company keeps escrowed copies of employees' encryption keys so it can still decrypt business data after an employee leaves.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > PKI
Key Points: Recovery and legal access to encrypted data; the escrow holder must be highly trusted; contrast with key management system, which handles the whole key lifecycle

Definition: Transforming plaintext into ciphertext with an algorithm and a key so only someone with the right key can read it. SY0-701 covers where it is applied (levels, transport), how (symmetric, asymmetric, key exchange) and its strength (algorithms, key length).
Example: A laptop uses full-disk encryption at rest, while its web traffic is encrypted in transit with TLS.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Protects confidentiality; reversible with the key, unlike hashing; data at rest vs data in transit

Definition: How much data a single encryption mechanism covers: a whole drive (full-disk), part of storage (partition, volume), or specific data (file, database, record).
Example: A laptop may use full-disk encryption, while a database server encrypts only the column holding credit card numbers.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Scope choice is the test; full-disk protects a lost device, record level protects specific fields; finer levels allow different keys per item

Definition: Encrypting everything on a storage drive, including the operating system, swap and temporary files, so the whole drive is unreadable without the key.
Example: BitLocker or FileVault on a laptop keeps all data safe if the laptop is stolen.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: FDE protects lost or stolen devices; often paired with a TPM; data is readable once the system is unlocked and running

Definition: Encrypting one specific partition of a drive while other partitions may remain unencrypted.
Example: A drive has an unencrypted system partition and a separately encrypted data partition holding customer files.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Narrower than full-disk; protects selected partitions only; BitLocker can encrypt a single data partition

Definition: Encrypting individual files rather than a whole drive or partition, so protection follows those specific files.
Example: Windows Encrypting File System (EFS) encrypts a single folder of HR documents on an otherwise unencrypted drive.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Per-file protection; EFS on NTFS is the common example; a copy moved to a non-NTFS drive (such as FAT32) or sent over the network is no longer EFS-encrypted

Definition: Encrypting a logical volume, which may span part of a disk or several physical disks, rather than one physical drive or partition.
Example: A BitLocker-encrypted removable USB volume (BitLocker To Go) or an encrypted volume spanning two disks.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Logical storage unit, not a physical disk; trap: a partition is a section of one physical disk, while a volume is a logical storage unit that can be one partition or span several disks

Definition: Encrypting an entire database, including its data files and backups, typically transparently by the database server.
Example: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) in Microsoft SQL Server encrypts the database files on disk.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Whole database at rest; transparent to applications; contrast with record level, which encrypts selected fields

Definition: Encrypting individual records or fields (columns) inside a database, so only the sensitive parts are encrypted, possibly with different keys.
Example: Only the Social Security number column in a customer table is encrypted, while names remain readable for searches.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption > Level
Key Points: Most granular level; also called column or field-level encryption; keeps sensitive fields protected even from some database users

Definition: Encrypting data in transit as it moves across a network, so it cannot be read if intercepted.
Example: HTTPS uses TLS to protect web traffic, and a site-to-site IPsec VPN protects traffic between two offices.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Data in transit, not at rest; TLS, IPsec, SSH, VPNs; protects against eavesdropping and on-path attacks

Definition: Encryption that uses a mathematically related key pair: data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key, and the private key creates signatures the public key verifies. Also called public key cryptography.
Example: RSA or elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) is used in TLS to authenticate the server and help establish a shared session key.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Two keys, public and private; slower than symmetric, so used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk data; RSA and ECC; Diffie-Hellman is asymmetric key agreement, not encryption

Definition: Encryption that uses the same shared secret key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suited to large amounts of data, but the key must be shared securely.
Example: AES encrypts a laptop's drive and the bulk data of a TLS session after the session key is agreed.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: One shared key; fast, used for bulk data; key distribution is the weakness; AES is the standard; cannot provide non-repudiation

Definition: The method used to get a shared symmetric key to both parties securely, either out-of-band (another channel) or in-band (over the same network, protected with asymmetric cryptography or Diffie-Hellman).
Example: In TLS, the browser and server use Diffie-Hellman to agree on a session key without ever sending the key itself.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Solves symmetric key distribution; out-of-band (phone, courier) vs in-band (network); Diffie-Hellman agrees on a key, it does not encrypt data; session keys are temporary

Definition: The mathematical procedures used to encrypt and decrypt data. Security depends on a well-known, tested algorithm plus a secret key, not on hiding the algorithm.
Example: AES is a symmetric algorithm; RSA and ECC are asymmetric; DES and RC4 are outdated and should not be used.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Algorithms are public, keys are secret; choose current, vetted algorithms; symmetric: AES; asymmetric: RSA, ECC

Definition: The size of a cryptographic key in bits; longer keys mean far more possible keys and greater resistance to brute force. Symmetric and asymmetric keys are not comparable bit for bit.
Example: AES-256 uses a 256-bit key, while RSA keys are commonly 2048 bits or more; RSA-2048 is only about as strong as a 112-bit symmetric key.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Encryption
Key Points: Longer is stronger but slower; asymmetric keys must be much longer than symmetric for similar strength; ECC gives equal strength with shorter keys than RSA

Definition: Hardware and systems that generate, store and protect keys and perform cryptographic operations: Trusted Platform Module, hardware security module, key management system and secure enclave.
Example: A laptop's TPM protects its BitLocker key, while a bank's HSM protects payment card keys.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Tools
Key Points: TPM is a chip in one device; HSM is a dedicated, often clustered appliance for many systems; secure enclave is an isolated processor in a chip; KMS manages the key lifecycle

Definition: A dedicated security chip on a computer's motherboard that provides a hardware root of trust: secure key storage, a random number generator, key generation and integrity measurement for secure boot.
Example: BitLocker stores its key in the TPM so the drive unlocks only on the original, unmodified computer.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Tools
Key Points: Built into one device; protects keys used by that device, such as full-disk encryption keys; resists dictionary attacks with lockout; contrast with HSM for enterprise scale

Definition: A dedicated, tamper-resistant hardware device (appliance or plug-in card) that securely generates, stores and uses many keys for servers and applications, often clustered for redundancy and with crypto acceleration.
Example: A certificate authority keeps its root private key inside an HSM so the key never leaves the hardware.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Tools
Key Points: Enterprise scale, many keys, many systems; high availability and crypto acceleration; TPM is per-device, HSM serves many

Definition: A centralized system that manages the full lifecycle of cryptographic keys: creation, storage, distribution, rotation, expiration and revocation, often with logging and access control.
Example: A cloud provider's key management service lets an organization create, rotate and audit the keys used to encrypt its storage buckets.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Tools
Key Points: Lifecycle and central control; keeps keys separate from the data they protect; supports rotation and auditing

Definition: A hardware-isolated security processor or area inside a system on a chip that handles sensitive data such as keys and biometric data separately from the main processor and operating system.
Example: Apple's Secure Enclave stores fingerprint and face data and protects keys on iPhones, so even a compromised OS cannot read them.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Tools
Key Points: Isolated from the main OS; protects keys and biometrics; has its own boot and true random number generator; found in phones and modern CPUs

Definition: Making data hard to understand or find while keeping it usable for some purpose. SY0-701 lists steganography, tokenization and data masking.
Example: A payment processor replaces card numbers with tokens, and a help desk sees only the last four digits.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Obfuscation
Key Points: Hides meaning or presence of data; not the same as encryption; steganography hides existence, tokenization substitutes, masking hides part

Definition: Hiding data inside other, ordinary-looking data (images, audio, video or network traffic) so that the existence of the message is concealed.
Example: A message is hidden in the least significant bits of a photo's pixels, so the image looks unchanged.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Obfuscation
Key Points: Hides that a message exists, encryption hides what it says; cover image, audio, video or traffic; security through obscurity, not strong protection alone

Definition: Replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive substitute value (token) that has no mathematical relationship to the original; the real value is stored in a separate, secured token vault.
Example: A mobile payment sends a one-time token instead of the real card number; only the payment processor's vault maps it back.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Obfuscation
Key Points: Not encryption, the token cannot be decrypted; original kept in a token vault; reduces PCI DSS scope; contrast with masking, which hides part of the real value

Definition: Hiding some or all of a data value from view by replacing characters, so users see only what they need while the real data stays protected.
Example: A receipt or support screen shows a card number as **** **** **** 4321.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Obfuscation
Key Points: Hides part of the displayed data; often used for non-production copies or limited views; tokenization replaces the whole value with a substitute

Definition: A one-way function that turns input of any size into a fixed-length digest; the same input always gives the same digest, any change gives a different one, and the original cannot be recovered from it.
Example: A downloaded installer's SHA-256 hash is compared with the hash published by the vendor to confirm the file was not altered.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Hashing
Key Points: One-way, not reversible, unlike encryption; provides integrity; a collision is two inputs with the same hash (MD5 is broken); SHA-256 is current; used to store passwords, together with salting and key stretching

Definition: Adding a random value (salt) to each password before hashing it, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed attacks no longer work.
Example: Two users with the password 'Summer2024' get completely different stored hashes because each has a unique salt.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Salting
Key Points: Defeats rainbow tables; salt is unique per password and stored with the hash, it is not secret; does not slow brute force against a single hash, key stretching does

Definition: A hash of a message encrypted with the sender's private key; the recipient verifies it with the sender's public key. It proves integrity, authenticity of origin and non-repudiation.
Example: A software vendor signs its update; the operating system checks the signature with the vendor's public key before installing.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Digital signatures
Key Points: Sign with the sender's private key, verify with the sender's public key; provides integrity, authentication and non-repudiation; does not by itself provide confidentiality

Definition: Making a weak key or password stronger against brute force by running it through a hash or key derivation function many times, so each guess takes much longer.
Example: PBKDF2 or bcrypt hashes a password thousands of times, so an attacker can test far fewer guesses per second.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Key stretching
Key Points: Repeated hashing slows brute force; PBKDF2 and bcrypt are examples; salting stops rainbow tables, stretching slows guessing; both are used together

Definition: A distributed ledger of records (blocks) in which each block contains the hash of the previous block, chaining them so any change to past data is evident; copies are kept by many participants.
Example: Cryptocurrencies record transactions on a blockchain; supply chain systems use it to track goods.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Blockchain
Key Points: Each block includes the previous block's hash; tampering breaks the chain and is detected; distributed, no single central authority; provides integrity and transparency

Definition: The shared, publicly viewable record of all transactions in a public blockchain, copied to every participant so anyone can verify it.
Example: Anyone can look up a Bitcoin transaction on the public ledger, and every node holds a copy.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Open public ledger
Key Points: Distributed to everyone, not held by one party; transparent and verifiable; the ledger is the data, blockchain is the hash-chained technology behind it

Definition: Digitally signed files that bind a public key to an identity (person, server or device), issued by a certificate authority. The common format is X.509, holding the subject, public key, issuer, serial number and validity dates.
Example: A website's TLS certificate, signed by a trusted CA, proves the server is really example.com and provides its public key.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: X.509 standard; signed by a CA; contain the public key, never the private key; status checked by CRL or OCSP

Definition: A trusted entity that verifies identities and issues, signs and revokes digital certificates. Trust flows from a root CA through intermediate CAs to end-entity certificates (the chain of trust).
Example: A commercial CA validates a company's domain and issues it a TLS certificate signed by an intermediate CA.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Issues, signs and revokes certificates; root CA keys are heavily protected, often offline; intermediates issue day-to-day certificates; browsers trust preinstalled root CAs

Definition: A list, published and signed by a CA, of certificates revoked before their expiration date (for example because a private key was compromised); clients download it to check status.
Example: After a server's private key is stolen, its certificate's serial number is added to the CA's CRL.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Downloaded list, updated periodically, so not real-time; can grow large; OCSP checks a single certificate in real time instead

Definition: A protocol that lets a client ask an OCSP responder for the current status (good, revoked or unknown) of one specific certificate in real time. With OCSP stapling, the server attaches a signed, recent status to the TLS handshake.
Example: A browser checks a bank site's certificate status through OCSP, or receives a stapled OCSP response from the bank's server.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Real-time, single-certificate check; lighter than downloading a CRL; stapling moves the check to the server and improves privacy and speed

Definition: A certificate signed with its own private key rather than by a trusted CA, so other systems do not trust it unless it is manually installed as trusted.
Example: An admin creates a self-signed certificate for an internal test web server; browsers show a warning until it is added to the trust store.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Free and quick; not trusted by default; fine for internal or test use; an internal CA is a better way to manage many internal certificates

Definition: A certificate issued and signed by an external, publicly trusted certificate authority, so browsers and devices trust it automatically.
Example: An online store buys a certificate from a public CA so every customer's browser trusts its HTTPS site without warnings.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Trusted by default because the CA's root is in browser trust stores; used for public-facing services; contrast with self-signed

Definition: An inherently trusted component that everything else's trust is built on, such as a root CA certificate in a trust store or a hardware component like a TPM or HSM.
Example: A browser trusts a website because its certificate chains up to a root CA already in the browser's trust store.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: The foundation of a chain of trust; must be highly protected; can be a root CA or hardware (TPM, HSM, secure enclave)

Definition: Creating a key pair and a CSR, a file containing the public key and identity details (such as the domain name) signed with the private key, which is sent to a CA to obtain a certificate. The private key stays with the requester.
Example: A web admin generates a key pair and CSR on the server, submits the CSR to a CA, and installs the signed certificate the CA returns.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: The CSR contains the public key, never the private key; the requester generates the key pair; the CA validates identity before signing

Definition: A certificate whose name begins with an asterisk (for example *.example.com), so it covers any single-level subdomain of that domain.
Example: One certificate for *.example.com secures www.example.com, mail.example.com and shop.example.com.
Category: 1.4 Cryptographic solutions > Certificates
Key Points: Covers one subdomain level only, not a.b.example.com or the bare example.com unless also listed; easier management but one compromised key affects every subdomain; a SAN certificate lists specific names instead

items.front: SY0-701 Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%)
items.back:
Definition: The second Security+ SY0-701 domain, worth about 22% of the exam. It covers who attacks and why (2.1), how they get in (2.2), the weaknesses they exploit (2.3), how to recognize attacks in progress (2.4) and how organizations reduce the risk (2.5).
Example: A question gives a log excerpt showing many failed logins across hundreds of accounts with one password, and asks which attack it is (password spraying, 2.4) and which control helps (MFA, 2.5).
Category: 2.0 Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations
Key Points: Five objectives: 2.1 actors and motivations, 2.2 vectors and attack surfaces, 2.3 vulnerabilities, 2.4 indicators of malicious activity, 2.5 mitigations; 2.4 is a "given a scenario" objective, so expect performance-based log and symptom questions; many terms repeat across objectives (buffer overflow, brute force, supply chain, encryption), so read which context the question asks about

items.front: SY0-701 2.1: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations
items.back:
Definition: Objective 2.1 asks you to tell threat actors apart by who they are, their attributes (internal or external, resources and funding, sophistication) and what motivates them.
Example: Scenario: a well funded group quietly steals defense research for years without asking for money. Answer: nation-state actor motivated by espionage.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations
Key Points: Six actor types: nation-state, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, shadow IT; three attributes: internal/external, resources/funding, sophistication; match motive to actor: money points to organized crime, beliefs to hacktivists, espionage or war to nation-states, revenge often to insiders

Definition: A threat actor is the person or group responsible for a security event. SY0-701 lists six: nation-state, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime and shadow IT.
Example: A ransomware gang, a disgruntled employee and a government hacking unit are all threat actors with very different skills and goals.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations
Key Points: Compare actors by attributes (internal/external, funding, sophistication) and motivation; insiders and shadow IT are internal, the rest usually external; highest capability: nation-states; lowest: unskilled attackers

Definition: A government or government-sponsored group that attacks other countries, organizations or people. It has the most resources and sophistication and often runs long, stealthy campaigns called advanced persistent threats (APTs).
Example: Stuxnet, the worm that damaged Iranian uranium centrifuges, is widely attributed to nation-states.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Highest funding and capability; usual motives: espionage, data exfiltration, disruption, war; often linked to APTs that persist undetected for long periods; trap: a well funded criminal gang after money is organized crime, not a nation-state

Definition: An attacker with little technical skill who runs tools, scripts or exploits written by others. SY0-701 uses this term for what was once called a script kiddie.
Example: A teenager downloads a ready-made DDoS tool and points it at a school website.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Low sophistication and low funding, usually external; motives: notoriety, disruption, curiosity; can still do real damage with ready-made tools; old name: script kiddie

Definition: A hacker who attacks to promote a political, social or philosophical cause. Common methods are website defacement, DDoS and leaking documents.
Example: A group defaces a company website with a protest message after the company announces a controversial policy.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Motive: philosophical or political beliefs, not money; sophistication varies widely; usually external; Anonymous is the classic example

Definition: A current or former employee, contractor or partner who misuses legitimate access to harm the organization, on purpose or by carelessness.
Example: A system administrator who was passed over for promotion copies the customer database before resigning.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Internal actor with existing access and knowledge, so perimeter controls do not stop them; motives: revenge, financial gain, being bribed; mitigations: least privilege, separation of duties, monitoring, offboarding

Definition: Professional criminal groups that attack for profit. They are well funded, organized like businesses and often skilled.
Example: A ransomware group encrypts a hospital network and demands payment in cryptocurrency.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Motive: financial gain above all; high resources and sophistication; typical activities: ransomware, fraud, data theft for sale, extortion; tell apart from nation-state by the money motive

Definition: Employees or departments using hardware, software or cloud services without approval from the IT or security team. It is usually not malicious but creates unmanaged, unpatched and unmonitored risk.
Example: The marketing team signs up for an unapproved file sharing service and uploads customer lists to it.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Threat actors
Key Points: Internal, usually not malicious; risk comes from systems IT does not know about, patch or secure; often driven by convenience or a slow approval process; fix with clear policy and approved alternatives

Definition: The characteristics used to compare threat actors: whether they are internal or external, how much resources and funding they have, and their level of sophistication or capability.
Example: A nation-state is external, very well funded and highly capable; an unskilled attacker is external, poorly funded and low capability.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations
Key Points: Three attributes on the exam: internal/external, resources/funding, sophistication/capability; funding usually drives capability; used to predict what an actor can do and how persistent it will be

Definition: Describes where the actor sits relative to the organization. Internal actors (insiders, shadow IT) already have access inside; external actors must first get in from outside.
Example: An employee abusing database rights is internal; a criminal sending phishing emails from abroad is external.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Attributes of actors
Key Points: Internal actors bypass perimeter defenses and know the environment; external actors need an initial access vector; an external attacker using stolen credentials is still external

Definition: How much money, people, time and tooling a threat actor can spend on attacks. More resources allow custom tools, zero-day exploits and long campaigns.
Example: A nation-state can buy or develop zero-day exploits; a lone hacktivist relies on free tools.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Attributes of actors
Key Points: Highest: nation-states and organized crime; lowest: unskilled attackers and many hacktivists; high funding enables persistence and APT-style operations

Definition: How technically skilled an actor is, from running others' scripts to writing custom malware and discovering zero-day vulnerabilities.
Example: An APT group writes custom implants that evade antivirus, while an unskilled attacker uses a public exploit kit.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Attributes of actors
Key Points: Ranges from unskilled attacker (lowest) to nation-state (highest); often follows funding; sophisticated attacks are stealthy and persistent

Definition: Why attackers attack. Money drives most of it (financial gain, often through blackmail). Others want secrets (espionage, data exfiltration), to stop a service (service disruption, disruption/chaos), to make a point (philosophical/political beliefs), to get even (revenge), or to help (ethical hacking); nations may attack as an act of war.
Example: A hacktivist is motivated by beliefs, organized crime by money, an angry ex-employee by revenge.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations
Key Points: Questions often give the behavior and ask the motive; one actor can have several motives; match: money to organized crime, beliefs to hacktivists, espionage/war to nation-states, revenge to insiders

Definition: Stealing data by moving it out of the organization without authorization, for sale, leverage or intelligence.
Example: Attackers copy millions of customer records and credit card numbers and sell them on a dark web market.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Exfiltration is the unauthorized transfer out; data can be sold, used for blackmail or espionage; detected by unusual outbound traffic volume (see resource consumption); mitigated by DLP and encryption

Definition: Spying to gain secret information, such as government intelligence or a competitor's trade secrets.
Example: A foreign intelligence unit breaks into a defense contractor to steal aircraft designs.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Typical of nation-states (and corporate competitors); stealth matters more than speed; differs from data exfiltration for profit by its intelligence goal

Definition: Making a system or service unavailable to its users, attacking availability.
Example: A DDoS attack takes an online bank offline during a holiday weekend.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Targets availability in the CIA triad; methods: DDoS, ransomware, sabotage; used by hacktivists, nation-states and extortionists

Definition: Forcing a victim to pay or act by threatening to release damaging information or keep harming them.
Example: Attackers steal embarrassing executive emails and threaten to publish them unless paid.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Closely tied to stolen data and double-extortion ransomware (encrypt plus threaten to leak); ultimately often financial

Definition: Attacking to make money through ransom, fraud, theft or selling stolen data.
Example: A criminal group runs business email compromise to trick finance staff into wiring money.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: The most common motive overall; the defining motive of organized crime; can also drive insiders

Definition: Attacking to advance a cause, ideology or political position rather than for money.
Example: A group leaks an energy company's internal documents to protest its environmental record.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: The defining motive of hacktivists; often public actions such as defacement, DDoS and leaks

Definition: Hacking with good intentions: finding weaknesses to get them fixed, with permission or through responsible disclosure.
Example: A researcher finds a flaw in a web app through the vendor's bug bounty program and reports it.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: White-hat or authorized hacking: penetration testers, bug bounty hunters; goal is improving security; permission and disclosure separate it from malicious hacking

Definition: Attacking to get back at a person or organization for a perceived wrong.
Example: A fired employee uses an account that was never disabled to delete project files.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Typical of insider threats, especially disgruntled or terminated staff; mitigate with prompt offboarding and least privilege

Definition: Attacking simply to cause trouble, confusion or damage, with no financial or political goal.
Example: An attacker floods a gaming server with traffic just to watch players get disconnected.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Common with unskilled attackers seeking notoriety; differs from service disruption by having no further goal; differs from hacktivism by having no cause

Definition: Cyber attacks used by one nation against another as part of armed conflict or military strategy, often against critical infrastructure.
Example: Malware takes down parts of a country's power grid during a military conflict.
Category: 2.1 Threat actors and motivations > Motivations
Key Points: Nation-state motive; targets: power, communications, government, military systems; cyberwarfare can accompany physical conflict

items.front: SY0-701 2.2: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces
items.back:
Definition: Objective 2.2 covers threat vectors (the paths an attacker uses to get in) and attack surfaces (all the points where a system could be attacked), including human vectors and social engineering.
Example: Scenario: an attacker leaves infected USB sticks in a company parking lot. Vector: removable device; it relies on human curiosity.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Vector = the path or method; attack surface = the sum of exposed points; reduce the surface by removing unused services, software and accounts; social engineering items (phishing, vishing, smishing, BEC, pretexting, watering hole, typosquatting) are heavily tested

Definition: Attacks delivered through messaging: email, Short Message Service (SMS) and instant messaging (IM). They carry malicious links, attachments or social engineering.
Example: A fake package-delivery text asks the user to tap a link and pay a "redelivery fee".
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Three channels: email, SMS, IM; email-based is phishing, SMS-based is smishing; filtering and user training are the main defenses

Definition: The most common attack vector: messages carrying phishing links, malicious attachments or fraudulent requests.
Example: An email that appears to come from IT asks users to "verify your password" on a fake login page.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Message-based
Key Points: Defenses: spam and malware filtering, SPF, DKIM and DMARC, link rewriting, user training; vector for phishing and business email compromise

Definition: Text messages to phones used to deliver malicious links or social engineering. Phishing by SMS is called smishing.
Example: A text claims your bank account is locked and links to a fake bank site.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Message-based
Key Points: SMS has no built-in sender authentication, so spoofing is easy; mobile screens hide full URLs; attack name: smishing

Definition: Chat platforms (workplace chat, consumer messengers, social media DMs) used to send malicious links, files or impersonation messages.
Example: An attacker with a compromised colleague's chat account sends coworkers a "shared document" link that installs malware.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Message-based
Key Points: Messages from known contacts are trusted more, which attackers exploit; may bypass email filtering; files and links in chat need scanning too

Definition: Malicious content hidden in or delivered by image files, such as scripts embedded in SVG images or data concealed with steganography.
Example: An SVG "image" attached to an email contains embedded JavaScript that redirects the viewer to a phishing page.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: SVG is XML and can carry HTML and JavaScript; steganography hides data inside images; images may slip past filters that trust picture formats

Definition: Malicious code delivered inside files such as executables, documents with macros, PDFs, scripts or compressed archives.
Example: A Word document asks the user to "enable content", which runs a macro that downloads malware.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Common carriers: Office macros, PDFs, ZIP/RAR archives, executables; defenses: attachment scanning, sandboxing, disabling macros, application allow lists

Definition: Phone calls used to deceive victims into revealing information or taking actions. Phishing by voice is called vishing.
Example: A caller claiming to be from the help desk asks an employee to read out the MFA code just sent to their phone.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Attack name: vishing; caller ID is easily spoofed; also includes war dialing and call tampering; verify by calling back a known number

Definition: USB drives and other removable media used to bring malware in or carry data out, including across air gaps.
Example: An attacker drops USB sticks labeled "Salaries 2026" in the lobby; an employee plugs one in and malware runs.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Can cross air-gapped networks (Stuxnet spread this way); some devices act as keyboards (USB keystroke injection); defenses: disable USB storage, device control policies, training

Definition: Software with flaws an attacker can exploit, on clients, servers or apps. Every installed program adds to the attack surface.
Example: An unpatched browser plugin lets a malicious website run code on the visitor's computer.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Patch and update; remove unneeded software to shrink the attack surface; scan for known vulnerabilities; contrast client-based (installed) vs agentless

items.front: Client-based vs. agentless software (vulnerable software vector)
items.back:
Definition: Two ways vulnerable software reaches users. Client-based software is installed on each device, so a flaw or infected executable sits on every endpoint and every copy needs updates. Agentless software installs nothing locally: users connect to a central system (such as a web app) each time, so one compromised server can infect every client that connects.
Example: A flawed desktop chat app must be patched on all 2,000 laptops (client-based); a hacked web portal serves malicious code to every employee who signs in (agentless).
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Vulnerable software
Key Points: Client-based: risk spread across every endpoint, each copy must be updated; agentless: nothing to patch on the client, but one compromised central system reaches every user; the difference is where the code runs and where it gets fixed

Definition: Systems or software past their support period that no longer get security patches, so new vulnerabilities stay open forever.
Example: A factory still runs Windows XP on a control workstation, which receives no updates.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: No patches means known exploits keep working; related to end-of-life and legacy hardware (2.3); mitigate with upgrade, isolation or segmentation and compensating controls

Definition: Networks that let attackers listen in, connect without authorization or tamper with traffic: wireless, wired and Bluetooth.
Example: A user joins open coffee-shop Wi-Fi where an attacker captures unencrypted traffic.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Three types listed: wireless, wired, Bluetooth; fixes: strong encryption (WPA3), 802.1X network access control, disabling unused ports and pairing

Definition: Wi-Fi networks that are open, use weak encryption such as WEP, or allow rogue and evil twin access points.
Example: An attacker sets up an evil twin access point named like the hotel Wi-Fi to capture guests' traffic.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Unsecure networks
Key Points: Weak or no encryption (open, WEP, old WPA) is the problem; use WPA3 and 802.1X; watch for rogue APs and evil twins

Definition: Physical network ports and cabling that let anyone who plugs in reach the network when there is no port security or network access control.
Example: A visitor plugs a laptop into an open Ethernet jack in a conference room and gets an IP address on the internal network.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Unsecure networks
Key Points: Physical access to a jack equals network access without 802.1X or port security; disable unused switch ports; monitor for unknown devices
