Definition: Short-range wireless connections that can be abused when devices are discoverable, use weak pairing or have unpatched Bluetooth flaws.
Example: An attacker in a train station exploits an unpatched phone's Bluetooth stack to take control of it (as with BlueBorne).
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Unsecure networks
Key Points: Attacks: bluejacking (unsolicited messages), bluesnarfing (data theft); reduce risk by turning off discoverability and patching

Definition: Network ports listening for connections. Each open port is a service that can be attacked, so unneeded ones enlarge the attack surface.
Example: A scan finds Telnet (port 23) open on a router; an attacker connects and tries default credentials.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Every open port is a potential entry point; close or firewall unused services; find them with port scans (nmap); related mitigation: disabling ports/protocols

Definition: Factory-set usernames and passwords (such as admin/admin) that are publicly documented. Leaving them unchanged lets anyone log in.
Example: The Mirai botnet took over hundreds of thousands of IoT cameras and routers by logging in with default passwords.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Default passwords are published in manuals and online lists; change them at installation; Mirai is the classic example; mitigation: default password changes (2.5)

Definition: Attacking an organization through the third parties it relies on: managed service providers (MSPs), vendors and suppliers.
Example: Attackers compromise an IT management vendor and push malware to all its customers through a software update.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Exploits trust in a third party; examples: SolarWinds Orion (2020), Target breach via an HVAC vendor (2013); mitigate with vendor risk assessment and least privilege for third parties; 2.3 lists supply chain as a vulnerability too

Definition: Companies that remotely manage customers' IT. Compromising one MSP can give an attacker access to every client it manages.
Example: The 2021 Kaseya VSA attack used an MSP remote management tool to deliver ransomware to many downstream businesses.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Supply chain
Key Points: One breach, many victims; MSPs often hold privileged remote access; limit and monitor their access and require MFA

Definition: Third parties that provide products or services and may have network access or supply software, creating a path into the customer.
Example: In the 2013 Target breach, attackers used credentials stolen from an HVAC vendor to enter Target's network.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Supply chain
Key Points: Vendor access must follow least privilege and be segmented; assess vendor security before onboarding; monitor vendor accounts

Definition: Providers of hardware, components or materials. A tampered or counterfeit part can introduce a hidden weakness before the product even arrives.
Example: Counterfeit network switches bought from an unauthorized reseller contain modified firmware.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Supply chain
Key Points: Risks: counterfeit or tampered hardware; buy from trusted, authorized sources; verify integrity on receipt

Definition: Manipulating people into revealing information or performing actions that help an attacker, exploiting trust, urgency, authority or fear.
Example: A caller posing as a senior manager pressures a new help desk worker to reset a password immediately.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces
Key Points: Messages that trick people: phishing (email), smishing (text), vishing (voice), business email compromise; pretending to be someone: impersonation, brand impersonation, pretexting (a made-up story); traps on the web: watering hole sites and typosquatted look-alike domains; false information: misinformation/disinformation; levers: authority, urgency, scarcity, familiarity, trust; best defense: security awareness training plus verification procedures

Definition: Fraudulent messages, usually email, that pretend to be from a trusted source to steal credentials, money or install malware. Spear phishing targets specific people; whaling targets executives.
Example: An email that looks like a Microsoft 365 alert links to a fake sign-in page that captures passwords.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Email channel; vishing is voice, smishing is SMS; spear phishing = targeted, whaling = high-level executives; signs: urgency, mismatched links and sender domains

Definition: Voice phishing: using phone calls or voicemail to trick people into giving information or taking action.
Example: A caller spoofing the bank's number asks the victim to confirm their card PIN to "stop fraud".
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Vishing = voice; smishing = SMS; caller ID can be spoofed; AI voice cloning makes it more convincing; verify by calling a known number

Definition: SMS phishing: text messages that lure victims to malicious links or ask for personal information.
Example: A text says "Your toll payment is overdue, pay now" with a link to a fake payment site.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Smishing = SMS text; vishing = voice call; phishing = email; short links hide the real destination

Definition: False information spread to influence people. Misinformation is false but shared without intent to deceive; disinformation is created and spread deliberately to mislead.
Example: A coordinated campaign of fake social media accounts spreads a false story that a company's product is dangerous.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Key difference is intent: disinformation is deliberate, misinformation is not; spread via social media, bots, fake reviews; aimed at reputation, elections or public opinion

Definition: Pretending to be someone else, such as IT support, an executive, a vendor or a delivery person, to gain trust or access.
Example: An attacker in a high-visibility vest says he is from the electricity company and is let into the server room.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Often uses authority or familiarity; usually part of pretexting; defense: verify identity through a separate known channel

Definition: An attack using a compromised or spoofed business email account, often an executive's or vendor's, to trick staff into wiring money or sending sensitive data.
Example: A finance clerk gets an email from the CFO's real (hacked) mailbox asking to urgently change a supplier's bank details.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Goal is usually financial fraud through wire transfers or invoice changes; may use a real compromised account, so the sender looks legitimate; defense: out-of-band verification of payment changes, MFA

Definition: Creating a made-up scenario (a pretext) with a believable story to get the victim to give information or access.
Example: A caller says, "Hi, I'm from your car insurer, we just need to confirm your address and date of birth for your claim."
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: The invented story is the defining feature; often combined with impersonation; attacker may have done research to sound credible

Definition: An attacker compromises a website that the target group is known to visit and infects it, then waits for the victims to come.
Example: Attackers infect an industry association's website frequented by engineers at defense companies.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Attacker does not contact the victim directly; targets a group via a trusted third-party site; defense: patching, web filtering, layered endpoint protection

Definition: Pretending to be a well known company, using its logos, look and style in emails, ads or websites to fool people.
Example: A fake "PayPal" email with the real logo says your account is limited and links to a fake login page.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Copies trusted brands to lower suspicion; often in phishing and fake ads; differs from typosquatting, which relies on a misspelled domain

Definition: Registering domain names that are common misspellings of legitimate ones, so users who mistype land on the attacker's site. Also called URL hijacking.
Example: An attacker registers "gooogle.com" or "micorsoft.com" to host a phishing page.
Category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Human vectors/social engineering
Key Points: Relies on typing mistakes or look-alike names; also known as URL hijacking; defenses: register common misspellings, DNS filtering, user care

items.front: SY0-701 2.3: Explain various types of vulnerabilities
items.back:
Definition: Objective 2.3 covers the categories of weaknesses that attackers exploit: application, operating system, web, hardware, virtualization, cloud, supply chain, cryptographic, misconfiguration, mobile and zero-day.
Example: Scenario: a guest VM user breaks out and accesses the hypervisor. Vulnerability: VM escape (virtualization).
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat exploits it; know each category with its examples; tell apart: SQLi (database) vs XSS (browser), TOC vs TOU, side loading vs jailbreaking

Definition: Flaws in how software is written or updated that let attackers run code or change its behavior: memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions and malicious updates.
Example: A program that does not check input length lets an attacker overwrite memory and run code.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Listed: memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOC/TOU), malicious update; fixes: secure coding, input validation, code review, patching

Definition: Inserting malicious code into the memory of a running, often trusted, process so it runs with that process's rights. DLL injection is a common form.
Example: Malware injects a DLL into a legitimate browser process so its activity looks like normal browser traffic.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application
Key Points: Code runs inside a legitimate process, helping it hide and evade detection; often fileless; DLL injection is the usual example; detected by EDR behavior monitoring

Definition: A flaw where a program writes more data into a memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting nearby memory. Attackers use it to crash the program or run their own code.
Example: A login field accepts 5,000 characters into a 64-byte buffer, overwriting the return address so the attacker's code runs.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application
Key Points: Cause: no bounds or input-length checking; result: crash (DoS) or code execution; defenses: input validation, safe functions, DEP and ASLR; as a 2.4 indicator it appears as crashes and odd long inputs

Definition: A flaw where the result depends on the timing of two or more events, so an attacker can act in the gap between them. The classic form is time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU).
Example: Two simultaneous withdrawal requests both check the same balance before either deducts it, allowing the account to be overdrawn.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application
Key Points: Exploits the window between checking a condition and using the result; TOC = check moment, TOU = use moment; fix with locking and atomic operations

Definition: The moment a program verifies something, such as a file's permissions or an account balance, before acting on it. The race condition exists if that result can change before it is used.
Example: A program checks that a user may write to /tmp/report at 10:00:00.000.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application > Race conditions
Key Points: TOC is the CHECK; TOU is the USE that follows; vulnerability is the gap between them (TOCTOU); trap: TOC itself is not the attack, the change in the gap is

Definition: The moment a program acts on the result of an earlier check. If the attacker changed things after the check, the program uses something it never verified.
Example: After the permission check, the attacker swaps /tmp/report for a link to /etc/passwd, and the program writes to that file at time of use.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application > Race conditions
Key Points: TOU comes after TOC; the attacker strikes between the two; prevent by making check and use one atomic step or locking the resource

Definition: A software update that has been tampered with to include malware, so trusted update channels deliver the attack.
Example: In 2020 attackers inserted a backdoor into SolarWinds Orion updates, which up to about 18,000 customers downloaded.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Application
Key Points: Abuses trust in vendor updates; ties to supply chain; defenses: verify digital signatures and hashes, test updates, monitor vendor advisories; even signed updates can be malicious if the vendor's build is compromised

Definition: Weaknesses in the operating system itself, such as kernel flaws or privilege escalation bugs. The OS is a large, complex attack surface that touches everything on the system.
Example: Microsoft Patch Tuesday regularly fixes Windows flaws that would let a normal user gain SYSTEM rights.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Mitigate by patching quickly (test first), hardening and removing unneeded features; OS bugs can expose every application on the host

Definition: Flaws in web applications, mainly from failing to validate input, that let attackers inject commands or scripts. SY0-701 lists SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Example: A search box that passes text straight into a database query lets an attacker dump the user table.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Two listed: SQLi (attacks the database/server) and XSS (attacks other users' browsers); root cause: untrusted input not validated or encoded; OWASP Top 10 is the reference

Definition: An attack where SQL code is inserted into an application's input so the database runs the attacker's commands, exposing or changing data.
Example: Typing ' OR 1=1 -- into a login field makes the query return every row, logging the attacker in without a password.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Web-based
Key Points: Targets the database behind the app; look for quote characters, OR 1=1, UNION SELECT in logs; fix: parameterized queries (prepared statements), input validation, least privilege for the DB account; XSS targets browsers instead

Definition: A flaw where a site includes untrusted input in its pages without encoding it, so an attacker's script runs in other users' browsers. Types: reflected (non-persistent), stored (persistent) and DOM-based.
Example: An attacker posts a comment containing a script tag on a forum; every visitor's browser runs it and sends their session cookie to the attacker.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Web-based
Key Points: Script runs in the victim's browser, trusting the site; stored XSS is saved on the server, reflected XSS comes back in a crafted link; look for script tags in input; fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy

Definition: Weaknesses in physical devices and their low-level software: firmware flaws and devices that are end-of-life or legacy.
Example: A network printer's firmware has a known flaw the manufacturer never fixed.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Listed: firmware, end-of-life, legacy; hardware is often hard or impossible to patch; isolate devices you cannot update

Definition: Flaws in the embedded software that controls hardware (BIOS/UEFI, device controllers). Only the manufacturer can fix it, and updates are often rare or ignored.
Example: A flaw in a server's management controller firmware lets attackers take remote control below the operating system.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Hardware
Key Points: Runs below the OS, so OS security tools may not see it; fix depends on the vendor releasing updates; keep firmware updated and verify its integrity (secure boot)

Definition: Hardware the manufacturer no longer sells. Support and patches may continue for a set time; once support ends (end of service life, EOSL), new flaws stay unfixed.
Example: A router model reached end of life years ago and its support has now ended; a new remote-code flaw is found but no firmware fix is released.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Hardware
Key Points: EOL = no longer sold, support may continue for a while; EOSL = support and patches have stopped; plan replacement before support ends; legacy hardware is often EOL too

Definition: Old hardware still in use, often because a critical system depends on it, that may be outdated, unsupported or unable to run modern security controls.
Example: A hospital keeps a 20-year-old MRI controller running an old OS because replacing it costs millions.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Hardware
Key Points: Often kept for business reasons; may be EOL too; mitigate with segmentation, isolation and compensating controls

Definition: Weaknesses in hypervisors and virtual machines that break the separation between VMs or between a VM and the host: VM escape and resource reuse.
Example: A flaw in a hypervisor's virtual device driver lets code in one VM read another VM's memory.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Listed: VM escape, resource reuse; the hypervisor is a high-value target because it controls every VM; patch hypervisors and limit VM sprawl

Definition: Breaking out of a virtual machine to reach the hypervisor or host, and from there other VMs. It is one of the most serious virtualization flaws.
Example: At the Pwn2Own hacking contest, researchers ran code in a guest VM that broke out to the host by exploiting a flaw in the hypervisor's emulated hardware.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Virtualization
Key Points: Defeats VM isolation; attacker gains control of host and other guests; mitigate by patching hypervisors and limiting guest features

Definition: When memory, storage or other resources are reassigned from one VM to another without being fully cleared, so leftover data can be read by the new VM.
Example: A new VM is given disk blocks that previously belonged to another customer and recovers fragments of their files.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Virtualization
Key Points: Risk from shared, overcommitted or reallocated resources; leaks data between tenants or VMs; hypervisor must wipe resources before reuse

Definition: Weaknesses that arise in cloud environments: misconfigured storage or permissions, insecure APIs, weak authentication, and confusion over the shared responsibility model.
Example: A company leaves a cloud storage bucket publicly readable, exposing customer records to anyone with the URL.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Most cloud breaches come from customer misconfiguration, not the provider; know the shared responsibility model; protect APIs and identities with MFA

Definition: Weaknesses introduced by the third parties an organization depends on: service providers, hardware providers and software providers.
Example: A widely used open-source library contains a flaw, making every application that includes it vulnerable (as with Log4j in 2021).
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Trust in third parties extends the attack surface; listed: service, hardware and software providers; mitigate with vendor assessments, SBOMs, integrity checks; 2.2 lists supply chain as a vector too

Definition: Risk from external providers of services, such as cloud, payroll or IT support, that hold your data or access. Their weaknesses become yours.
Example: A payroll processing company is breached, exposing every client's employee bank details.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Supply chain
Key Points: You cannot outsource accountability; assess providers and set security terms in contracts; limit what access and data they get

Definition: Risk that hardware is counterfeit, tampered with or built with flawed components before it reaches you.
Example: In 2020, F-Secure found counterfeit Cisco Catalyst switches that were built to bypass Cisco's software authentication checks; they were found when they failed after an update.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Supply chain
Key Points: Buy from trusted, authorized sources; check device integrity and firmware; hard to detect after deployment

Definition: Risk that software you buy or include contains vulnerabilities, malicious code or compromised updates, including open-source components and libraries.
Example: The Log4j flaw affected thousands of products that bundled the logging library without their users knowing.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Supply chain
Key Points: Includes third-party libraries and dependencies; track components with a software bill of materials (SBOM); verify code signatures; malicious update is a related 2.3 item

Definition: Weaknesses in how cryptography is chosen or used: outdated algorithms, short keys, poor key management, weak random numbers or bad certificates.
Example: A site still accepts SSL 3.0 and uses MD5 hashes, letting attackers break or forge protected data.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Examples: weak algorithms (DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1), short keys, exposed private keys, expired or self-signed certs; usually the implementation fails, not the math; ties to downgrade, collision and birthday attacks (2.4)

Definition: Insecure settings on otherwise sound systems: open permissions, unnecessary services, default settings or accounts, or disabled security features.
Example: A database server is exposed to the internet with no password because remote access was enabled for testing and never turned off.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Among the most common causes of breaches, especially in the cloud; fixes: secure baselines, configuration management and enforcement, regular audits

Definition: Weaknesses in smartphones and tablets, especially from installing apps outside official stores (side loading) and removing built-in restrictions (jailbreaking or rooting).
Example: An employee jailbreaks a company iPhone to install an unofficial app, which turns out to contain spyware.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: Listed: side loading, jailbreaking; both bypass the platform's security model; control with mobile device management (MDM) that detects and blocks them

Definition: Installing apps from outside the official app store, skipping the store's security review.
Example: A user installs an Android APK downloaded from a forum to get a "free premium" version of an app; it contains malware.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Mobile device
Key Points: Bypasses app store vetting; easier on Android than iOS; does not require jailbreaking; block with MDM

Definition: Removing the manufacturer's restrictions on a mobile device (on iOS; the Android equivalent is rooting) to gain full control and install anything.
Example: A user jailbreaks an iPhone, which disables protections and lets any app reach system files.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities > Mobile device
Key Points: Jailbreaking = iOS, rooting = Android; gives root-level access and weakens the security model; side loading only installs outside apps, jailbreaking removes OS limits; MDM can detect it

Definition: A vulnerability unknown to the vendor or with no patch available yet, so defenders have had zero days to fix it. An exploit for it is a zero-day exploit.
Example: Attackers exploit an unknown browser flaw for weeks before the vendor learns of it and releases a fix.
Category: 2.3 Types of vulnerabilities
Key Points: No patch exists, so signature-based tools miss it; defenses: layered security, behavior-based detection, least privilege, rapid patching once released; valuable to nation-states

items.front: SY0-701 2.4: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity
items.back:
Definition: Objective 2.4 asks you to look at a scenario (symptoms, logs, behavior) and identify the attack: malware, physical, network, application, cryptographic and password attacks, plus general indicators of compromise.
Example: Scenario: logs show one user logged in from New York and Tokyo within ten minutes. Indicator: impossible travel, suggesting stolen credentials.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Performance-based style: read the clues; know the distinguishing feature of each attack (worm self-spreads, virus needs a user, spraying uses one password on many accounts); account clues: lockouts, concurrent sessions, impossible travel; system clues: resource consumption, resources becoming inaccessible, blocked content; log clues: missing logs or out-of-cycle logging; outside clues: your data published/documented online

Definition: Malicious software designed to harm systems or steal data. SY0-701 lists ransomware, Trojan, worm, spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb and rootkit.
Example: A user opens a fake invoice, a Trojan installs, and it later drops ransomware across the network.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Tell apart: virus needs user action and a host file, worm spreads by itself over networks, Trojan disguises itself as legitimate, rootkit hides deep in the OS, logic bomb waits for a trigger; bloatware is unwanted preinstalled software, often not malicious

Definition: Malware that encrypts the victim's files (or locks the system) and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the key. Many groups also steal data and threaten to leak it (double extortion).
Example: WannaCry (2017) encrypted hundreds of thousands of computers worldwide and demanded Bitcoin payments.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Indicators: files renamed with odd extensions, ransom notes, mass file changes; best recovery: tested offline backups; defenses: patching, EDR, least privilege; paying does not guarantee recovery

Definition: Malware disguised as legitimate or desirable software. It does not replicate itself; it relies on the user installing it, then opens access or runs harmful code.
Example: A "free video converter" installs fine but also installs a remote access Trojan (RAT) giving the attacker control.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Disguise is the defining feature; does not self-replicate (unlike worms and viruses); RAT = remote access Trojan, a backdoor; common source: pirated or free software

Definition: Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks on its own by exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action and no host file needed.
Example: WannaCry spread worm-style through an SMB vulnerability, jumping from computer to computer inside networks.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Spreads automatically without user action (virus needs a user and a host file); indicators: sudden network traffic spikes, many infected hosts quickly; defenses: patching, firewalls, segmentation

Definition: Malware that secretly watches the user and collects information such as browsing, keystrokes, location or credentials, and sends it to the attacker.
Example: A free browser toolbar records every website visited and sells the data, while also capturing form entries.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Purpose is surveillance and data theft; often bundled with free software or Trojans; keyloggers are a type of spyware; differs from bloatware, which is unwanted but not spying

Definition: Unnecessary software preinstalled by the manufacturer or bundled with other apps. It uses storage and resources and can add vulnerabilities, even if it is not malicious.
Example: A new laptop arrives with trial antivirus, games and a vendor updater that has a known security flaw.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Usually not malicious, just unwanted; risk: wasted resources and extra attack surface; fix: uninstall it (removal of unnecessary software, 2.5)

Definition: Malware that attaches to a host file or program and spreads when the user runs or opens it. Types include program, boot sector, script, macro and fileless viruses.
Example: A macro virus in a spreadsheet infects other documents each time an infected file is opened.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Needs user action and a host to spread; a worm needs neither; fileless viruses live in memory and use tools like PowerShell; defense: antivirus/EDR with current signatures

Definition: Malware (or a hardware device) that records keystrokes to capture passwords, card numbers and messages, then sends them to the attacker.
Example: A keylogger on a hotel business center PC captures a guest's webmail password.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Captures input before encryption, so HTTPS does not help; can be software or a USB hardware dongle; MFA limits the value of stolen passwords

Definition: Malicious code that waits until a specific condition is met, such as a date, an event or a user being removed, then runs its payload.
Example: An administrator plants code that deletes the payroll database if his account is ever disabled.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Defined by its trigger (time, event, condition); often planted by insiders; hard to detect with signatures because it is custom; defense: change management, code review, monitoring

Definition: Malware that hides deep in the operating system, often in the kernel, to conceal itself and other malware while keeping privileged access.
Example: A rootkit modifies the kernel so its files and processes do not show in Task Manager or antivirus scans.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
Key Points: Main feature is stealth at the kernel level; normal tools may not see it; defenses: secure boot, UEFI, scanning from outside the OS, often reimaging the system

Definition: Attacks on physical security: forcing entry (brute force), copying access badges (RFID cloning) and attacking the environment (power, heating, cooling).
Example: An attacker clones a staff badge from a few centimeters away in a coffee line and walks into the office.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Listed: brute force, RFID cloning, environmental; physical access often defeats digital controls; defenses: locks, guards, cameras, badge plus PIN, environmental monitoring

Definition: Using physical force to get in: breaking doors, windows, locks or barriers, or forcing open equipment.
Example: An intruder pries open a rear fire door and kicks in the wiring closet door.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Physical attacks
Key Points: Physical force, not password guessing (that is brute force under password attacks); indicators: damaged doors, broken locks, alarms; defenses: reinforced doors, bollards, alarms, cameras

Definition: Copying the data from an RFID access badge or key fob with a reader, then writing it to a blank card to impersonate the owner.
Example: An attacker uses a hidden reader to capture an employee's badge ID in an elevator, then opens the server room with a clone.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Physical attacks
Key Points: Many badges send a fixed ID without encryption, so they are easy to copy; indicator: badge used in two places at once or at odd hours; defenses: encrypted badges, MFA (badge plus PIN or biometric), shielded sleeves

Definition: Attacking the environment systems support: power, heating and cooling (HVAC), humidity or fire suppression, to cause outages or damage.
Example: Attackers hack a data center's HVAC controls and turn off cooling, causing servers to overheat and shut down.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Physical attacks
Key Points: Targets availability; HVAC and building systems are often networked and poorly secured; defenses: segment building systems, monitor temperature and power, backup power

Definition: Attacks against network traffic and services: DDoS (amplified, reflected), DNS attacks, wireless attacks, on-path, credential replay and malicious code.
Example: An attacker poisons ARP tables on a LAN so all traffic passes through their laptop.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Listed: DDoS, DNS attacks, wireless, on-path, credential replay, malicious code; look for traffic anomalies, unusual DNS answers, duplicate MAC addresses

Definition: Overwhelming a target with traffic or requests from many sources, often a botnet, so legitimate users cannot reach it. A DoS uses one source; a DDoS uses many.
Example: The 2016 Mirai botnet of hacked IoT devices flooded DNS provider Dyn, knocking major websites offline.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: Attacks availability; DoS = one source, DDoS = many (botnet); variants: amplified and reflected; defenses: upstream filtering, scrubbing services, CDN, rate limiting

Definition: A DDoS that sends small requests to services that return much larger responses, multiplying the traffic the attacker generates. DNS, NTP and memcached are common amplifiers.
Example: Attackers send tiny NTP "monlist" queries that each trigger a response hundreds of times larger, aimed at the victim.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks > Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)
Key Points: Amplified = small request, big response (traffic multiplied); usually combined with reflection (spoofed source IP); UDP protocols are favored because they need no handshake

Definition: A DDoS where the attacker spoofs the victim's IP as the source of requests to third-party servers, so those servers send their replies to the victim. It hides the attacker and spreads the traffic across many sources.
Example: Attackers send DNS queries with the victim's IP as the source to thousands of open resolvers, which all answer the victim.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks > Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)
Key Points: Reflected = spoofed source makes others reply to the victim (hides the attacker); amplified = responses bigger than requests; most real attacks are both ("reflected amplification")

Definition: Attacks that tamper with name resolution to send users to the wrong place: DNS poisoning or spoofing, domain hijacking, and abusing DNS for amplification or tunneling.
Example: Attackers poison a resolver's cache so the bank's domain points to a phishing server, and users see the right URL but the wrong site.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: DNS poisoning = false records in cache or hosts file; domain hijacking = taking over the domain registration; defenses: DNSSEC, registrar locks and MFA, monitoring DNS changes

Definition: Attacks on Wi-Fi networks, such as deauthentication (kicking users off), jamming (radio interference), rogue access points and evil twins.
Example: An attacker sends forged deauthentication frames so clients disconnect and reconnect to his evil twin access point.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: Deauth uses unprotected 802.11 management frames (802.11w protects them, required in WPA3); jamming is radio interference (DoS); evil twin mimics a legitimate SSID; rogue AP is unauthorized

Definition: An attacker secretly sits between two parties, reading or changing their traffic. Formerly called man-in-the-middle; ARP poisoning is a common LAN technique and on-path browser (man-in-the-browser) is a malware variant.
Example: ARP poisoning on a café network makes a victim's laptop send all its traffic through the attacker's machine.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: Old name: man-in-the-middle; indicators: duplicate MAC addresses in ARP tables, certificate warnings; defenses: encryption (TLS), certificate validation, dynamic ARP inspection

Definition: Capturing valid credentials, password hashes or authentication tokens and reusing them to log in as the victim, without needing to know the plaintext password.
Example: An attacker captures an NTLM hash from network traffic and uses it to authenticate to other servers (pass the hash).
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: Reuses captured authentication data; pass the hash is the classic example; defenses: encryption, MFA, timestamps and nonces, Kerberos instead of NTLM; differs from application replay of session tokens/cookies

Definition: Harmful code in any form (executables, scripts, macros, injected website code) used to exploit systems over the network.
Example: Attackers injected card-skimming JavaScript into an airline's payment page, stealing customers' card details (a Magecart attack).
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
Key Points: Broad category: scripts, executables, macros, injected web code; can arrive by email, web or worm; defenses: anti-malware, patching, application allow lists, input validation

Definition: Attacks against applications and their logic: injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery and directory traversal.
Example: A web server log shows requests containing ../../ and SQL keywords against the login page.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Listed: injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, directory traversal; root causes: poor input validation and weak session handling; defenses: secure coding, WAF, patching

Definition: Sending crafted input that the application passes to an interpreter as code: SQL, LDAP, XML, command or DLL injection.
Example: Logs show the input admin'; DROP TABLE users;-- submitted to a web form.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: Indicators: code fragments in input fields and logs (quotes, semicolons, OR 1=1); types: SQL, LDAP, XML, command, DLL; defenses: input validation, parameterized queries, least privilege

Definition: An attack that sends more data than an input buffer can hold, to crash the application or run attacker code.
Example: An application keeps crashing and logs show requests with thousands of "A" characters in a username field.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: Indicators: crashes or restarts, very long input strings, unexpected code execution; defenses: input validation, patching, DEP and ASLR; the 2.3 card covers the vulnerability itself

Definition: Capturing a valid session token, cookie or transaction and sending it again to impersonate the user or repeat the action.
Example: An attacker steals a session cookie over unencrypted Wi-Fi and uses it to take over the victim's logged-in session (session hijacking).
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: Reuses captured session data; defenses: encryption (HTTPS), session timeouts, tokens tied to one use, nonces and timestamps; network credential replay is the 2.4 network version

Definition: Gaining higher access than intended. Vertical escalation moves to a higher privilege level (user to admin); horizontal escalation accesses another user's resources at the same level.
Example: A standard user exploits a flaw in a service running as SYSTEM to get administrator rights.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: Vertical = up a level; horizontal = sideways to another user; indicators: unexpected admin rights or new admin accounts; defenses: patching, least privilege, monitoring

Definition: Tricking a system into sending a request it should not. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) makes a logged-in user's browser send unwanted requests; server-side request forgery (SSRF) makes a server request internal or external resources for the attacker.
Example: A malicious page silently submits a funds-transfer form to the victim's bank while the victim is logged in (CSRF).
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: CSRF abuses the trust a site has in the user's browser; SSRF abuses the server to reach internal systems; defenses: anti-CSRF tokens, same-site cookies, validating server-side URLs; XSS runs script, CSRF sends requests

Definition: Manipulating file paths in input (for example with ../) to read files outside the folder the application is supposed to serve.
Example: A request for /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd returns the server's password file.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
Key Points: Indicator: ../ or encoded %2e%2e%2f sequences in URLs or logs; defenses: input validation, least privilege file permissions, no direct user-controlled paths

Definition: Attacks that weaken or bypass encryption and hashing: downgrade, collision and birthday attacks.
Example: An on-path attacker forces a browser and server to use an old, breakable protocol version.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Listed: downgrade, collision, birthday; defenses: modern protocols and algorithms, disabling legacy options, longer hashes

Definition: Forcing two systems to fall back to an older, weaker protocol or cipher that the attacker can break. SSL stripping, which turns HTTPS into HTTP, is a related on-path technique.
Example: The POODLE attack (2014) forced connections to fall back to SSL 3.0, whose padding flaw let the attacker decrypt data such as session cookies.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Cryptographic attacks
Key Points: Requires an on-path position; defenses: disable old protocols and ciphers (SSL, early TLS), HSTS against SSL stripping

Definition: Finding two different inputs that produce the same hash value, so a forged item can pass as legitimate.
Example: Researchers created two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash (SHAttered, 2017); MD5 collisions were used to forge certificates.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Cryptographic attacks
Key Points: Breaks the integrity guarantee of hashing; MD5 and SHA-1 are vulnerable; use SHA-256 or stronger; the birthday attack is the math that makes collisions easier to find

Definition: An attack based on the birthday paradox: finding any two inputs with the same hash takes far fewer tries than finding a match for one specific hash (about the square root of the possible outputs).
Example: In a room of 23 people there is about a 50% chance two share a birthday; similarly, a 64-bit hash yields a collision after about 2^32 attempts.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Cryptographic attacks
Key Points: Explains why collisions are easier than expected; defense: longer hash outputs (SHA-256 or more); collision = the result, birthday = the method that finds it

Definition: Attempts to guess or crack passwords. SY0-701 lists spraying (few passwords, many accounts) and brute force (many passwords against one account or hash).
Example: Logs show failed logins for 500 different accounts, each tried with "Spring2026!".
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Spraying = one or a few common passwords across many accounts, avoids lockout; brute force = many guesses per account, triggers lockout online; offline brute force cracks stolen hashes; defenses: MFA, lockout, strong password policy, salted hashing

Definition: Trying one or a few common passwords against many accounts, staying under each account's lockout threshold.
Example: An attacker tries "Welcome1" once against every account in a company's directory, then waits an hour and tries "Password123".
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Password attacks
Key Points: Few passwords, many accounts; avoids account lockout; indicator: many accounts with one or two failures each from the same source; defenses: MFA, banning common passwords, monitoring

Definition: Trying every possible password combination, or a very large list, until one works. Online brute force targets a live login; offline brute force cracks a stolen password hash file.
Example: An attacker steals a hash database and runs billions of guesses per second on GPUs to recover passwords.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Password attacks
Key Points: Online: slow and triggers account lockout; offline: no lockout, limited only by computing power; defenses: lockout, long passwords, salted slow hashes; physical brute force is forcing doors

items.front: Indicators of malicious activity (indicators of compromise)
items.back:
Definition: Signs that an attack is happening or has happened. Watch accounts (lockouts, the same user signed in twice at once, impossible travel between logins), systems (unusual resource consumption, resources suddenly inaccessible, security tools or updates being blocked), logs (missing logs, logging at odd times) and the outside world (your data published or documented online).
Example: An analyst sees log files deleted for a two-hour window, plus an admin logged in from two countries at once.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity
Key Points: Indicators of compromise (IoCs) are evidence of an intrusion; combine several before concluding; know each indicator's likely cause

Definition: Accounts getting locked after too many failed logins, which may mean someone is trying to guess passwords.
Example: Several users call the help desk the same morning because their accounts are locked, though they did not mistype anything.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Suggests brute force (spraying deliberately avoids lockout); attacker may also lock accounts on purpose as a DoS; check the source of failed attempts

Definition: One account logged in more than once at the same time from different places or devices, when that is not normal for the user.
Example: A user's account shows active sessions on her office PC and on an unknown laptop at the same time.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Suggests stolen credentials or session hijacking; compare with impossible travel (logins too far apart in too little time)

Definition: Content being blocked in a suspicious way. Malware often blocks antivirus updates and security websites so it can stay on the host. Security tools may also log repeated blocked downloads or connections from an infected host.
Example: The web proxy logs repeated blocked connections from one PC to a known command-and-control domain.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: A host that suddenly cannot reach antivirus updates or security sites suggests malware protecting itself; repeated proxy blocks from one host suggest malware calling out

Definition: Logins for the same account from locations so far apart in so short a time that no one could physically travel between them.
Example: A user logs in from Chicago at 9:00 and from Moscow at 9:20.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Strong sign of compromised credentials; VPNs can cause false positives; differs from concurrent sessions: impossible travel is about time and distance between logins

Definition: Unusual use of CPU, memory, disk or network bandwidth, which can signal malware, cryptomining, data exfiltration or a DoS.
Example: A file server sends 50 GB to an unknown external IP at 2 a.m.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Spikes in outbound traffic suggest exfiltration; constant high CPU suggests cryptomining; compare to a baseline of normal use

Definition: Systems, services or files that suddenly cannot be reached or opened.
Example: Users cannot open shared files, which now have strange extensions and a ransom note in each folder.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Can indicate ransomware (encrypted files), DoS, or an attacker locking out admins; differs from resource consumption, which is about unusual usage

Definition: Log activity at unexpected times or outside normal schedules, such as updates, backups or admin actions that should not be happening then.
Example: Logs show an OS patch installed at 3 a.m. on a Sunday, though patching only happens on Tuesday nights.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Activity outside the normal schedule or change window is suspicious; compare to change management records

Definition: Evidence of an attack that is made public: the attacker publishing stolen data, or researchers or vendors documenting the attack and its indicators.
Example: The company learns of its breach when its customer database appears for sale on a dark web forum.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Sometimes the first a victim hears of a breach; threat intelligence feeds publish IoCs to check against your systems

Definition: Gaps or deleted entries in log files, often a sign an attacker covered their tracks.
Example: The security log on a domain controller has no entries between 1:00 and 3:00 a.m., and the log-clear event appears at 3:01.
Category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Indicators
Key Points: Attackers delete or alter logs to hide activity; defenses: send logs to a central SIEM or write-once storage, alert on log clearing

items.front: SY0-701 2.5: Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise
items.back:
Definition: Objective 2.5 covers why organizations use controls that reduce risk: segmentation, access control, application allow lists, isolation, patching, encryption, monitoring, least privilege, configuration enforcement, decommissioning and hardening techniques.
Example: Scenario: a company wants to stop employees running unapproved programs. Mitigation: application allow list.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Know the PURPOSE of each technique and which threat it reduces; segmentation vs isolation; allow list (only approved runs) vs deny list; hardening reduces attack surface on each system

Definition: Dividing a network into separate zones (with VLANs, subnets, firewalls) so systems with different risk or roles are separated and traffic between them is controlled.
Example: Point-of-sale terminals are placed on their own VLAN so a breach of office PCs cannot reach card systems.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Limits lateral movement and contains breaches; improves performance and compliance (PCI DSS); segmentation controls traffic between zones, isolation cuts a system off completely

Definition: Controlling who or what can reach which resources and what they can do there, using access control lists and permissions.
Example: Only HR staff can open the personnel folder; everyone else is denied.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Listed: access control list (ACL), permissions; enforces least privilege; covers network and file system access

Definition: A list of rules that allow or deny access to a resource. On network devices it filters traffic by IP, port and protocol; on file systems it lists which users or groups may access an object.
Example: A router ACL blocks all inbound traffic to the database subnet except TCP 1433 from the application servers.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Access control
Key Points: Rules are processed in order, with an implicit deny at the end on most devices; used on firewalls, routers and file systems

Definition: The specific rights granted to a user or group on a resource, such as read, write, modify, execute or full control.
Example: Interns get read-only access to the policy library so they cannot change documents.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Access control
Key Points: Grant the minimum needed (least privilege); assign to groups rather than individuals; review regularly to remove permission creep

Definition: A policy that lets only approved applications run; anything not on the list is blocked by default. Formerly called whitelisting.
Example: A kiosk PC only allows the browser and the check-in app to run, so downloaded malware cannot execute.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Default deny, very strong against unknown malware; deny list (blocklist) blocks only known bad apps; harder to manage where software changes often

Definition: Separating a system, process or device completely so it cannot interact with others, either as protection or to contain a threat.
Example: An infected laptop is moved to a quarantine network with no access to company resources; a browser runs untrusted pages in an isolated sandbox.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Contains compromised systems and protects sensitive ones (air gap, sandbox, quarantine); stronger than segmentation, which allows controlled traffic

Definition: Applying vendor updates that fix security flaws in operating systems, applications and firmware.
Example: IT deploys an emergency browser patch within 24 hours of a zero-day exploit being reported.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Closes known vulnerabilities; test before production, but prioritize critical fixes; automate where possible; does not help against unpatched zero-days

Definition: Encoding data so only authorized parties with the key can read it, protecting it at rest and in transit.
Example: Full disk encryption keeps data safe when a laptop is stolen; TLS protects web traffic.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Protects confidentiality even if data is stolen; at rest (disk, database) and in transit (TLS, VPN); key management is critical

Definition: Continuously watching systems, networks and logs to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly.
Example: A SIEM alerts the security team when an admin account logs in from a new country.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Detective, not preventive; tools: SIEM, IDS/IPS, EDR, log aggregation; needs a baseline to spot anomalies

Definition: Giving users, processes and systems only the minimum access needed to do their job, and nothing more.
Example: A help desk technician can reset passwords but cannot change domain admin group membership.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Limits damage from compromised accounts and insiders; reduces privilege escalation impact; review access regularly

Definition: Making sure systems match an approved secure baseline configuration and correcting or blocking those that drift, often checked before devices are allowed on the network.
Example: Network access control checks that a laptop has current antivirus and patches before letting it connect, sending it to remediation otherwise.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Uses secure baselines and tools like group policy, MDM and posture assessment; detects and fixes configuration drift

Definition: Retiring systems securely: removing them from service, wiping or destroying data and storage, and updating inventories and access.
Example: Before old servers are recycled, their drives are wiped and shredded, and their DNS records and firewall rules are removed.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Prevents data leaks from discarded hardware and forgotten systems still running; sanitize or destroy media; document the process

Definition: Steps that reduce a system's attack surface and strengthen its defenses: encryption, endpoint protection, host-based firewall, HIPS, disabling ports and protocols, changing default passwords and removing unnecessary software.
Example: A new web server gets unused services removed, the admin password changed, a host firewall turned on and EDR installed before going live.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques
Key Points: Goal: smallest possible attack surface per system; use vendor or CIS benchmarks as baselines; seven listed techniques

Definition: Encrypting a system's storage and communications as part of hardening, such as full disk encryption, encrypted file systems and encrypted protocols.
Example: Every company laptop is configured with BitLocker full disk encryption before being issued.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Applied per device: full disk encryption, file encryption, encrypted protocols (SSH instead of Telnet); protects data if the device is lost

Definition: Installing security software such as antivirus, anti-malware or endpoint detection and response (EDR) on each device to detect and block threats.
Example: An EDR agent spots a process encrypting many files rapidly and isolates the laptop automatically.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: EDR adds behavior detection and response beyond signature-based antivirus; covers servers, laptops and mobile devices

Definition: A software firewall running on the individual device that controls traffic in and out of that host, regardless of the network it is on.
Example: Windows Defender Firewall blocks inbound file sharing on a laptop when it connects to public Wi-Fi.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Protects the device even off the corporate network; can be application-aware; complements network firewalls

Definition: Software on a host that watches system and network activity for attacks and actively blocks them, not just alerts.
Example: HIPS stops a program that tries to modify system files and inject code into another process.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Prevention (blocks), unlike HIDS which only detects and alerts; uses signatures and behavior; often built into endpoint protection suites

Definition: Turning off network ports, services and protocols that are not needed, so they cannot be attacked.
Example: Telnet and FTP are disabled on a server, leaving only SSH (TCP 22) and HTTPS (TCP 443) open.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Reduces the attack surface (open service ports are a 2.2 vector); also disable insecure protocols; includes disabling unused physical switch ports

Definition: Replacing factory-set default passwords on devices, applications and accounts with strong unique ones at installation.
Example: A new IP camera's admin/admin login is changed to a long unique password before it is mounted.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Directly counters the default credentials vector (Mirai botnet); applies to routers, IoT, databases and apps; also rename or disable default accounts

Definition: Uninstalling applications, services and features a system does not need, since every program can contain vulnerabilities.
Example: A new laptop has its preinstalled trial apps and games (bloatware) removed before being issued.
Category: 2.5 Mitigation techniques > Hardening techniques
Key Points: Fewer programs means fewer vulnerabilities to patch; removes bloatware; part of building a minimal secure baseline

areas.title: Security Architecture
areas.theme: Cloud, network and infrastructure design, protecting data, and resilience and recovery.
story: A secure system is built, not bolted on.
Design networks, protect data in every state, and keep things running when they break.
canDo: Compare architecture models and their risks
Protect data at rest, in transit and in use

sections.title: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models
Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure
Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

items.back:
Definition: The exam domain about designing and securing systems: architecture models (cloud, on-premises, IoT, ICS), secure enterprise network design, data protection, and resilience and recovery. It is 18% of the SY0-701 exam.
Example: A question asks which design keeps a factory control network safe from internet malware: the answer (air gap or segmentation) comes from this domain.
Category: 3.0 Security architecture
Key Points: Four objectives: 3.1 architecture models, 3.2 securing infrastructure, 3.3 protecting data, 3.4 resilience and recovery; mostly compare and contrast and scenario questions; tests trade-offs, not configuration syntax

items.front: SY0-701 3.1: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers the security trade-offs of architecture choices such as cloud, IaC, serverless, microservices, on-premises, containers, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS and embedded systems, and the considerations used to choose between them.
Example: Choosing between running an app on on-premises servers or as serverless functions, weighing patch control, cost and the shared responsibility split.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models
Key Points: Know who is responsible for what in each model; know which systems cannot be patched easily (ICS, RTOS, embedded, IoT); weigh each model on staying up (availability, resilience, ease of recovery), growing and launching (scalability, ease of deployment, responsiveness), money and risk (cost, risk transference) and the hardware it needs (power, compute, patching)

Definition: The set of ways a system can be built and hosted: cloud, infrastructure as code, serverless, microservices, network infrastructure, on-premises, centralized or decentralized designs, containers, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, embedded systems and high availability. Each has its own security implications.
Example: A company compares hosting its customer portal in containers in the cloud versus on virtual machines in its own data center.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models
Key Points: Each model changes who controls and patches what; more distributed models add attack surface (APIs, management interfaces); specialized systems (ICS, RTOS, embedded) trade patchability for reliability

Definition: Computing resources (servers, storage, applications) delivered on demand by a provider over a network, in service models IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and deployment models public, private, community and hybrid. Security is shared between the provider and the customer.
Example: A startup runs its web servers on a public cloud IaaS platform instead of buying hardware.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS), software as a service (SaaS); misconfiguration (open storage buckets) is the top cloud risk; customer is always responsible for its data and access

Definition: A table showing which security tasks belong to the cloud provider and which to the customer for each service model. The provider always secures the physical data center; the customer always owns its data, accounts and access.
Example: In IaaS the customer patches the guest OS; in SaaS the provider patches everything and the customer manages user accounts and data.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Cloud
Key Points: Customer responsibility shrinks from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS; data and identity are always the customer's; a breach from a misconfigured bucket is the customer's fault, not the provider's

Definition: Security issues when combining on-premises systems with one or more clouds: consistent identity and policy across environments, secure connections between them, data moving between locations, and different tools and logs in each.
Example: A firm keeps its database on-premises and its web front end in a public cloud, linked by a site-to-site VPN, and must sync user accounts across both.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Cloud
Key Points: Hard part is consistency: same authentication, monitoring and policies everywhere; data in transit between sites must be encrypted; more complexity means more chance of misconfiguration

Definition: Outside companies that provide or connect to cloud services (the cloud provider, SaaS apps, managed service providers). Their security, access and contracts become part of your risk.
Example: A managed service provider with admin access to your cloud tenant is breached, and attackers use its access to reach your systems.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Cloud
Key Points: Vet vendors and set security requirements in contracts (right to audit, SLAs); limit and monitor vendor access; supply chain risk links to objective 5.3

Definition: Defining servers, networks and other infrastructure in machine-readable template or script files so environments are built automatically and identically every time. The files can be version-controlled, reviewed and tested like software.
Example: A team deploys the same hardened web tier to test and production from one Terraform template stored in Git.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Benefits: consistency, repeatability, fewer manual errors, easy rebuild; risks: one bad template spreads a misconfiguration everywhere, secrets hard-coded in templates; scan templates before deploying

Definition: A cloud model where code runs as functions triggered by events and the provider manages all servers, operating systems and scaling. The customer only writes and secures the code, its permissions and its data. Also called function as a service (FaaS).
Example: An image upload triggers a cloud function that creates a thumbnail; no server is ever managed by the company.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: No OS to patch for the customer; security focus moves to function permissions (least privilege), input validation and API/event security; functions are short-lived (ephemeral)

Definition: An application built as many small independent services, each doing one job and talking to others through APIs. Services can be updated, scaled and fail independently.
Example: An online store splits into separate inventory, payment and shipping services, so a bug in shipping does not take down payments.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: More resilient and scalable than a monolith; many more APIs to authenticate, authorize and monitor; compare with a monolithic app where one flaw or failure affects everything

Definition: How the network that connects systems is built and separated: physically isolated networks (including air gaps), logically segmented networks (VLANs, subnets) and software-defined networking.
Example: A hospital places medical devices on their own segment, separate from guest Wi-Fi and staff workstations.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Physical isolation is strongest but costly and inflexible; logical segmentation is cheaper and common; SDN separates control from data for central, programmable management

Definition: Keeping networks or devices on completely separate hardware with no shared switches or cables, so traffic cannot cross between them. The most extreme form is an air gap.
Example: A bank keeps its card-processing systems on separate physical switches from the office network.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Network infrastructure
Key Points: Stronger than logical segmentation (no VLAN hopping or misconfiguration crossing); higher cost and harder to manage; contrast with logical segmentation, which shares hardware

Definition: A system or network with no physical or wireless connection to any other network, especially the internet. Data moves in or out only by hand, usually on removable media.
Example: A uranium enrichment plant's control systems were air-gapped, yet Stuxnet reached them through infected USB drives.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Network infrastructure > Physical isolation
Key Points: Protects against network attacks, not against removable media or insiders; updates and data transfer are slow and manual; often used for ICS, military and highly classified systems

Definition: Dividing one physical network into separate logical networks using VLANs, subnets, firewall rules or ACLs, so devices on shared hardware cannot talk freely to each other.
Example: Guest Wi-Fi users are placed on VLAN 50 and blocked by ACLs from reaching the finance VLAN, though both use the same switches.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Network infrastructure
Key Points: Cheaper and more flexible than physical isolation; a misconfiguration or VLAN hopping can break it; limits lateral movement and the scope of a breach

Definition: A network design that separates the control plane (decides where traffic goes) from the data plane (forwards traffic), with a central controller programming the network devices through software. A management plane configures and monitors it.
Example: An administrator pushes a new segmentation policy to hundreds of switches at once from the SDN controller.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts > Network infrastructure
Key Points: Planes: control, data, management; central, automated, programmable and consistent; the controller is a high-value target and single point of failure, so protect it

Definition: Systems hosted in the organization's own facilities on hardware it owns and runs. The organization has full control and full responsibility for security, maintenance and costs.
Example: A defense contractor keeps classified file servers in its own locked data center rather than in a cloud.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Full control over data location, hardware and patching; full responsibility and high upfront cost; scaling and recovery are slower than in the cloud

Definition: Centralized architecture puts control, data or processing in one place; decentralized spreads them across many locations or nodes. Centralized is easier to manage and secure consistently; decentralized avoids a single point of failure.
Example: A single central authentication server (centralized) versus a blockchain ledger copied across many nodes (decentralized).
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Centralized: easier visibility and control, but a single point of failure and an attractive target; decentralized: resilient, but harder to manage and keep consistent

Definition: Packaging an application with its libraries and settings into a container that runs on a shared host operating system kernel through a container engine (for example Docker). Containers are lighter and start faster than virtual machines.
Example: A team ships its API as a container image that runs the same on a laptop, a test server and a cloud cluster.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Containers share the host kernel (VMs each have their own OS); a kernel flaw or container escape can affect all containers; secure images from trusted sources and scan them; isolate with namespaces

Definition: Running multiple virtual machines, each with its own operating system, on one physical host through a hypervisor. Type 1 hypervisors run on bare metal; Type 2 run on top of a host OS.
Example: One physical server hosts separate web, database and mail VMs.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Risks: VM escape (break out to the hypervisor or other VMs), VM sprawl (unmanaged VMs), resource reuse; patch the hypervisor; stronger isolation than containers

Definition: Everyday network-connected devices and sensors such as smart cameras, thermostats, wearables and building systems. They often have weak default credentials, limited processing power and few or no security updates.
Example: Thousands of IP cameras with default passwords were taken over by the Mirai botnet for DDoS attacks.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Change default credentials; put IoT on its own segment; often hard or impossible to patch; large attack surface from many devices

items.front: Industrial control systems (ICS)/supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)
items.back:
Definition: Systems that monitor and control physical industrial processes such as power grids, water treatment and manufacturing. SCADA covers large, often geographically spread systems, using PLCs, sensors and HMIs.
Example: A water utility uses SCADA to control pumps and chemical dosing at stations across a city.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Availability and safety come first (an outage can harm people); often legacy and hard to patch; protect with segmentation or air gaps and strict access; attacks have physical consequences

Definition: An operating system built to process inputs within guaranteed, deterministic time limits, used where a delay is unacceptable. Found in vehicles, industrial equipment, medical devices and military systems.
Example: A car's anti-lock braking system runs on an RTOS that must react within milliseconds.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Deterministic timing is the defining feature; security add-ons can break timing, so they are minimal; hard to patch; isolate it from other networks

Definition: Computers built into a device to perform one dedicated function, usually with firmware and limited resources. Examples include printers, smart meters, traffic lights and medical pumps.
Example: A hospital infusion pump runs embedded firmware that the vendor rarely updates.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Limited CPU and memory restrict security features; firmware updates may be rare or unavailable; often long service life; segment and monitor them

Definition: Designing a system so it stays running and accessible nearly all the time, using redundancy so that one failed component does not cause an outage. Usually measured as uptime percentage (for example 99.999%).
Example: A web service runs on two servers behind a load balancer in different zones so one can fail without users noticing.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Architecture and infrastructure concepts
Key Points: Achieved through redundancy (servers, power, network, sites); higher availability costs more; differs from fault tolerance, which aims for zero interruption; covered again in 3.4

Definition: The factors used to compare architecture models. Staying up: availability, resilience, ease of recovery. Growing and launching: scalability, ease of deployment, responsiveness. Money and risk: cost and risk transference. Upkeep and hardware: patch availability or an inability to patch, power and compute.
Example: Choosing cloud over on-premises for a seasonal app because of scalability and cost, while accepting less control over patching.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models
Key Points: Every model is a trade-off: no option wins on all factors; exam scenarios name a priority (cost, uptime, patching) and ask which model fits it

Definition: How reliably a system is up and usable when needed. Architecture choices such as redundancy, multiple zones and cloud hosting change how available a system can be.
Example: An e-commerce site chooses a multi-region cloud deployment because any downtime loses sales.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: The A in the CIA triad; improved by redundancy and failover; balanced against cost; ICS puts availability first

Definition: A system's ability to keep working, perhaps in a degraded state, through failures or attacks, and to recover quickly. Built with redundancy, diversity and fault-tolerant design.
Example: A microservices app keeps taking orders even when its recommendation service crashes.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Resilience is about surviving and bouncing back; availability is the uptime result; microservices and distributed designs usually increase resilience

Definition: The money needed to build and run an architecture, including upfront capital expense, ongoing operating expense, licenses, staff and the cost of security controls.
Example: A small business picks SaaS email to avoid buying servers and hiring a mail administrator.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: On-premises: high upfront capital cost; cloud: pay-as-you-go operating cost; more availability and redundancy cost more; controls should not cost more than the asset they protect

Definition: How quickly a system reacts to requests and changes in load. Location, design and scaling ability all affect it.
Example: A trading platform hosts servers near the exchange so orders are processed with minimal delay.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Linked to performance and latency; elastic cloud and load balancing help keep systems responsive under load; heavy security inspection can add latency

Definition: The ability to add or remove capacity as demand changes. Elasticity is scaling automatically and quickly, both up and down.
Example: A ticket site automatically adds cloud servers when concert tickets go on sale and removes them afterward.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Scale up (bigger machine) vs scale out (more machines); cloud, containers and microservices scale easily; on-premises scaling needs hardware purchases

Definition: How simply and quickly a system can be set up or changed. Automation, templates and managed services make deployment easier and more consistent.
Example: With IaC a new branch office network is deployed in minutes from a tested template.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: IaC, containers and cloud services ease deployment; easy deployment can also spread mistakes fast; complex systems (ICS, hybrid) are harder to deploy securely

Definition: Shifting some of the impact of a risk to another party, such as a cloud provider or an insurer, through contracts and service agreements. Accountability for the data still stays with the organization.
Example: Moving email to a SaaS provider transfers responsibility for server patching and hardware failure to that provider.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Cloud and outsourcing transfer some operational risk; you cannot transfer accountability for your data; also a risk response strategy in 5.2 (with accept, avoid, mitigate)

Definition: How quickly and simply a system can be restored after a failure or attack. Architectures with automation, snapshots and redundancy recover faster.
