Example: A cloud VM rebuilt from an IaC template and restored from a snapshot is back online in minutes.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Supports low RTO; cloud, IaC and containers usually recover easily; ICS and legacy systems can be hard to restore

Definition: Whether the vendor actually releases security updates for a system and how quickly. Unsupported or end-of-life products get none.
Example: A vendor stops releasing patches for an old operating system, so a newly found flaw stays open forever.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Check vendor support lifecycle before choosing; end-of-life means no patches; cloud SaaS providers patch for you

Definition: Situations where a system cannot be patched even if fixes exist, because of uptime needs, vendor certification, limited resources or fixed firmware. Compensating controls must cover the gap.
Example: A certified medical device cannot be updated without losing its regulatory approval, so it is placed on an isolated network.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Common with ICS/SCADA, RTOS, embedded, IoT and medical devices; use compensating controls: segmentation, air gap, monitoring, strict access; different from patch availability (patch may exist but cannot be applied)

Definition: The electrical needs of an architecture: how much power it draws and how dependable its supply is. Data centers need enough capacity and backup power, and small devices may be limited by battery.
Example: Moving to the cloud removes the need for a company to buy more power capacity and generators for its server room.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: On-premises means you supply and back up power; low-power IoT and embedded devices cannot run heavy security software; power resilience is detailed in 3.4

Definition: The processing power available to a system (CPU, memory). It limits what workloads and security functions can run, and cloud compute can be scaled on demand.
Example: A small sensor lacks the CPU to perform strong encryption, while a cloud workload can add more virtual CPUs at peak times.
Category: 3.1 Architecture models > Considerations
Key Points: Constrained devices (IoT, embedded) limit encryption and agents; cloud offers elastic compute; affects cost and responsiveness

items.front: SY0-701 3.2: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers designing a secure network: device placement, zones, attack surface, connectivity, failure modes, device attributes, network appliances, port security, firewall types, secure remote communication and choosing effective controls.
Example: Deciding where to put a WAF, an IPS and a jump server in a new data center design.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure
Key Points: Scenario based: pick the right device and where to place it; know fail-open vs fail-closed, inline vs tap, IPS vs IDS, WAF vs NGFW vs UTM, TLS vs IPSec, SD-WAN vs SASE

Definition: The design decisions that shape network security: where devices go, how the network is split into zones, how large the attack surface is, how sites connect, how devices behave when they fail, how they attach to traffic, which appliances to use, port security and firewall types.
Example: A network architect plans zones, firewall placement and failure behavior before building a new office network.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure
Key Points: Defense in depth: layered controls at zone boundaries; reduce attack surface; choose behavior on failure deliberately

Definition: Choosing where in the network each security device sits so it sees and controls the right traffic, usually at the boundaries between security zones.
Example: A firewall is placed between the internet and the screened subnet, and another between the screened subnet and the internal network.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Firewalls at zone boundaries; IPS inline where traffic must be blocked; IDS sensors where they can see the traffic of interest; a WAF in front of web servers

Definition: Areas of the network grouped by trust level and purpose, with controls on traffic between them, such as untrusted (internet), screened subnet (DMZ) and trusted (internal) zones.
Example: Public web servers sit in the screened subnet; the database they use sits in the internal trusted zone, reachable only on one port.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Traffic between zones is filtered by policy; CompTIA calls the DMZ a screened subnet; zones support least privilege and limit lateral movement

Definition: All the points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data: open ports, services, applications, user accounts, devices and connections. Smaller is safer.
Example: Disabling unused services and closing unused firewall ports on a server reduces its attack surface.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Reduce by hardening, removing unneeded services, segmentation and least privilege; every new device, app or API adds to it; cloud, IoT and remote work enlarge it

Definition: How networks, sites, users and clouds are linked (internet, VPN, leased lines, wireless, SD-WAN) and how those links are secured and kept available.
Example: Branch offices connect to headquarters over encrypted site-to-site VPN tunnels with a backup cellular link.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Encrypt links over untrusted networks; redundant links improve availability; each connection is part of the attack surface

Definition: How a security device behaves when it fails or loses power: fail-open lets traffic pass, fail-closed blocks it. The choice trades availability against security.
Example: An inline IPS is configured to fail-open so a crash does not cut off the business website.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Fail-open favors availability; fail-closed favors security (confidentiality and integrity); pick based on what matters more for that link

Definition: A failure mode where a device lets all traffic through when it fails. The network keeps working, but traffic is no longer inspected or filtered.
Example: An inline IPS fails and switches to pass-through, so the store keeps taking orders but attacks are not blocked.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Failure modes
Key Points: Prioritizes availability; risk: unprotected traffic during the failure; contrast with fail-closed

Definition: A failure mode where a device blocks all traffic when it fails. Nothing unsafe gets through, but the connection is down until the device is fixed.
Example: A firewall protecting a classified network stops all traffic when it crashes.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Failure modes
Key Points: Prioritizes security over availability; causes an outage on failure; contrast with fail-open; do not confuse with door locks (fail-safe/fail-secure)

Definition: Characteristics describing how a security device interacts with traffic: active vs. passive (can it act on traffic) and inline vs. tap/monitor (is traffic going through it or copied to it).
Example: An IPS is active and inline; an IDS is passive and connected to a tap or SPAN port.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Active usually requires inline to block; passive monitoring cannot stop traffic; inline devices can become a bottleneck or point of failure

Definition: An active security device can respond to and change traffic, for example by blocking or resetting connections. A passive device only watches and reports, without affecting traffic.
Example: An active IPS drops a malicious packet; a passive IDS only logs an alert about it.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Device attribute
Key Points: Active can stop attacks but can also block legitimate traffic (false positives); passive has no impact on traffic; IPS = active, IDS = passive

Definition: An inline device sits directly in the traffic path, so all traffic passes through it and can be blocked. A tap or monitor device receives a copy of traffic (network tap or switch port mirror/SPAN) and can only observe.
Example: An IPS is cabled between the router and the core switch (inline); an IDS sensor is plugged into a switch mirror port (tap/monitor).
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Device attribute
Key Points: Inline can block, adds latency and needs a failure mode; tap/monitor cannot block and does not affect traffic; port mirror is also called SPAN

Definition: Dedicated devices or virtual appliances that perform a network security job: jump servers, proxy servers, IPS/IDS, load balancers and sensors.
Example: A data center uses a load balancer for its web servers, an IPS at the edge and a jump server for admin access.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Know each appliance's purpose and placement; many are now virtual or cloud based; firewalls are covered separately under firewall types

Definition: A hardened, closely monitored host that administrators connect to first and then use to reach systems in a secure zone. It is the single controlled entry point for administration.
Example: Admins SSH into a jump server in the management zone, then from there into the database servers, which accept admin connections only from it.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Network appliances
Key Points: Also called jump box or bastion host; reduces exposure by funneling admin access through one point; must be hardened, patched and logged, since compromise exposes everything behind it

Definition: A server that makes requests on behalf of clients, so it can filter content, cache, log and hide internal addresses. A forward proxy serves internal users going out; a reverse proxy sits in front of internal servers for incoming requests.
Example: All employee web traffic goes through a forward proxy that blocks known malicious sites and logs visits.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Network appliances
Key Points: Forward proxy: users out to internet (content filtering, URL filtering); reverse proxy: internet in to servers (protects and load-balances web servers); explicit vs transparent proxies

Definition: Systems that inspect traffic for attacks using signatures, anomaly (behavior) detection or both. An IDS alerts only; an IPS sits inline and can block the malicious traffic.
Example: An IPS drops packets that match a known SQL injection signature; an IDS on a mirror port alerts the SOC about a port scan.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Network appliances
Key Points: IPS: inline and active; IDS: tap/monitor and passive; signature-based misses new (zero-day) attacks, anomaly-based has more false positives; HIDS/HIPS run on hosts, NIDS/NIPS on the network

Definition: A device or service that spreads incoming requests across multiple servers to improve performance and availability, and removes failed servers from the pool. It can also offload TLS and cache content.
Example: A load balancer sends visitors to whichever of four web servers is least busy and stops using one that fails a health check.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Network appliances
Key Points: Active/active (all serve traffic) vs active/passive (standby takes over); scheduling: round robin, weighted, least connections; affinity keeps a user on one server; supports high availability

Definition: Devices or software components placed in the network to collect traffic or event data and send it to a monitoring system such as an IDS, SIEM or NDR platform.
Example: Sensors on each network segment forward traffic metadata to a central console that spots unusual connections.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Network appliances
Key Points: Placement decides visibility: put sensors where the traffic of interest flows; sensors collect, a central system analyzes and correlates; often passive (tap/monitor)

Definition: Protection of individual switch ports and wireless access point connections, so only authenticated devices or users get network access. On SY0-701 this means 802.1X with EAP authentication.
Example: A visitor plugs a laptop into a wall jack and gets no network access because it cannot authenticate with 802.1X.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: Stops unauthorized devices at the point of connection; 802.1X with EAP is what the exam item lists; switch MAC address limiting is a separate, weaker control because MACs can be spoofed

Definition: An IEEE standard for port-based network access control: a device gets network access only after authenticating. Roles are the supplicant (client), the authenticator (switch or access point) and the authentication server (usually RADIUS).
Example: An employee laptop connects to the office Wi-Fi and is authenticated against RADIUS with its certificate before the access point opens the port.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Port security
Key Points: Three roles: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server; uses EAP to carry credentials (EAP over LAN, EAPoL); works for wired and wireless (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise); until authenticated, only authentication traffic passes

Definition: An authentication framework that carries many different authentication methods, used by 802.1X and enterprise Wi-Fi. Common methods include EAP-TLS, PEAP, EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST.
Example: A company uses EAP-TLS so both the server and each client prove their identity with certificates.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Port security
Key Points: EAP is a framework, not one method; EAP-TLS needs certificates on server and clients (strongest); PEAP and EAP-TTLS need a server certificate and protect a password inside a TLS tunnel; EAP-FAST uses a PAC instead of certificates

Definition: The kinds of firewalls the exam compares: web application firewall (WAF), unified threat management (UTM), next-generation firewall (NGFW) and Layer 4 vs Layer 7 firewalls. They differ in what traffic they understand and what else they do.
Example: A company uses an NGFW at its internet edge and a WAF in front of its public web application.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations
Key Points: WAF protects web apps (HTTP); NGFW is application-aware with built-in IPS; UTM is an all-in-one box for smaller sites; Layer 4 filters by IP, port and protocol, Layer 7 by application content

Definition: A firewall that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from web applications and blocks application attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It works at Layer 7 and protects the app rather than the whole network.
Example: An online store puts a WAF in front of its checkout pages to block SQL injection attempts and meet PCI DSS.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Firewall types
Key Points: Protects web servers and apps, not general network traffic; blocks SQLi, XSS and similar; often required or recommended for PCI DSS; differs from an NGFW, which protects the whole network edge

Definition: An all-in-one security appliance combining many functions, such as firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, content and URL filtering, spam filtering and VPN, in one device. Common in small and medium businesses.
Example: A 20-person office buys one UTM box to provide its firewall, VPN, web filtering and antivirus scanning.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Firewall types
Key Points: Simple and cheap to manage; single point of failure; performance drops when all features are on; older all-in-one concept compared to NGFW

Definition: A firewall that identifies and controls traffic by application, not just by port and IP address, and usually includes intrusion prevention, URL filtering and TLS decryption. Also called an application layer gateway or Layer 7 firewall.
Example: An NGFW allows the company's video conferencing app but blocks file-sharing apps, even though both use port 443.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Firewall types
Key Points: Application awareness is the key feature; integrates IPS; can decrypt and inspect TLS; contrast with a traditional Layer 4 firewall that sees only ports and addresses

Definition: A Layer 4 firewall filters on transport information: source and destination IP address, port and protocol (TCP/UDP), often statefully tracking connections. A Layer 7 firewall understands the application data itself and can allow or block specific applications or content.
Example: A Layer 4 rule allows TCP port 443; a Layer 7 rule allows only the company's approved web apps over that same port.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Infrastructure considerations > Firewall types
Key Points: Layer 4: fast, simple, cannot tell apps apart on the same port; Layer 7: application-aware (NGFW, WAF), more processing; stateful firewalls track sessions, stateless check each packet alone

Definition: Ways to connect users and sites securely over untrusted networks: VPNs, remote access methods, tunneling with TLS or IPSec, SD-WAN and SASE.
Example: Remote staff connect through a TLS VPN, while branches use IPSec tunnels managed by SD-WAN.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure
Key Points: Encrypt traffic across untrusted networks; know TLS (application/transport, port 443) vs IPSec (network layer); SD-WAN is about connectivity, SASE adds cloud-delivered security

Definition: An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network (usually the internet) that makes a remote user or site appear to be on the private network. It can be site-to-site or remote access, and is often terminated on a VPN concentrator.
Example: Two offices link their networks with an always-on site-to-site VPN between their firewalls.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access
Key Points: Site-to-site (network to network) vs remote access (user to network); full tunnel (all traffic through VPN) vs split tunnel (only corporate traffic); built on IPSec or TLS

Definition: Letting users or administrators reach internal systems from outside, for example through a VPN, remote desktop, SSH or a jump server. It must be protected with strong authentication and encryption.
Example: An administrator connects through the VPN with MFA, then uses SSH to manage a server.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access
Key Points: Always require MFA; never expose RDP directly to the internet; use encrypted protocols (SSH not Telnet); log and limit remote sessions

Definition: Encapsulating one network protocol inside another so traffic can cross a network privately, usually with encryption. The main secure tunneling protocols on the exam are TLS and IPSec.
Example: A remote worker's traffic is wrapped in an encrypted TLS tunnel across hotel Wi-Fi to the corporate network.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access
Key Points: Tunneling hides and protects the inner traffic; TLS tunnels usually run over port 443 and pass most firewalls; IPSec tunnels protect all IP traffic at the network layer

Definition: A cryptographic protocol that encrypts traffic between two endpoints, the successor to SSL. As a VPN it usually runs over TCP port 443 and can be used from a client app or a browser (clientless).
Example: Contractors open a browser to the company's TLS VPN portal and reach internal web apps without installing software.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access > Tunneling
Key Points: TLS VPN (often still called SSL VPN) usually uses port 443, so it rarely gets blocked; clientless or light client; SSL is deprecated, TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are current; contrast with IPSec

Definition: A suite of protocols that secures IP traffic at the network layer with authentication, integrity and encryption, commonly used for site-to-site VPNs. It uses Authentication Header (AH) for integrity and authentication, Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for encryption, and IKE to set up keys.
Example: Two data centers connect with an IPSec tunnel-mode VPN between their routers.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access > Tunneling
Key Points: AH = integrity and authentication only, no encryption; ESP = encryption (plus integrity); tunnel mode protects the whole original packet inside a new IP header (site-to-site), transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original header; IKE (Internet Key Exchange) negotiates keys

Definition: A WAN that uses software to manage and choose among several connection types (broadband, cellular, MPLS) between sites and the cloud, steering traffic over the best path. It is built for cloud-based applications.
Example: A retail chain's stores send cloud app traffic straight to the internet over broadband and fall back to LTE automatically if broadband fails.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access
Key Points: About efficient, resilient connectivity, not a full security stack; central management and dynamic path selection; contrast with SASE, which adds cloud-delivered security to SD-WAN

Definition: A cloud-delivered model that combines SD-WAN networking with security services such as secure web gateway, cloud access security broker (CASB), zero trust network access and firewall as a service. Users get the same protection wherever they connect.
Example: Remote employees connect through a SASE provider's nearby cloud point of presence, which applies company security policy before traffic reaches any app.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure > Secure communication/access
Key Points: SASE = networking (SD-WAN) plus security delivered from the cloud; follows users anywhere, supports zero trust; SD-WAN alone does not provide the security services

Definition: Choosing security controls that fit the risk, requirements, environment and budget, often in layers (defense in depth). When the ideal control is not possible, a compensating control is chosen.
Example: Because an ICS controller cannot be patched, the team selects network segmentation and monitoring as compensating controls.
Category: 3.2 Securing enterprise infrastructure
Key Points: Base the choice on risk and business needs, not on the newest product; consider cost, performance and availability impact; compensating controls fill gaps; layered controls avoid single points of failure

items.front: SY0-701 3.3: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers data types, data classifications, data states, data sovereignty and geolocation, and methods to secure data such as encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation and permission restrictions.
Example: Deciding to tokenize stored card numbers, encrypt laptops and restrict a database to EU data centers for GDPR.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data
Key Points: Match the method to the goal: encryption (reversible with a key), hashing (one-way), masking (hide part), tokenization (replace with a token); know the three data states; sovereignty is about laws, geolocation about location

Definition: Categories of data by content and the rules that apply to them: regulated, trade secret, intellectual property, legal information, financial information, and human- and non-human-readable data.
Example: A hospital holds regulated health records, legal contracts and financial billing data, each with different handling rules.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data
Key Points: The type drives which laws and protections apply; one record can belong to several types; differs from classification, which labels sensitivity

Definition: Data whose handling is governed by laws or industry rules, such as personal data (PII), health data (PHI) and payment card data. Mishandling it can bring fines and legal penalties.
Example: A clinic must protect patient records under HIPAA and report breaches.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Examples: PII (GDPR, state laws), PHI (HIPAA), cardholder data (PCI DSS); compliance requirements set minimum controls; regulators may audit

Definition: Confidential business information that gives a company a competitive advantage because it is kept secret, such as formulas, processes or customer lists. It stays protected only while secrecy is maintained.
Example: A soft-drink formula known by only a few employees and protected by NDAs.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Protected by secrecy and NDAs, not by registration; once disclosed, protection can be lost; differs from patents, which are public

Definition: Creations of the mind owned by a person or company, such as software code, designs, inventions, brands and written works. Legally protected by copyrights, trademarks and patents.
Example: A game studio's source code and character designs are its intellectual property and are targeted by competitors and nation-state actors.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Protected by law (copyright, trademark, patent) and by security controls; theft of IP is a common espionage motive; trade secrets are a related form of IP protected by secrecy

Definition: Data related to legal matters, such as contracts, court documents, case files and attorney-client communications. It is often confidential and may be subject to legal holds.
Example: A law firm keeps privileged client communications on restricted file shares.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Often privileged and confidential; may be under legal hold (must not be deleted); some court records are public

Definition: Data about money: company financial records, payroll, bank account and payment card details. It is a prime target for fraud and often regulated.
Example: Attackers steal a company's unreleased quarterly earnings report to trade on it.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Includes internal company finances and customer payment data; card data falls under PCI DSS; public company reporting falls under laws like SOX

Definition: Human-readable data can be read directly by people (text documents, spreadsheets). Non-human-readable data needs a machine to interpret it, such as barcodes, QR codes, images, binary or encoded files.
Example: A DLP system must decode a QR code or scan an image to find a credit card number that a keyword search on text would miss.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data types
Key Points: Both can contain sensitive data; non-human-readable data is harder for people and simple DLP rules to inspect; encoding is not encryption

Definition: Labels that describe how sensitive data is and how it must be handled. SY0-701 lists sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private and critical; each organization defines its own scheme and the controls for each label.
Example: A company labels its press releases public, its HR files confidential and its merger plans restricted.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data
Key Points: Classification drives controls (access, encryption, retention); the data owner assigns it; schemes differ by organization; government uses unclassified, confidential, secret, top secret

Definition: Data that would cause harm if disclosed and needs protection, such as PII, PHI and intellectual property. Access is limited to those who need it.
Example: Employee home addresses and Social Security numbers are classified sensitive.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: Broad label for data needing protection; often includes PII and PHI; exact meaning set by each organization

Definition: Highly sensitive data whose disclosure could seriously harm the organization or individuals. Access must be specifically approved.
Example: Source code for an unreleased product is classified confidential and shared only with the development team.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: Need-to-know and approval required; usually encrypted and access-logged; disclosure has serious impact

Definition: Data meant to be shared freely with anyone, so disclosure causes no harm. Also called unclassified.
Example: Product brochures and the company's published annual report.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: No confidentiality controls needed; integrity still matters (no defacement); lowest classification level

Definition: Data with access strictly limited to specific, named people, often requiring extra approval or an NDA. Disclosure could cause severe damage.
Example: Merger negotiation documents are restricted to the executive team and legal counsel.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: Tightest access controls; often individual approval or NDA required; terms overlap with confidential, so read how the question defines them

Definition: Data with restricted access that needs extra rights or permissions to view, and sometimes a signed NDA. It is not for public release and often covers personal information about employees or customers.
Example: Employee salary records can be viewed only by HR staff who have been granted access.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: Professor Messer groups private with classified and restricted (extra permissions, possibly an NDA); not for public release; exact meaning set by each organization

Definition: Data the organization cannot operate without, so its availability and integrity must be protected above all. Loss or downtime would stop essential operations.
Example: A hospital's patient medication records must always be available, so they are replicated and backed up frequently.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Data classifications
Key Points: Focus on availability and integrity, not just confidentiality; drives backups, redundancy and recovery priority; links to business impact analysis

Definition: Factors that affect how data must be protected wherever it is: its state (at rest, in transit, in use), data sovereignty and geolocation.
Example: A cloud architect checks which country customer data is stored in and encrypts it at rest and in transit.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data
Key Points: Different states need different protections; sovereignty is legal, geolocation is physical location; both affect cloud region choices

items.front: Data states (at rest, in transit, in use)
items.back:
Definition: The three conditions data can be in: at rest (stored), in transit (moving across a network) and in use (being processed in memory). Each needs its own protections.
Example: A customer record is encrypted on disk (at rest), sent over TLS (in transit) and decrypted in RAM while an app processes it (in use).
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations
Key Points: At rest: full-disk, database, file encryption; in transit: TLS, IPSec, VPN; in use: hardest to protect, data is decrypted in memory; secure enclaves and access controls help

Definition: Data stored on a device or medium, such as hard drives, SSDs, databases, backups or cloud storage. Protected by encryption and access permissions.
Example: A stolen laptop with full-disk encryption (BitLocker) does not expose its files.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations > Data states
Key Points: Protect with full-disk, volume, file or database encryption plus permissions; backups and removable media count as data at rest

Definition: Data moving across a network, between systems or locations. Also called data in motion. Protected by transport encryption.
Example: Employee logins to a web app are protected by HTTPS (TLS) so they cannot be sniffed on public Wi-Fi.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations > Data states
Key Points: Protect with TLS, IPSec, VPNs, SSH; threats are sniffing and on-path attacks; also called data in motion

Definition: Data actively being processed, held in memory (RAM), CPU caches or registers. It is usually unencrypted at that moment, which makes it hard to protect.
Example: Malware scrapes card numbers from a point-of-sale terminal's memory while transactions are processed.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations > Data states
Key Points: Most difficult state to protect; RAM scraping is the classic attack; protections include secure enclaves, memory protection and limiting access

Definition: The principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or collected. Some laws require certain data to stay within national or regional borders.
Example: GDPR restricts transferring EU residents' personal data to countries without adequate protection, so a company stores it in EU cloud regions.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations
Key Points: About legal jurisdiction; affects cloud region choice and backups abroad; contrast with geolocation, which is the physical location itself

Definition: Determining the physical location of a device, user or data, using GPS, IP address, Wi-Fi or cell data. Used to enforce location-based rules and to know where data resides.
Example: A login attempt geolocated to another continent minutes after a local login is flagged as impossible travel.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > General data considerations
Key Points: Supports location-based access policies and impossible travel detection; IP geolocation can be fooled by VPNs; informs data sovereignty compliance

Definition: Techniques for protecting data: geographic restrictions, encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation and permission restrictions.
Example: A payment company tokenizes card numbers, masks them on receipts, hashes passwords and encrypts databases.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data
Key Points: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way; tokenization swaps in a meaningless token; masking hides part of the data; pick by whether the original must be recovered

Definition: Allowing or blocking access to data or systems based on location, such as country, region or a defined area (geofencing).
Example: A company blocks logins from countries where it has no employees, and a mobile app works only inside the office geofence.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Uses geolocation and geofencing; can be bypassed with VPNs, so combine with other controls; also used to meet data sovereignty rules

Definition: Turning readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext with an algorithm and key, so only those with the right key can read it. It protects confidentiality and is reversible.
Example: Customer records in a database are encrypted with AES-256, so a stolen copy is useless without the key.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Reversible with the key (unlike hashing); symmetric (AES) vs asymmetric (RSA, ECC); protecting the keys is critical; used for data at rest and in transit

Definition: A one-way function that turns data of any size into a fixed-length digest. The same input always gives the same hash, and the original cannot be recovered from it.
Example: A website stores salted password hashes, compares the hash at login and never stores the actual passwords.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: One-way, not reversible (not encryption); used for integrity checks and password storage; salt defeats rainbow tables; collisions mean weak algorithms (MD5, SHA-1); SHA-256 is common

Definition: Hiding part or all of data by replacing characters with symbols or fake values, so people see only what they need. The underlying data still exists elsewhere.
Example: A receipt shows a card number as ************4321.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Limits exposure on screens, reports and test data; often one-way for the viewer; does not protect the stored original; contrast with tokenization, which replaces the stored value

Definition: Replacing sensitive data with a random token that has no mathematical relationship to the original. The real value is kept in a secure token vault and looked up only when needed.
Example: A mobile payment app sends a one-time token instead of the real card number, so a merchant breach exposes no card data.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Token is not derived from the data, so it cannot be decrypted (unlike encryption); original lives in a token vault; widely used for card data to reduce PCI DSS scope

Definition: Making data or code hard to understand while keeping it usable, so it is hard to read or reverse-engineer. Masking, tokenization and steganography are forms of obfuscation.
Example: A developer obfuscates JavaScript so competitors cannot easily read its logic.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Hides meaning but is not strong protection on its own (security through obscurity); umbrella term covering masking, tokenization, steganography; code obfuscation slows reverse engineering

Definition: Separating data into different locations, databases or network segments based on sensitivity, so a breach of one area does not expose everything.
Example: Card data is kept on an isolated network segment, separate from the rest of the company's systems, which also shrinks PCI DSS scope.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Limits the blast radius of a breach; sensitive data gets stronger controls in its own segment; related to network segmentation in 3.1

Definition: Limiting who can read, change or delete data through access controls such as file permissions, ACLs and role-based access, following least privilege.
Example: Only payroll staff have read access to the salary folder, and only the payroll manager can modify it.
Category: 3.3 Protecting data > Methods to secure data
Key Points: Apply least privilege and need to know; review permissions regularly; controls access but not what happens if storage is stolen (pair with encryption)

items.front: SY0-701 3.4: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers keeping systems running and recovering them: high availability, site considerations, platform diversity, multi-cloud, continuity of operations, capacity planning, testing, backups and power.
Example: A company designs a warm site, daily offsite backups, UPS and generator power, and yearly failover tests for its core systems.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Know hot vs warm vs cold sites; load balancing vs clustering; test types (tabletop, failover, simulation, parallel processing); backup terms (snapshots, replication, journaling); UPS vs generator

Definition: Keeping systems up and running nearly all the time through redundant components, so one failure does not cause downtime. On SY0-701 3.4 it focuses on load balancing and clustering.
Example: Two clustered database servers share storage so the standby takes over automatically if the active node fails.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Redundancy at every level (servers, power, network, sites); more nines of uptime costs more; load balancing and clustering are the two main techniques

Definition: Load balancing spreads requests across independent servers that do not need to know about each other. Clustering links servers to work together as one system, usually sharing storage and aware of each other, so one node can take over another's work.
Example: Web servers sit behind a load balancer; a database runs as a failover cluster sharing the same storage.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > High availability
Key Points: Load balancer: front-end device distributing traffic, servers independent; cluster: servers cooperate as one logical unit, often with shared storage; both give high availability and scale

Definition: Choosing alternate locations to resume operations after a disaster, by how ready they are (hot, warm, cold) and how far away they are (geographic dispersion). Readiness trades cost against recovery speed.
Example: A bank keeps a hot site in another state; a small firm contracts a cold site and plans to bring in equipment.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Hot = fastest and most expensive; cold = slowest and cheapest; warm in between; distance protects against regional disasters

Definition: A fully equipped, ready-to-run alternate site with hardware, software, network and current data, so operations can switch over within minutes or hours.
Example: An airline's reservation system fails over to a hot site with real-time replicated data.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Site considerations
Key Points: Fastest recovery, highest cost; data kept current (replication); used when RTO is very short; often a mirror of production

Definition: An empty alternate facility with space, power and connectivity but no ready systems or data. Equipment and data must be brought in, so recovery takes days or weeks.
Example: A small company rents empty office space it can move into, then installs servers and restores backups after a disaster.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Site considerations
Key Points: Cheapest, slowest; no hardware or current data; suits long RTOs and low budgets

Definition: An alternate site with some equipment and connectivity in place but not fully current, needing data restoration and setup before use. Recovery takes hours to days.
Example: A warm site has servers and network gear installed; staff restore last night's backups to bring it online.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Site considerations
Key Points: Between hot and cold in both cost and speed; hardware present, data not fully current; most common compromise

Definition: Placing data centers, recovery sites and backups far enough apart that one regional event (hurricane, earthquake, power grid failure) cannot take them all out.
Example: A company on the US East Coast keeps its recovery site in the Midwest, outside the same hurricane zone.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Site considerations
Key Points: Protects against regional disasters; too far can add latency and legal (sovereignty) issues; cloud regions and availability zones support it

Definition: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies for the same function so one vulnerability or failure cannot bring everything down.
Example: Using firewalls from two different vendors in layers, so one vendor's zero-day does not open the whole network.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Reduces single points of failure and common-mode vulnerabilities; adds management complexity and training cost; part of defense in depth

Definition: Using services from more than one cloud provider so an outage, price change or problem at one provider does not stop the business.
Example: An app runs in two different cloud providers, so a major outage at one leaves the other serving users.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Avoids vendor lock-in and single-provider outages; more complex security, identity and monitoring across providers; different from hybrid cloud, which mixes on-premises and cloud

Definition: Planning to keep essential business functions running during and after a disruption, including alternate processes when technology is unavailable.
Example: When the ordering system goes down, staff switch to paper order forms and phone calls until it returns.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Part of business continuity planning; focuses on essential functions; includes manual or alternate processes, not only IT recovery; disaster recovery is the IT restoration part

Definition: Making sure enough people, technology and infrastructure exist to meet normal and peak demand and to keep running during disruptions.
Example: Before a holiday sale, a retailer adds cloud capacity, extra support staff and more bandwidth.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Three areas: people, technology, infrastructure; both too little (outage) and too much (waste) are problems; cloud elasticity eases technology capacity

Definition: Having enough staff with the right skills and cross-training to handle workloads and incidents, including backups for key roles.
Example: A SOC cross-trains analysts so the night shift can still respond if one analyst is sick during a major incident.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Capacity planning
Key Points: Avoid single points of failure in people (one admin who knows everything); cross-training and succession planning; staffing for peak or incident load

Definition: Making sure applications, servers and services can handle the expected demand, scaling up or out as needed.
Example: An online store adds application servers and uses autoscaling so the site stays fast during a flash sale.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Capacity planning
Key Points: Plan for peak load, not average; cloud elasticity scales on demand; monitor usage trends to predict needs

Definition: Making sure the underlying facilities and services, such as network bandwidth, power, cooling, data center space and cloud resources, can support the load.
Example: A data center adds cooling and power capacity before installing new server racks.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Capacity planning
Key Points: Includes network, power, cooling, physical space; long lead times for physical upgrades; cloud can shift some of this to the provider

Definition: Checking that recovery and continuity plans actually work, using tabletop exercises, failover tests, simulations and parallel processing, from low risk discussions to real switchovers.
Example: A company runs a tabletop exercise each quarter and a full failover test once a year.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Untested plans often fail; tabletop is discussion only and lowest risk; failover actually switches systems; simulations practice realistic scenarios; document lessons learned

Definition: A discussion-based exercise where key staff talk through how they would respond to a scenario, step by step, without touching any systems.
Example: Managers sit in a conference room and walk through their response to a ransomware scenario to find gaps in the plan.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Testing
Key Points: Cheapest and least disruptive test; no systems affected; finds gaps in roles, communication and procedures; contrast with simulation and failover, which involve action

Definition: Actually switching operations from a primary system or site to the redundant one to prove it takes over correctly, then usually switching back.
Example: The team shuts down the primary database server to confirm the cluster moves work to the secondary node without data loss.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Testing
Key Points: Real switchover, so it carries risk and needs planning; proves redundancy works; measure against RTO and RPO

Definition: A realistic practice run of an event where people carry out their actions as if it were real, but in a controlled way that does not affect production.
Example: IT sends a simulated phishing email and a fake malware alert to see if staff report it and the SOC responds correctly.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Testing
Key Points: More hands-on than a tabletop, less risky than real failover; tests people and processes; examples include phishing simulations and simulated attacks

Definition: Splitting work across multiple processors or systems that run at the same time. If one fails, the others carry the load, and a faulty system can be found and taken out while processing continues. Some study guides also use the term for a parallel test: running the backup system alongside production and comparing results without cutting over.
Example: Transactions are spread across four servers; one starts returning errors, so it is removed and the other three keep processing.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Testing
Key Points: Professor Messer: multiple CPUs or processes handle transactions at once, improving performance and recovery; a failed processor is isolated without stopping work; parallel test meaning: backup runs beside production and outputs are compared, safer than a full failover

Definition: Copies of data and systems kept so they can be restored after loss, corruption, ransomware or disaster. SY0-701 covers onsite/offsite, frequency, encryption, snapshots, recovery, replication and journaling.
Example: A company keeps nightly backups onsite for quick restores and a weekly encrypted copy offsite.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: Follow 3-2-1 (three copies, two media types, one offsite); keep an offline or immutable copy against ransomware; test restores; frequency sets RPO

Definition: Onsite backups are stored at the same location as the original data, so restores are fast. Offsite backups are stored at another location or in the cloud, so they survive a site disaster.
Example: Local backup appliance for quick file restores, plus nightly copies to a cloud provider in another region.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: Onsite: fast, but lost in fire or flood; offsite: survives site disasters, slower restore; use both

Definition: How often backups are taken. It decides how much data could be lost, which ties to the recovery point objective (RPO).
Example: An RPO of one hour means backups or replication must happen at least hourly.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: More frequent = less data lost, more cost and storage; match frequency to RPO and data importance; full, incremental and differential backups mix frequency and size

Definition: Encrypting backup data so a lost or stolen backup cannot be read. The keys must be protected and available for recovery.
Example: Backup tapes sent offsite are encrypted, so a tape lost in transit does not cause a breach.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: Backups are data at rest and often hold everything; lose the key and the backup is useless; store keys separately from the backups

Definition: A point-in-time copy of a system or volume, common for virtual machines and storage, that can be rolled back to quickly. Often stores only changes since the previous snapshot.
Example: An admin takes a VM snapshot before patching and reverts to it when the patch breaks the application.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: Fast to take and restore; often depend on the original storage, so they are not a full substitute for separate backups; common in virtualization and cloud

Definition: Restoring data or systems from backups to a working state. Restores must be tested regularly to prove backups are complete and recovery meets the RTO.
Example: A quarterly test restore reveals a corrupted backup job before a real outage needs it.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: A backup is only as good as a successful restore; test restores regularly; measure against RTO (time) and RPO (data loss)

Definition: Continuously or frequently copying data to another system or location, keeping a near-current copy available. It supports fast failover.
Example: A database replicates in real time to a hot site in another region.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: Very low data loss and fast recovery; replicates corruption and deletions too, so it does not replace point-in-time backups; synchronous vs asynchronous

Definition: Recording each change in a journal (log) before or as it is applied, so data can be rebuilt or rolled to a consistent point after a failure. Used by file systems, databases and backup systems.
Example: After a crash, a database replays its journal to restore all committed transactions.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Backups
Key Points: Allows recovery to a consistent state or a specific point in time; protects against corruption from crashes mid-write; journal must itself be protected

Definition: Keeping systems running when utility power fails, using an uninterruptible power supply for short-term power and generators for long outages, along with redundant power feeds and supplies.
Example: A data center's UPS carries the load for the seconds it takes the diesel generator to start.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery
Key Points: UPS bridges the gap, generator runs long term; dual power supplies and multiple feeds add redundancy; power distribution units (PDUs) distribute power to racks

Definition: Fuel-powered machines that produce electricity for long power outages, from hours to days, as long as fuel lasts. They take time to start, so a UPS covers the gap.
Example: A hospital's diesel generators power critical systems through a two-day grid outage.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Power
Key Points: Long-term power; startup delay requires a UPS; needs fuel supply contracts and regular testing

Definition: A battery-based device that provides immediate power when utility power fails, for minutes, enough for a clean shutdown or for a generator to start. It also smooths out surges and sags.
Example: When the power flickers, servers keep running on the UPS without rebooting.
Category: 3.4 Resilience and recovery > Power
Key Points: Short-term, immediate power; types: offline/standby, line-interactive, online (double-conversion, always on battery path); pair with a generator for long outages

Example: A security analyst who applies a hardened baseline to new laptops, reviews SIEM alerts, patches a critical CVE, and then documents an incident is doing Domain 4.0 work.
Category: 4.0 Security Operations

items.front: SY0-701 4.1: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers how to secure individual computing resources: building and keeping secure baselines, hardening different device types, securing wireless and mobile devices, choosing wireless security settings, writing secure applications, sandboxing, and monitoring.
Example: Given a scenario where a company is rolling out tablets to field staff over public Wi-Fi, choose MDM, a COPE model, WPA3 on company networks and a VPN.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Scenario objective: pick the right technique for the device or situation; know the baseline life cycle (establish, deploy, maintain); know BYOD vs COPE vs CYOD; know WPA3, RADIUS and EAP basics

Definition: A secure baseline is a documented, approved set of security settings (services, permissions, patches, policies) that a system type must meet. It gives every system of that type the same known-good starting point and a reference to measure drift against.
Example: A company defines a Windows 11 workstation baseline that disables SMBv1, enforces BitLocker and sets password policy, then checks every laptop against it.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Life cycle: establish, deploy, maintain; often built from CIS Benchmarks or vendor guides; drift from the baseline is a finding to fix; a baseline is per system type, not one for everything

Definition: Establishing a baseline means deciding and documenting the secure configuration for a system type, usually starting from trusted guidance such as CIS Benchmarks or manufacturer security guides and adjusting it to business needs.
Example: The security team starts from the CIS Benchmark for Ubuntu Server, removes settings that would break the web app, and records the approved list as the server baseline.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
Key Points: First step of the baseline life cycle; based on industry or vendor guidance plus testing; must be documented and approved; output is the reference for deploy and maintain

Definition: Deploying a baseline means applying the approved settings to systems consistently, usually with central tools such as Group Policy, MDM, configuration management or golden images rather than by hand.
Example: An administrator pushes the workstation baseline to 2,000 domain computers with Active Directory Group Policy objects.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
Key Points: Use automation for consistency at scale (Group Policy, MDM, Ansible, images); manual setup invites drift and mistakes; deployment happens after the baseline is established and tested

Definition: Maintaining a baseline means keeping it current and keeping systems compliant with it: updating it for new patches, threats and software versions, and regularly checking systems for configuration drift.
Example: After a new OS release changes default settings, the team revises the baseline and runs a compliance scan that flags 40 servers which no longer match.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
Key Points: Baselines are not set and forget; update when software, threats or guidance change; scan for drift (SCAP and compliance tools help); changes to the baseline go through change management

Definition: The kinds of systems that must be hardened, meaning their attack surface is reduced by removing unneeded services and software, changing defaults, patching and restricting access. They range from user devices (workstations, mobile devices) and network gear (routers, switches) to servers and cloud infrastructure, and to specialised systems that are hard to patch (ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, IoT devices).
Example: Before deployment, a team disables unused ports on switches, removes default accounts from routers, and turns off unneeded services on servers.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Common steps for all: patch, change default credentials, disable unused services and ports, least privilege, logging; each target has its own constraints (ICS cannot be patched easily, IoT may not be patchable at all); hardening reduces attack surface

Definition: Hardening phones and tablets means keeping the OS and apps updated, requiring screen locks and encryption, limiting app sources, and managing settings centrally through MDM so lost or stolen devices can be locked or wiped.
Example: An MDM policy forces a 6-digit passcode, full device encryption, automatic updates and remote wipe on all company phones.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: MDM is the main tool to enforce mobile hardening; segment work and personal data (containerization); updates depend on carrier and manufacturer support; remote wipe for loss or theft

Definition: Hardening desktops and laptops means applying regular OS and application patches, removing unnecessary software, enforcing least privilege (no daily admin rights), and running endpoint protection such as antivirus or EDR, plus host firewall and disk encryption.
Example: IT removes local admin rights from users, enables BitLocker, turns on the host firewall and installs EDR on every laptop.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Patch management and automatic updates; remove unneeded apps and services; standard user accounts, not admin; endpoint protection, host firewall and encryption, usually enforced with Group Policy

Definition: Hardening a network switch means changing default credentials, using secure management (SSH instead of Telnet, SNMPv3), disabling unused ports, keeping firmware updated, and using port security or 802.1X to control what connects.
Example: An administrator shuts down every unused switch port, enables 802.1X on user ports and disables Telnet in favor of SSH for management.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Default passwords and plaintext management (Telnet, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c) are classic exam findings; disable unused ports; firmware updates; restrict management access to a management network

Definition: Hardening a router means changing default credentials, using encrypted management, disabling unused services and interfaces, applying firmware updates, and using access control lists to filter traffic and limit who can manage the device.
Example: A network engineer applies an ACL so only the IT management subnet can SSH to the edge router and updates its firmware to fix a known flaw.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Like switches: defaults, encrypted management, firmware; ACLs filter traffic and management access; routers sit at network boundaries, so a compromise affects many hosts

Definition: Hardening cloud infrastructure means securing the customer-controlled parts of the cloud: least-privilege identity and access policies, secure configuration of storage and network security groups, MFA on admin accounts, logging, and endpoint protection on cloud instances.
Example: A security review finds a storage bucket open to the public and an admin account without MFA; both are fixed and cloud audit logging is enabled.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Shared responsibility: the customer still secures its configuration, identities and data; misconfiguration (public buckets, open security groups) is the top cloud risk; least privilege on IAM roles; enable logging and monitoring

Definition: Hardening servers means patching the OS and applications, removing unneeded services and software, enforcing strong authentication and least privilege for administrators, using host firewalls and endpoint protection, and monitoring logs.
Example: A new web server is built with only the web service installed, remote desktop restricted to a jump host, and the host firewall allowing only ports 443 and management traffic.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Minimize installed roles and services; strict admin access and MFA; patching cadence plus monitoring; servers hold valuable data, so they are prime targets

Definition: Industrial control systems (ICS) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems run physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing. Because they often run old software that cannot be patched or rebooted easily, they are hardened mostly by network segmentation and strict access control.
Example: A water utility places its SCADA network on an isolated segment with no direct internet access and only one tightly controlled jump server.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Segmentation or air gaps are the main control; availability and safety come first, so patching is slow and must be planned; legacy protocols often lack authentication; compromise can cause physical harm

Definition: Embedded systems are computers built into a device for one purpose, such as a printer, medical device or car controller. They often have limited updates and resources, so hardening relies on firmware updates from the manufacturer where available, changing defaults, and isolating them on the network.
Example: A hospital puts its infusion pumps on a separate network segment because the manufacturer releases firmware updates only rarely.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Limited or no patching, so segment them; change default credentials; depend on the vendor for firmware; often overlooked in inventories

Definition: A real-time operating system (RTOS) is an operating system built to respond to inputs within strict, predictable time limits, used in things like industrial controllers, vehicles and medical equipment. It is hardened by isolating it on the network, applying vendor updates carefully, and limiting access, since added security software could affect timing.
Example: A factory robot controller runs an RTOS; it is placed on an isolated network and updates are tested before installation so timing is not disrupted.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: RTOS = deterministic timing; often embedded, so hard to patch; isolate it and limit access; security tools must not break timing guarantees

Definition: Internet of Things (IoT) devices are network-connected everyday devices such as cameras, smart sensors, thermostats and speakers. They often ship with weak defaults and poor update support, so they are hardened by changing default credentials, updating firmware, disabling unused features and placing them on a separate network segment.
Example: Smart cameras in an office are moved to their own VLAN with no access to the corporate network, and their default admin passwords are changed.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
Key Points: Default credentials are a classic IoT weakness (Mirai botnet); segment IoT onto its own network; update firmware where possible; buy from vendors with security support

Definition: Securing wireless devices starts with how access points are installed: planning placement, coverage and channels so the network performs well and does not leak signal where attackers can use it.
Example: Before installing access points in a new office, the network team does a site survey and reviews a heat map to place APs where coverage is good but signal does not spill into the parking lot.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Installation considerations include site surveys and heat maps; goal is good coverage, minimal interference and minimal signal leakage; also find rogue APs during surveys

Definition: Installation considerations are the planning steps before and after placing wireless access points, mainly site surveys and heat maps, to decide AP location, channels and power levels and to spot interference and unauthorized APs.
Example: A warehouse full of metal racks needs a site survey to see where signal is blocked before choosing AP locations.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices
Key Points: Two listed tools: site surveys and heat maps; check for interference from other networks and devices; adjust channels and power; repeat surveys as the building or usage changes

Definition: A wireless site survey examines a location to learn how radio signals behave there: existing networks, interference, obstacles and channel use. It guides where to place access points and can also reveal rogue or unknown access points.
Example: A technician walks a building with a wireless analyzer, finds a neighboring network on the same channel and an unauthorized AP plugged in by an employee.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices > Installation considerations
Key Points: Done before installation and periodically after; identifies interference, channel overlap and rogue APs; often produces the data used for heat maps

Definition: A wireless heat map is a visual floor plan that shows signal strength in colors, making it easy to see strong coverage, dead zones and places where signal leaks outside the intended area.
Example: A heat map shows strong red coverage reaching the street outside, so the team lowers AP power on that side of the building.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices > Installation considerations
Key Points: Visual output of a site survey; shows coverage gaps and signal leakage; used to adjust AP placement and power; do not confuse with a SIEM dashboard

Definition: Mobile solutions are the ways an organization secures smartphones and tablets: managing them with MDM, choosing a deployment (ownership) model such as BYOD, COPE or CYOD, and securing how they connect (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth).
Example: A company picks a COPE model, enrolls every phone in MDM, and requires a VPN when phones use public Wi-Fi.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Three parts: MDM, deployment models, connection methods; ownership model decides how much control the company has; MDM enforces policy whatever the model

Definition: MDM is a centralized system for managing and securing mobile devices: enrolling them, pushing security policies (passcodes, encryption), controlling apps, separating work and personal data, tracking location, and remotely locking or wiping lost devices.
Example: An employee loses a company tablet in a taxi; IT uses the MDM console to locate it and then remotely wipe it.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
Key Points: Enforces policy centrally on many devices; features: remote wipe, geolocation, app allow lists, containerization (work data separated from personal); works with BYOD, COPE and CYOD

Definition: Mobile deployment models define who owns a device and how it may be used. Security+ lists bring your own device (BYOD), corporate-owned personally enabled (COPE) and choose your own device (CYOD).
Example: A company weighs BYOD to save money against COPE for more control over the data on each phone.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
Key Points: BYOD: user owns it; COPE: company owns and supplies it, personal use allowed; CYOD: user picks from an approved list, company owns it; more company ownership means more control and less user privacy concern

Definition: BYOD is a model where employees use their own personal devices for work. It saves the company hardware costs but makes control harder, so work data is usually separated with MDM containerization and the user must accept company policies.
Example: Staff use their own iPhones for work email, with the company app container that IT can wipe without touching personal photos.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
Key Points: User owns the device; hardest to control and secure, with many device types to support; privacy conflict when the company wants to wipe or monitor; containerization separates work data

Definition: COPE is a model where the company buys, owns and manages the device but allows the employee to use it for personal activities too. The company keeps full control and can wipe it, since the device is company property.
Example: A firm hands every salesperson a company-owned phone that is fully managed but may also be used for personal apps and calls.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
Key Points: Company owns and chooses the device; personal use allowed; company has full control; vs CYOD: in COPE the company picks the device, in CYOD the user picks from an approved list

Definition: CYOD is a model where the employee chooses a device from a company-approved list, and the company buys, owns and manages it. It balances user choice with company control and support.
Example: New hires can pick either an approved Android or iPhone model; the company purchases it and enrolls it in MDM.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
Key Points: User chooses, but only from an approved list; company owns and manages it; middle ground between BYOD and COPE; trap: CYOD does not mean the user owns it

Definition: Connection methods are the ways mobile devices communicate, each with its own risks. Security+ lists cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Example: A phone may be on the carrier network, then join hotel Wi-Fi, while paired to a Bluetooth headset, creating three separate attack paths.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
Key Points: Cellular: carrier network, traffic bypasses corporate monitoring; Wi-Fi: rogue APs, evil twins, on-path attacks, use encryption or VPN; Bluetooth: short range, pairing attacks, disable when not needed

Definition: Cellular connections use a mobile carrier network (such as 4G or 5G). Traffic is encrypted between the phone and the tower, but it bypasses the company network, so corporate filtering and monitoring cannot see it, and devices can be tracked by location.
Example: An employee tethers a laptop to a phone hotspot, sending traffic over cellular and around the corporate web filter.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
Key Points: Bypasses corporate security controls; location tracking risk; SIM swapping and fake cell towers are related threats; control with MDM and VPN policies

Definition: Wi-Fi connects mobile devices to local wireless networks. Public or unknown networks risk eavesdropping, rogue access points, evil twins and on-path attacks, so devices should use strong wireless encryption and a VPN on untrusted networks.
Example: A user joins "Free_Airport_WiFi", which is actually an attacker's evil twin AP capturing their traffic.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
Key Points: Prefer WPA3 or at least WPA2 encrypted networks; VPN on public Wi-Fi; watch for evil twin and rogue APs; MDM can restrict which networks devices join

Definition: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless link used for headsets, watches and file transfer. Risks include unwanted pairing, bluejacking (sending unsolicited messages) and bluesnarfing (stealing data), so it should be turned off or set non-discoverable when not needed and pairing should be controlled.
Example: An attacker in a cafe uses a flaw in an unpatched phone's Bluetooth stack to read its contacts.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
Key Points: Short range, but still an attack path; bluejacking = unsolicited messages, bluesnarfing = data theft; disable or make non-discoverable; keep devices patched

Definition: Wireless security settings decide how a Wi-Fi network authenticates users and protects traffic. Security+ covers WPA3, AAA with RADIUS, cryptographic protocols and authentication protocols.
Example: A company configures WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, authenticating users against a RADIUS server tied to Active Directory.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Personal mode uses a shared passphrase, enterprise mode uses 802.1X with RADIUS and individual credentials; WPA3 replaces WPA2; know which protocol does encryption vs authentication

Definition: WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard. In personal mode it replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key exchange with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), which resists offline password guessing and gives forward secrecy; it also requires protected management frames and offers a stronger 192-bit enterprise mode.
Example: An attacker captures a WPA3-Personal handshake but cannot run an offline dictionary attack on it, unlike with a WPA2-PSK handshake.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
Key Points: SAE (dragonfly handshake) replaces the PSK 4-way handshake guessing weakness; forward secrecy: a later stolen password does not decrypt old captures; WPA3-Personal still requires at least AES-CCMP-128, like WPA2; the optional WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode uses AES-GCMP-256; study guides (including Professor Messer) teach "WPA3 uses GCMP", so pick GCMP if asked; WPA3 is the best answer for new Wi-Fi

Definition: AAA stands for authentication, authorization and accounting. RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a common AAA protocol: the access point passes the user's login to a central RADIUS server, which checks credentials (often against Active Directory) and logs the session.
Example: With WPA3-Enterprise, each employee logs in to Wi-Fi with their own domain account, verified by the RADIUS server, so a departing employee is blocked by disabling one account.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
Key Points: Used in enterprise Wi-Fi with 802.1X; RADIUS uses UDP (1812 authentication, 1813 accounting); it encrypts only the password, while TACACS+ (TCP 49) encrypts the whole payload; individual credentials beat a shared passphrase

Definition: Wireless cryptographic protocols encrypt and integrity-protect Wi-Fi traffic. WPA2 uses CCMP, based on AES; WPA3-Personal requires at least AES-CCMP-128, and the WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode uses the stronger AES-GCMP-256. Old options such as WEP and TKIP are broken and should not be used.
Example: An audit finds an old access point still offering TKIP; it is reconfigured to allow only AES-based encryption.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
Key Points: CCMP-128 (AES) for WPA2 and the WPA3-Personal minimum, GCMP-256 for WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit (study guides shorten this to "WPA3 uses GCMP"); WEP and TKIP are insecure; cryptographic protocol = protects data, authentication protocol = proves identity

Definition: Wireless authentication protocols prove who is connecting. Enterprise Wi-Fi uses IEEE 802.1X port-based access control with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) family, such as EAP-TLS (certificates on both sides), PEAP and EAP-TTLS (a TLS tunnel protecting another login method) and EAP-FAST.
Example: A company uses EAP-TLS so each laptop presents its own certificate to the RADIUS server before joining Wi-Fi.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
Key Points: 802.1X is the framework, EAP carries the method, RADIUS checks the credentials; EAP-TLS needs client and server certificates and is the strongest; PEAP and EAP-TTLS need only a server certificate

Definition: Application security means building software so it resists attack. Security+ 4.1 lists input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis and code signing as techniques.
Example: A development team validates all form input, sets secure cookie flags, runs a static analyzer in its build pipeline and signs its release installer.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Four techniques: input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis, code signing; these are developer-side protections; 4.3 covers application security as a way to find vulnerabilities

Definition: Input validation checks every piece of data an application receives (type, length, format, allowed characters) and rejects or cleans anything unexpected before using it. It is the main defense against injection attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
