Example: A login form rejects a username containing ' OR 1=1 -- because only letters and digits are allowed, stopping a SQL injection attempt.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
Key Points: Validate on the server side (client-side checks are easy to bypass); prefer allow lists over deny lists; defends against SQL injection, XSS, buffer overflows; pair with parameterized queries

Definition: A secure cookie is a browser cookie protected with attributes: Secure (sent only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (not readable by page scripts, which limits theft through XSS) and SameSite (limits sending it with cross-site requests). They protect session tokens and other sensitive values stored in cookies.
Example: A web app marks its session cookie Secure and HttpOnly, so it is never sent over plain HTTP and an XSS script cannot read it.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
Key Points: Secure flag = HTTPS only; HttpOnly = no JavaScript access; SameSite helps against cross-site request forgery; do not store sensitive data in cookies in plain text

Definition: Static code analysis, also called static application security testing (SAST), examines source code without running it to find security flaws such as injection risks, buffer overflows and hard-coded secrets, often automatically in the build pipeline.
Example: A static analyzer flags a line where user input is concatenated into a SQL query before the code is ever deployed.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
Key Points: Code is not executed (vs dynamic analysis, which runs the app); finds issues early in development; produces false positives that need human review; cannot find runtime or configuration problems

Definition: Code signing is when a developer digitally signs software with a private key tied to a certificate from a trusted certificate authority. Users and systems verify the signature with the public key to confirm who published the code and that it has not been changed since it was signed.
Example: Windows shows the verified publisher name when installing a signed application, and warns if a downloaded installer was altered after signing.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
Key Points: Provides integrity and authenticity (who signed it, unchanged since); does not prove the code is safe or bug-free; relies on protecting the private signing key; uses public key infrastructure

Definition: Sandboxing runs an application or file in an isolated, restricted environment so it cannot reach the rest of the system or network. It limits damage from untrusted code and is used for testing, malware analysis and in browsers and mobile apps.
Example: A suspicious email attachment is opened inside a sandbox, where analysts watch it try to contact a command-and-control server without risking the real network.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Isolation contains damage; used by browsers, mobile OSs, and malware analysis; test new code in a sandbox before production; virtual machines and containers are common ways to sandbox

Definition: Monitoring computing resources means continuously collecting and reviewing logs, performance data and security events from systems so problems and attacks are detected quickly. Secure baselines and hardening reduce risk, and monitoring confirms they keep working.
Example: An admin sees in the logs that a hardened server suddenly has a new service listening and investigates.
Category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources
Key Points: Detective control that complements preventive hardening; logs feed a SIEM; watch for configuration drift and unusual activity; 4.4 goes deeper into monitoring tools

items.front: SY0-701 4.2: Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers managing assets through their whole life: buying them securely, assigning owners and classifications, tracking and inventorying them, and disposing of them so no data is left behind.
Example: An organization buys laptops only from approved vendors, tags each one to an owner, tracks it in an inventory, and gets a certificate of destruction when its drive is shredded.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
Key Points: Asset life cycle: acquisition, assignment, tracking, disposal; you cannot protect what you do not know you have; know sanitization vs destruction vs certification

Definition: Acquisition or procurement is how an organization buys hardware, software and services. A secure process uses approved vendors, checks security requirements and supply chain risk before purchase, and records new assets so they enter management from day one.
Example: A purchase request for new network switches must go through IT and security approval, use a vetted vendor, and the switches are added to inventory on arrival.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
Key Points: Security should be part of purchasing, not added later; approved vendor lists reduce supply chain risk; prevents shadow IT; new assets go straight into inventory

Definition: Assignment and accounting mean recording each asset against a responsible owner and a classification, so the organization knows who is accountable for it and how it must be protected.
Example: Each laptop record lists the employee responsible and the department that owns it, and each database is labeled with its data classification.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
Key Points: Two parts: ownership and classification; supports accountability; classification drives which controls apply

Definition: Ownership means a specific person or group is named as responsible for an asset, including its security, approving access and deciding how it is used.
Example: The HR director is listed as owner of the payroll system and must approve every access request to it.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Assignment/accounting
Key Points: Every asset needs a named owner; the owner is accountable, even if IT runs the system day to day; unowned assets tend to go unpatched and unmonitored

Definition: Classification labels an asset or its data by sensitivity and importance (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so the right protection is applied.
Example: A server holding customer credit card data is classified as restricted, so it requires encryption, extra monitoring and limited access.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Assignment/accounting
Key Points: Classification decides controls, handling and disposal method; set by the owner; data classifications are covered more in 3.3

Definition: Asset tracking keeps an up-to-date view of every asset the organization has, where it is, who has it and its status, using inventory records and automated discovery (enumeration).
Example: An asset management system shows 1,050 laptops issued, while a network scan finds 1,080, revealing 30 unrecorded devices.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
Key Points: Two parts: inventory and enumeration; finds lost, stolen and unauthorized devices; accurate tracking is the base for patching and vulnerability scanning

Definition: An inventory is the recorded list of assets with details such as asset tag, serial number, owner, location, configuration and software installed, kept current as assets change.
Example: Each laptop has an asset tag and a record listing its serial number, assigned user and OS version in the inventory database.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Monitoring/asset tracking
Key Points: The record of what you have; must be updated when assets move or change; supports audits, patching and incident response

Definition: Enumeration is actively discovering and listing assets, for example by scanning the network or querying management tools, to find what is really present, including devices and software missing from the inventory.
Example: A discovery scan enumerates all devices on the network and finds an unknown wireless access point an employee plugged in.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Monitoring/asset tracking
Key Points: Discovers what is actually there, compared with the inventory, which records what should be there; finds shadow IT and rogue devices; done with scanners and agents

Definition: Disposal or decommissioning is retiring an asset securely: removing it from service and inventory and making sure no data on it can be recovered, through sanitization or destruction, with proof (certification), while keeping any data the organization must retain.
Example: Old servers are retired: required records are archived, drives are wiped or shredded, a certificate of destruction is filed, and the inventory is updated.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
Key Points: Four parts: sanitization, destruction, certification, data retention; data left on discarded drives is a common breach; NIST SP 800-88 guides media sanitization

Definition: Sanitization removes data from storage media so it cannot be recovered while the media may still be reused, for example by overwriting, secure erase commands or cryptographic erase. NIST SP 800-88 names three sanitization levels: clear and purge keep the media reusable, destroy does not.
Example: Before donating old laptops, IT runs a secure erase on each SSD so the drives can be reused without exposing data.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
Key Points: Sanitization can keep the device usable, destruction cannot; simple file deletion or quick formatting is not sanitization; degaussing wipes magnetic media (and usually ruins hard drives), it does not work on SSDs

Definition: Destruction physically ruins storage media so data can never be read, for example by shredding, pulverizing, drilling or incinerating. It is used for the most sensitive data or media that cannot be reliably sanitized.
Example: Hard drives from a bank's card processing servers are sent through an industrial shredder.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
Key Points: Physical, permanent, media not reusable; vs sanitization, which removes data but can keep the media usable; often done by a third party who then provides certification

Definition: Certification is documented proof that media was properly sanitized or destroyed, often a certificate of destruction from a disposal vendor listing the assets, method and date.
Example: A recycling vendor provides a certificate of destruction listing the serial numbers of 200 shredded drives, which the company keeps for its auditors.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
Key Points: Provides evidence for audits and compliance; especially important when a third party does the disposal; ties disposal back to inventory records

Definition: Data retention means keeping data for the period required by law, regulation or business policy, and disposing of it once that period ends. Before an asset is destroyed, any data that must be kept is preserved elsewhere.
Example: Before wiping an old finance server, seven years of financial records required by regulation are moved to an archive.
Category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
Key Points: Keep data as long as required, but not longer (extra data is extra risk); legal holds can override normal disposal; retention policy should be checked before sanitization or destruction

items.front: SY0-701 4.3: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers the vulnerability management cycle: finding vulnerabilities, analyzing and prioritizing them, responding and remediating, validating that fixes worked, and reporting.
Example: A team scans weekly, confirms findings, ranks them by CVSS and business impact, patches or applies compensating controls, rescans to verify, and reports progress to management.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: Cycle: identify, analyze, respond, validate, report; know false positive vs false negative; CVE is the identifier, CVSS is the score; remediation options include patching, segmentation, compensating controls, insurance, exceptions

Definition: Identification methods are the ways an organization discovers vulnerabilities: vulnerability scans, application security testing, threat feeds, penetration testing, responsible disclosure programs and system or process audits.
Example: A company combines automated scans, a yearly penetration test, a bug bounty program and threat intelligence feeds to find weaknesses.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: No single method finds everything; scans are automated and broad, pen tests are manual and deep; threat feeds tell you about new threats; audits check processes as well as systems

Definition: A vulnerability scan uses an automated tool to check systems for known weaknesses such as missing patches, misconfigurations and open services, comparing what it finds against a database of known vulnerabilities. Scans can be credentialed or non-credentialed, and internal or external.
Example: A weekly scan reports that 12 servers are missing a critical OpenSSL patch.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Credentialed scans log in and see more (fewer false positives); non-credentialed shows the attacker view; scans identify, they do not exploit (that is pen testing); keep scanner signatures updated

Definition: In vulnerability management, application security means finding flaws in software, through static analysis of code, dynamic analysis of the running application, and package monitoring of third-party components.
Example: A company runs SAST on each code commit, DAST against its staging site, and monitors its open-source libraries for new CVEs.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Three methods: static analysis, dynamic analysis, package monitoring; static = code not running, dynamic = running app; package monitoring covers dependencies and the software supply chain

Definition: Static analysis (SAST) inspects source code or binaries without running them to find vulnerabilities such as injection flaws, unsafe functions and hard-coded credentials.
Example: A static analysis tool reports that a function uses strcpy without bounds checking, a possible buffer overflow.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
Key Points: No execution; finds flaws early and points to the exact line; can produce false positives; misses runtime and environment problems that dynamic analysis catches

Definition: Dynamic analysis (DAST) tests an application while it is running, sending inputs and observing behavior to find vulnerabilities such as injection, authentication flaws and crashes. Fuzzing, which sends large amounts of random or malformed input, is a common form.
Example: A fuzzer sends thousands of malformed requests to a web API and finds one that crashes the service.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
Key Points: App is running (vs static: code only); finds runtime and configuration issues; fuzzing is a dynamic technique; does not point to the exact line of code

Definition: Package monitoring tracks the third-party libraries and packages an application uses and alerts when one has a known vulnerability or is compromised, so it can be updated or replaced.
Example: A dependency monitoring tool alerts the team that a logging library in their app has a newly published critical CVE.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
Key Points: Covers software supply chain risk from open-source and third-party code; often uses a software bill of materials (SBOM) or software composition analysis; verify packages come from trusted sources

Definition: A threat feed is a stream of threat intelligence, such as new vulnerabilities, malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes, and attacker techniques, that helps an organization learn about threats relevant to it. Feeds come from open sources, commercial vendors, sharing organizations and the dark web.
Example: A SIEM imports a threat feed of known malicious IPs and alerts when a workstation connects to one.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Sources: OSINT, proprietary/third-party, information-sharing organizations, dark web; often shared in standard formats such as STIX over TAXII; feeds are only useful if relevant and acted upon

Definition: OSINT is intelligence gathered from publicly available sources such as websites, social media, news, public vulnerability databases, forums and government advisories. It is free but must be checked for accuracy.
Example: An analyst follows public vulnerability advisories and security researchers' blogs to learn about a new exploit the same day it is published.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
Key Points: Public and free (vs proprietary, paid); quality varies, so verify it; attackers use OSINT too, for reconnaissance

Definition: A proprietary or third-party threat feed is commercial threat intelligence from a security vendor, usually paid, often curated, more timely and tailored, and delivered in formats ready to load into security tools.
Example: A company subscribes to a vendor feed that pushes newly seen malicious domains straight into its firewall and SIEM.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
Key Points: Paid and curated (vs OSINT, free and public); may include vendor research not available elsewhere; still needs tuning to be relevant

Definition: An information-sharing organization is a group where members, often in the same industry or sector, share threat intelligence with each other, such as an Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) or government programs.
Example: A bank receives a warning from the financial sector ISAC about a phishing campaign that hit another member bank yesterday.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
Key Points: Industry focused, so very relevant; members share what they see; examples: sector ISACs, government partnerships such as CISA programs

Definition: The dark web is the part of the internet reachable only through special software such as Tor. Monitoring it can reveal stolen credentials, leaked company data, or attackers planning or selling access to an organization.
Example: A dark web monitoring service finds employee usernames and passwords from the company for sale on a criminal forum, so passwords are reset.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
Key Points: Early warning of breaches and leaked credentials; often done by specialized services; content is hard to verify and access carries risks

Definition: A penetration test is an authorized, simulated attack where testers actively try to exploit vulnerabilities to show what a real attacker could achieve. It follows agreed rules of engagement and may be done with known, partially known or unknown knowledge of the environment.
Example: Hired testers exploit an unpatched web server, move to a database, and report how they reached customer data.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Exploits vulnerabilities (a scan only identifies them); needs written authorization and rules of engagement; known (white box), partially known (gray box), unknown (black box) environment; more in 5.5

Definition: A responsible disclosure program gives outside researchers a clear, safe way to report vulnerabilities they find to the organization, which then has time to fix them before details are made public.
Example: A researcher finds a flaw in a company's website and reports it through the published security contact page instead of posting it online.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Defines how to report and what is allowed; gives the vendor time to patch before public disclosure; bug bounty programs add rewards; reduces chance of a flaw being made public before it is fixed

Definition: A bug bounty program pays rewards to outside researchers who find and responsibly report vulnerabilities in an organization's systems, within a defined scope and rules.
Example: A software company pays a researcher $5,000 for reporting an authentication bypass in its mobile app.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Responsible disclosure program
Key Points: Rewarded form of responsible disclosure; scope and rules define what may be tested; adds many testers at low cost; out-of-scope testing is not authorized

Definition: A system or process audit reviews systems, configurations and procedures against policies, standards or regulations to find gaps, such as missing controls, weak processes or noncompliant settings.
Example: An internal audit finds that the account removal process takes weeks, so former employees keep access, a process vulnerability.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods
Key Points: Finds process weaknesses that scanners cannot; compares against a standard or policy; can be internal or external

Definition: Analysis is deciding what each discovered vulnerability really means: confirming it is real, scoring and classifying it, and prioritizing it based on severity, exposure, the environment, business impact and the organization's risk tolerance.
Example: Two findings share a CVSS 9.8, but one is on an internet-facing server and the other on an isolated lab system, so the internet-facing one is fixed first.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: Steps: confirm, classify, score, prioritize; CVSS alone is not enough, context matters; inputs include exposure factor, environmental variables, organizational impact, risk tolerance

Definition: Confirmation checks whether a reported vulnerability actually exists before effort is spent fixing it, weeding out false positives and considering whether real issues were missed (false negatives).
Example: An analyst checks the server version by hand and finds the scanner wrongly flagged a patched service.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Verify before acting; false positive = reported but not real; false negative = real but not reported; credentialed scans and manual checks improve accuracy

Definition: A false positive is when a scanner or security tool reports a vulnerability or threat that does not actually exist. It wastes time but does not leave the organization exposed.
Example: A scanner reports a vulnerable Apache version because it reads the banner, but the server has a backported security patch.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis > Confirmation
Key Points: Reported but not real; wastes effort, causes alert fatigue; reduce with credentialed scans, updated signatures and tuning; less dangerous than a false negative

Definition: A false negative is when a real vulnerability or threat exists but the scanner or security tool does not detect it. It is more dangerous because the organization believes it is safe.
Example: A scan reports a server as clean, but it is vulnerable to a flaw the scanner's outdated signatures do not cover.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis > Confirmation
Key Points: Real but missed; most dangerous error because nothing gets fixed; caused by outdated signatures, non-credentialed scans, limited scope; combine methods (scans plus pen tests)

Definition: Prioritizing means ordering vulnerabilities for remediation, since not everything can be fixed at once, based on severity scores, whether exploits exist, how exposed the system is and how important the affected asset is.
Example: A team fixes an actively exploited flaw on its public VPN gateway before a higher-scored flaw on an isolated internal test machine.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Fix highest risk first, not simply highest score; consider active exploitation, exposure and asset value; limited time and staff make prioritization necessary

Definition: CVSS is a standard way to rate the severity of a vulnerability with a score from 0.0 to 10.0, built from metrics such as attack vector, complexity, privileges needed, user interaction and impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. It is maintained by FIRST.
Example: A vulnerability that is remotely exploitable without credentials and gives full system control gets a CVSS base score of 9.8, rated Critical.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Score, not an identifier (CVE is the identifier); v3.x ratings: None 0.0, Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9, Critical 9.0 to 10.0; base score can be adjusted with environmental metrics; NVD publishes CVSS scores for CVEs

Definition: CVE is a public list that gives each publicly known vulnerability a unique identifier, such as CVE-2021-44228, so everyone refers to the same flaw by the same name. The program is run by MITRE with US government sponsorship.
Example: A vendor advisory, a scanner report and a news article all reference CVE-2021-44228, so the team knows they all mean the Log4Shell flaw.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Identifier, not a score (CVSS is the score); format CVE-year-number; officially named Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, but CompTIA's acronym list writes Enumeration; scanners map findings to CVE IDs

Definition: Vulnerability classification groups vulnerabilities by type or category, such as injection, misconfiguration, missing patch, or weak cryptography, and by severity, so similar issues can be handled together and root causes found.
Example: Classification shows that 60% of findings are misconfigurations, pointing to a weak baseline process rather than missing patches.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Classifies by type (for example using CWE categories) and severity; helps find root causes and patterns; supports reporting and prioritization

Definition: Exposure factor (EF) is the percentage of an asset's value that would be lost if a specific threat succeeded, expressed from 0% to 100%. It is used in quantitative risk calculations: single loss expectancy (SLE) equals asset value times exposure factor.
Example: If a $100,000 database would lose 40% of its value in a breach, the EF is 0.4 and the SLE is $40,000.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: EF is a percentage of value lost; SLE = AV x EF; ALE = SLE x ARO; higher exposure means higher priority

Definition: Environmental variables are facts about where a vulnerable system sits and how it is used, such as whether it is internet-facing, what data it holds, and which other controls protect it, that make the real risk higher or lower than the generic score. CVSS has environmental metrics for this.
Example: A critical flaw on a server that is offline, isolated and behind multiple controls is lower real risk than the same flaw on a public web server.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Adjusts generic severity to your environment; the same CVE can be urgent in one company and minor in another; CVSS environmental metrics capture it

Definition: Industry or organizational impact is how much a vulnerability being exploited would hurt this particular organization, considering its industry, regulations, critical services, reputation and the data involved.
Example: A flaw in a patient records system has higher impact for a hospital, due to health data regulations and patient safety, than the same flaw would have elsewhere.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Business context drives priority; regulated industries (health, finance) face fines and legal impact; critical services and safety raise impact

Definition: Risk tolerance is how much risk an organization is willing to accept in a specific situation. It decides which vulnerabilities must be fixed immediately, which can wait, and which may be accepted.
Example: A low-risk-tolerance bank requires critical vulnerabilities to be patched within 48 hours, while a startup allows 30 days.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Analysis
Key Points: Set by leadership; shapes remediation timelines and whether exceptions are allowed; risk appetite and risk tolerance are covered more in 5.2

Definition: Response and remediation is deciding and carrying out what to do about each vulnerability: fix it by patching, reduce it with segmentation or compensating controls, transfer financial risk with insurance, or formally accept it with an exception or exemption.
Example: A legacy system that cannot be patched is placed on an isolated segment with extra monitoring, and a documented exception is approved.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: Options: patching, insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions and exemptions; patching is preferred when possible; every option except patching leaves the flaw in place

Definition: Patching applies vendor updates that fix the vulnerability itself. It is the most direct remediation, but patches should be tested and deployed through change management, with a rollback plan.
Example: After Microsoft releases a fix for a critical flaw, IT tests it on a pilot group and then deploys it to all servers.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
Key Points: Fixes the root cause; test before broad deployment; automate where possible; some systems (legacy, ICS, embedded) cannot be patched, so other controls are needed

Definition: Cybersecurity insurance transfers some of the financial impact of a security incident to an insurer. It does not fix the vulnerability, but it helps cover costs such as recovery, legal fees and some losses.
Example: A company buys cyber insurance that helps pay for incident response and customer notification after a ransomware attack.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
Key Points: Risk transfer, not risk reduction; does not remove the vulnerability; insurers often require baseline controls such as MFA and backups; policies may exclude some events

Definition: Segmentation places a vulnerable system on a separate, restricted network segment so attackers have fewer paths to reach it and a compromise cannot spread easily. It is often used when a system cannot be patched.
Example: An old manufacturing PC running an unsupported OS is moved to its own VLAN that can reach only the machine it controls.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
Key Points: Limits exposure without fixing the flaw; common for legacy, ICS and IoT systems; implemented with VLANs, firewalls, ACLs

Definition: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the normal fix is not possible, reducing the risk to an acceptable level by other means.
Example: Since a vulnerable application cannot be patched until next quarter, a web application firewall rule is added to block the known exploit.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
Key Points: Used when the primary control (often patching) is not possible; examples: WAF rules, extra monitoring, segmentation, disabling a feature; should be documented and reviewed

Definition: An exception or exemption is a formal, documented approval to leave a vulnerability unremediated, or not follow a policy, for a stated reason and usually for a limited time, with the risk accepted by someone with authority.
Example: A critical medical device cannot be updated without vendor approval, so management signs a six-month exception while compensating controls are applied.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
Key Points: Formal risk acceptance; must be documented, approved, time limited and reviewed; often paired with compensating controls; an undocumented unpatched system is not an exception

Definition: Validation of remediation confirms that a fix actually worked and did not create new problems, by rescanning, auditing and verifying the system's state.
Example: After patching, the team rescans the servers, confirms the finding is gone, and closes the ticket.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: Three methods: rescanning, audit, verification; never assume a patch worked; validation closes the loop before reporting

Definition: Rescanning means running the vulnerability scan again after remediation to confirm the vulnerability no longer appears and no new issues were introduced.
Example: A rescan after patching shows the critical finding has disappeared from all but one server, where the patch failed.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Validation of remediation
Key Points: Fastest way to confirm a fix; use the same scan settings as the original scan; can reveal failed patches or new findings

Definition: An audit, as validation, reviews records, configurations and remediation evidence to confirm fixes were done correctly and according to policy and compliance requirements.
Example: An auditor checks change tickets and system configurations to confirm every critical vulnerability was fixed within the policy deadline.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Validation of remediation
Key Points: Checks that the process was followed and documented, not only that a scan is clean; supports compliance; can be internal or external

Definition: Verification confirms by direct checking that a remediation is in place and effective, for example by checking the installed version, testing that the exploit no longer works, or confirming a compensating control is active.
Example: A tester tries the original exploit against the patched server and confirms it now fails.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Validation of remediation
Key Points: Direct confirmation the fix is effective; can include manual testing or retesting by the pen tester; complements rescans

Definition: Vulnerability reporting communicates findings, risk levels, remediation progress and trends to the right audiences, from technical detail for administrators to summary metrics for management and compliance.
Example: A monthly report shows management that critical vulnerabilities dropped from 45 to 8 and average time to patch fell to 6 days.
Category: 4.3 Vulnerability management
Key Points: Tailor to the audience (technical vs executive); track metrics such as open criticals and time to remediate; supports compliance and accountability; final step of the cycle

items.front: SY0-701 4.4: Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers what to monitor (systems, applications, infrastructure), the monitoring activities (log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, alert response) and the tools used (SCAP, benchmarks, agents, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow, vulnerability scanners).
Example: A SOC collects logs from servers, apps and firewalls into a SIEM, tunes its alerts, quarantines an infected laptop, and archives logs for a year.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring
Key Points: Know what each tool does and its look-alikes (SIEM vs NetFlow vs SNMP; agent vs agentless); alert tuning reduces false positives; quarantine is a response action

Definition: Monitoring computing resources means watching the health, performance and security events of systems, applications and infrastructure so that problems and attacks are noticed and handled quickly.
Example: A monitoring dashboard shows a server's CPU at 100%, a spike of failed application logins and a router interface going down, all at the same time.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring
Key Points: Three areas: systems, applications, infrastructure; covers both availability and security; feeds log aggregation and alerting

Definition: Monitoring systems means watching servers and endpoints: their availability, resource use (CPU, memory, disk), security logs, logins, running processes and configuration changes.
Example: Monitoring alerts when a domain controller logs hundreds of failed logins from one account in a minute.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
Key Points: Watch OS logs, authentication events, resource use and changes; sudden changes can indicate compromise or failure

Definition: Monitoring applications means watching application availability, response times, errors and application logs, including security events such as failed logins, access to sensitive functions and unusual transactions.
Example: Application logs show a single user downloading thousands of customer records, triggering an alert.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
Key Points: App logs show what users do inside the app; watch errors and unusual usage; uptime and performance matter for availability too

Definition: Monitoring infrastructure means watching the network devices and supporting systems, such as routers, switches, firewalls, wireless controllers, and cloud and virtualization platforms, for availability, performance and security events.
Example: An alert fires when a core switch reports an interface error spike and the firewall shows a flood of blocked connections.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
Key Points: Covers network and platform components; uses SNMP, NetFlow, device logs; infrastructure failure affects many systems at once

Definition: The alerting and monitoring activities are log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, and alert response and remediation or validation (including quarantine and alert tuning).
Example: A SOC collects logs, alerts on suspicious events, runs scans, reports metrics, archives old logs, and responds to alerts by quarantining hosts.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring
Key Points: Think of a pipeline: collect, alert, respond, report, keep; each activity has a separate card; SIEM supports most of them

Definition: Log aggregation collects logs from many sources, such as servers, applications, firewalls and endpoints, into one central place, usually a SIEM or log server, where they can be searched, correlated and kept safe from tampering.
Example: Firewall, VPN and Active Directory logs are all sent to a SIEM, so an analyst can see a VPN login followed by unusual file access in one view.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Centralizes logs for correlation and search; protects logs from being erased on a compromised host; often uses syslog; accurate time sync (NTP) is needed to correlate events

Definition: Alerting automatically notifies staff when monitored data matches a rule or threshold that suggests a problem or attack, so it can be investigated quickly.
Example: The SIEM sends an alert when an administrator account logs in at 3 a.m. from another country.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Rules and thresholds trigger alerts; too many alerts cause alert fatigue; tuning keeps alerts useful; alerts lead to response

Definition: Scanning as a monitoring activity regularly checks systems and networks for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, unauthorized devices and compliance with baselines.
Example: A nightly scan finds a server whose configuration no longer matches its secure baseline.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Regular and automated; finds vulnerabilities, rogue devices and drift; results feed alerts and reports

Definition: Reporting summarizes monitoring data into useful information, such as security events, trends, compliance status and incidents handled, for analysts, managers and auditors.
Example: A weekly SIEM report shows the top attacked systems and the number of blocked malware events.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Turns raw data into decisions; scheduled or on demand; supports compliance; dashboards show near-real-time views

Definition: Archiving stores older logs and monitoring data long term, protected from change, to meet legal and compliance retention requirements and to support later investigations.
Example: Logs older than 90 days move from the SIEM to cheaper archive storage and are kept for one year as required by policy.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Retention set by policy or regulation; archived data must stay intact and searchable when needed; helps investigate incidents discovered long after they began

Definition: Alert response is what happens after an alert: investigating it, containing the problem (for example quarantine), fixing it, validating the fix, and improving the alerts themselves through tuning.
Example: An alert on a malware detection leads an analyst to quarantine the laptop, clean it, confirm it is clean and adjust the rule that fired late.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities
Key Points: Listed parts: quarantine and alert tuning; validate before closing; feedback from each alert improves detection

Definition: Quarantine isolates a suspicious file, device or system so it cannot spread malware or reach other resources while it is investigated and fixed.
Example: EDR automatically cuts an infected laptop off from the network, allowing only communication with the security console.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities > Alert response and remediation/validation
Key Points: Containment action; can apply to files (antivirus moves them) or to whole hosts (network isolation); keeps evidence for investigation

Definition: Alert tuning adjusts detection rules and thresholds to cut false positives while still catching real threats, so analysts are not overwhelmed and important alerts are not missed.
Example: A rule alerting on every failed login is tuned to alert only after 10 failures in 5 minutes from one source.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities > Alert response and remediation/validation
Key Points: Reduces false positives and alert fatigue; over-tuning can create false negatives; an ongoing process, not a one-time fix

Definition: The alerting and monitoring tools listed are SCAP, benchmarks, agents or agentless collection, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow and vulnerability scanners.
Example: A SOC uses a SIEM for correlation, NetFlow for traffic patterns, SNMP traps for device faults and scanners for vulnerabilities.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring
Key Points: Correlation across logs = SIEM; traffic metadata = NetFlow, device fault alerts = SNMP traps; configuration checks = SCAP and benchmarks, known flaws = vulnerability scanners; malware = antivirus, sensitive data leaving = DLP

Definition: SCAP is a NIST suite of open standards that lets security tools describe vulnerabilities and configuration checks in a common format, so different tools can automatically check systems for compliance and known flaws. It includes standards such as CVE, CVSS, CPE, CCE, XCCDF and OVAL.
Example: A compliance tool loads a SCAP content file for a benchmark and automatically checks 500 servers against it.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Created by NIST; enables automated, tool-independent compliance and vulnerability checks; common language between scanners; pairs with benchmarks

Definition: Benchmarks are published, recommended secure configuration settings for specific operating systems, applications and devices, such as CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs. Systems are compared against them to find weak settings.
Example: A scan compares a Linux server with the CIS Benchmark and reports that SSH root login is still allowed.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Common sources: CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, vendor guides; used to establish secure baselines; often checked automatically with SCAP

Definition: Agent-based monitoring installs software on each system to collect data and enforce settings continuously; agentless monitoring collects data remotely, for example over the network or through management interfaces, with nothing installed on the system.
Example: An EDR agent runs on every laptop, while network devices that cannot run agents are monitored agentlessly through SNMP and syslog.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Agent: more detail, works offline and off network, but must be installed and maintained; agentless: nothing to install, good for devices that cannot run agents, but less detail and needs network access; NAC can use persistent or dissolvable agents too

Definition: A SIEM collects and aggregates logs and events from across the organization, correlates them to find suspicious patterns, raises alerts, provides dashboards and reports, and keeps data for investigations and compliance.
Example: The SIEM correlates a phishing email click, a new process on the same laptop, and a connection to a known bad IP into one high-priority alert.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Key functions: aggregation, correlation, alerting, dashboards, retention; correlation across sources is what sets it apart; needs tuning; SOAR (4.7) automates response on top

Definition: Antivirus software detects, blocks and removes malware on endpoints using signatures of known malware plus heuristic and behavior-based detection, and reports detections to central monitoring.
Example: Antivirus quarantines a malicious attachment and the central console alerts the security team.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Signature-based detection misses new malware, so heuristics and behavior help; keep definitions updated; EDR goes further with recording and response; alerts feed the SIEM

Definition: As a monitoring tool, DLP watches data in use, in motion and at rest for sensitive information, such as card numbers or confidential documents, and alerts on or blocks attempts to send or copy it where it should not go.
Example: DLP alerts the security team when an employee tries to email a spreadsheet full of Social Security numbers to a personal address.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Monitors data in use, in motion, at rest; detects patterns and labels of sensitive data; can alert or block; 4.5 covers DLP as a capability to configure

Definition: An SNMP trap is an unsolicited alert message that a network device's SNMP agent sends to the management station when a specific event occurs, such as an interface going down or a threshold being crossed, instead of waiting to be polled.
Example: A switch sends an SNMP trap to the network management system the moment a link to a server goes down.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Trap = device pushes an alert (vs polling, where the manager asks); traps use UDP 162, polling UDP 161; use SNMPv3 for authentication and encryption, v1 and v2c send community strings in clear text

Definition: NetFlow is a protocol, originally from Cisco, that collects metadata about network traffic flows, such as source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, times and byte counts, and sends it to a collector for analysis. It shows who talked to whom and how much, not packet contents.
Example: NetFlow data shows a workstation sending 20 GB to an unknown external IP overnight, suggesting data exfiltration.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Flow metadata, not full packet capture; good for baselining traffic, spotting exfiltration and DDoS; uses probes and collectors; IPFIX is the related open standard

Definition: Vulnerability scanners are tools that automatically probe systems and applications for known vulnerabilities, missing patches and misconfigurations, and report findings with severity ratings, often mapped to CVE and CVSS.
Example: A scheduled scanner run finds a web server with an expired TLS certificate and an outdated, vulnerable PHP version.
Category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Tools
Key Points: Identifies, does not exploit; credentialed vs non-credentialed; keep plugins updated; results can contain false positives that need confirmation

items.front: SY0-701 4.5: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security
items.back:
Definition: This objective covers changing and tuning enterprise security tools to improve protection: firewalls, IDS/IPS, web filters, operating system security, secure protocols, DNS filtering, email security, file integrity monitoring, DLP, NAC, EDR/XDR and user behavior analytics.
Example: Given a scenario where spoofed emails impersonate the CEO, publish SPF, DKIM and a DMARC reject policy for the company domain.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Scenario objective: choose the right control and setting; know firewall rule order and implicit deny; know SPF vs DKIM vs DMARC; know secure protocol and port pairs

Definition: A firewall controls traffic between networks or hosts by allowing or blocking it according to rules based on addresses, ports, protocols and, for next-generation firewalls, applications and users. Enhancing security means tuning its rules, access lists, allowed ports and protocols, and network zones such as screened subnets.
Example: An admin replaces an "allow any" rule with rules that permit only HTTPS to the web server and block everything else.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Rules read top to bottom, first match wins, implicit deny at the end; least privilege for traffic; NGFW adds application awareness; screened subnet isolates public-facing servers

Definition: Firewall rules are the individual statements that say which traffic to allow or deny, defined by source, destination, port, protocol and action. They are processed in order, the first match is applied, and traffic matching no rule is denied by an implicit deny.
Example: A broad "allow all from LAN" rule placed above a specific "deny LAN to finance server" rule means the deny never takes effect.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Firewall
Key Points: Order matters: specific rules above general ones; first match wins; implicit deny at the bottom; remove unused and overly broad rules

Definition: Access control lists (ACLs) are ordered lists of permit and deny entries applied to an interface or traffic direction on a firewall or router, filtering packets by criteria such as IP address, port and protocol.
Example: A router ACL permits traffic from the management subnet to port 22 and denies SSH from everywhere else.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Firewall
Key Points: Same logic as rules: ordered, first match, implicit deny; often stateless on routers; applied inbound or outbound per interface

Definition: Firewalls filter by port number and protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP) to allow only the services that are needed, for example TCP 443 for HTTPS, while blocking others such as Telnet on TCP 23.
Example: The firewall allows TCP 443 to the web server, but blocks TCP 3389 so Remote Desktop is not exposed to the internet.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Firewall
Key Points: Allow only needed ports and protocols; know common ports (22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP); port alone does not prove which application is in use, NGFWs inspect the application

Definition: A screened subnet, formerly called a DMZ, is a separate network zone between the internet and the internal network that holds public-facing servers. Firewalls control traffic so outsiders reach only those servers, and a compromised server cannot freely reach the internal network.
Example: The company web and email gateways sit in a screened subnet, and the firewall blocks them from starting connections to the internal database network.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Firewall
Key Points: Same idea as the older term DMZ; holds public services (web, email relay, DNS); limits damage if a public server is compromised; uses one firewall with three interfaces or two firewalls

Definition: An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches traffic or host activity and alerts on attacks; an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and can also block them. They detect using signatures and anomaly or behavior analysis, and show trends over time.
Example: An inline IPS drops packets matching a known exploit signature, while an IDS on a mirror port only alerts.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: IDS = detect and alert (passive, out of band); IPS = inline, can block; signature-based misses new attacks, anomaly-based catches them but has more false positives; network-based vs host-based

Definition: IDS/IPS trends are patterns in detections over time, such as rising attack types, top sources or most targeted systems, usually shown on dashboards. They help spot campaigns and decide where to strengthen defenses or tune rules.
Example: The IPS dashboard shows a steady rise in attempts against the VPN gateway over two weeks, so the team prioritizes patching it.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > IDS/IPS
Key Points: Look at patterns, not single alerts; helps prioritize and tune; changes from normal can signal a new campaign

Definition: IDS/IPS signatures are patterns that match known attacks, such as specific byte sequences or request formats. Signature detection is accurate for known threats but cannot catch new attacks without a signature, so signatures must be kept updated.
Example: A new signature for a recently published exploit lets the IPS block attempts against an unpatched server.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > IDS/IPS
Key Points: Matches known attacks; needs frequent updates; misses zero-days; vs anomaly or behavior-based detection, which compares to a baseline of normal

Definition: A web filter controls which websites users can reach, blocking malicious or inappropriate sites. It can run as an agent on each device or as a central proxy, and uses URL scanning, content categories, block rules and reputation.
Example: The web filter blocks gambling and known malware sites and warns users before they open newly registered domains.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Agent-based follows the device anywhere; centralized proxy covers traffic through the network; techniques: URL scanning, categorization, block rules, reputation

Definition: Agent-based web filtering installs software on each device that enforces web policy locally, so filtering works wherever the device is, including at home or on public Wi-Fi, without routing traffic through the office.
Example: A remote employee's laptop still blocks malicious sites at a hotel because the filtering agent runs on the laptop.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: Works on and off the corporate network; must be installed and updated on every device; vs centralized proxy, which only filters traffic that passes through it

Definition: A centralized proxy is a server that user web traffic passes through, where requests are checked against policy, filtered, logged and sometimes cached, before reaching the internet.
Example: All office browsers send traffic through the company proxy, which blocks malware sites and logs every visited URL.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: One place to manage and log; only filters traffic routed through it (remote users may bypass it); inspecting HTTPS needs TLS decryption; can be explicit or transparent

Definition: URL scanning checks the web address a user requests against lists and analysis of known malicious, phishing or disallowed sites, allowing or blocking the request.
Example: A user clicks a link in an email; the filter scans the URL, recognizes a known phishing page and blocks it.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: Checks the address itself; often combined with reputation and categories; CompTIA writes Universal, the standard term is Uniform Resource Locator

Definition: Content categorization groups websites into categories such as news, social media, gambling, adult or malware, so policy can allow or block whole categories instead of individual sites.
Example: The company blocks the gambling and adult categories and limits social media to the marketing team.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: Policy by category is easier to manage than per site; categories are maintained by the filter vendor; miscategorized sites may need manual overrides

Definition: Block rules are web filter policies that deny access to specific URLs, domains, categories or content types, sometimes for specific users or groups.
Example: A block rule stops downloads of executable files from file-sharing sites for all users except IT.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: Can target URLs, categories, file types, users or groups; exceptions should be documented; deny lists can be bypassed by new sites, so pair with reputation

Definition: Reputation filtering rates a site, domain or IP address by its history and characteristics, such as age, past malware hosting or spam, and blocks or warns about risky ones even if they are not yet on a known bad list.
Example: A domain registered yesterday has no history and a poor reputation score, so the filter blocks it.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Web filter
Key Points: Catches new or unknown bad sites better than static lists; scores come from vendors and threat intelligence; good sites can occasionally get poor scores

Definition: Operating system security means centrally hardening and controlling operating systems, for example with Group Policy on Windows domains and SELinux mandatory access control on Linux.
Example: An admin uses Group Policy to block USB storage on Windows PCs and enables SELinux in enforcing mode on Linux servers.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Group Policy = Windows Active Directory central settings; SELinux = Linux mandatory access control; both enforce secure baselines at scale

Definition: Group Policy is the Windows Active Directory feature that applies settings to many users and computers from one place, such as password rules, software restrictions, firewall settings and device controls, through Group Policy Objects (GPOs).
Example: A GPO linked to the Finance organizational unit enforces screen lock after 5 minutes and blocks USB storage devices.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Operating system security
Key Points: Windows and Active Directory; applied via GPOs to sites, domains and OUs; main tool to deploy Windows secure baselines; not used on Linux (that is SELinux in this list)

Definition: Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) is a Linux security module that enforces mandatory access control: a central policy decides what each process and user may access, even if normal file permissions would allow more. It was originally developed by the NSA.
Example: A compromised web server process cannot read users' home directories because the SELinux policy restricts it to web content.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Operating system security
Key Points: Mandatory access control (MAC), not discretionary; limits damage from compromised services; modes: enforcing, permissive (logs only), disabled; Linux, not Windows

Definition: Implementing secure protocols means choosing encrypted, authenticated protocols instead of insecure ones, using their proper ports, and deciding how traffic is protected in transit.
Example: An organization replaces Telnet with SSH, FTP with SFTP, and HTTP with HTTPS across all systems.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Three parts: protocol selection, port selection, transport method; prefer encrypted versions; know insecure to secure pairs

Definition: Protocol selection is choosing the secure version of a protocol for a task, one that encrypts data and authenticates the parties, such as SSH over Telnet, HTTPS over HTTP, SFTP or FTPS over FTP, LDAPS over LDAP, SNMPv3 over SNMPv1/v2c, and IMAPS or POP3S over IMAP or POP3.
Example: A scan finds LDAP traffic sending passwords in clear text, so directory queries are moved to LDAPS.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Implementation of secure protocols
Key Points: Insecure protocols send data, including passwords, in clear text; know pairs: Telnet to SSH, HTTP to HTTPS, FTP to SFTP or FTPS, LDAP to LDAPS, SNMPv1/v2c to SNMPv3; a protocol choice is the real security decision, not the port

Definition: Port selection means using the right, standard port for each secure protocol and opening only those ports, such as 22 for SSH and SFTP, 443 for HTTPS, 636 for LDAPS, 993 for IMAPS, 995 for POP3S, and 465 (implicit TLS) or 587 (STARTTLS) for mail submission.
Example: The firewall allows TCP 993 for IMAPS but blocks TCP 143, so mail clients must use the encrypted protocol.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Implementation of secure protocols
Key Points: Know secure ports: SSH/SFTP 22, HTTPS 443, LDAPS 636, IMAPS 993, POP3S 995, FTPS 989/990; a nonstandard port is not real security; the port number does not guarantee the protocol is secure

Definition: Transport method is how data is protected while it travels, for example by using TLS for an application's connection, a VPN tunnel such as IPsec to protect all traffic between sites, or strong wireless encryption on Wi-Fi.
Example: Branch offices connect to headquarters through an IPsec VPN so all traffic between sites is encrypted, even for older applications.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Implementation of secure protocols
Key Points: TLS protects one application connection; a VPN (IPsec, TLS VPN) protects everything in the tunnel; choose based on what needs protecting; protects data in transit

Definition: DNS filtering blocks access to malicious or disallowed domains by refusing to resolve their names, or by returning a safe address instead, so devices never connect to them. It works for any application that uses DNS, not only web browsers.
Example: Malware on a laptop tries to look up its command-and-control domain, but the DNS filter returns no address, so the connection fails.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Blocks at name resolution, before any connection; covers all applications that use DNS; can be bypassed by direct IP addresses or outside DNS servers, so block other DNS; vs web filter, which inspects web requests

Definition: Email security protects against spoofing, phishing, spam and malware in email. Security+ lists DMARC, DKIM and SPF, which are DNS-published records that help receivers verify who really sent a message, plus email gateways that filter mail.
Example: A company publishes SPF and DKIM records, sets a DMARC reject policy, and routes all mail through a secure email gateway.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: SPF = which servers may send for the domain; DKIM = cryptographic signature proves the message is from the domain and unchanged; DMARC = policy for failures plus reporting, needs SPF or DKIM to pass and align; gateway = filtering

items.front: Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
items.back:
Definition: DMARC is a DNS TXT record that tells receiving mail servers what to do with messages that fail authentication for a domain (none, quarantine or reject) and where to send reports. A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and the passing domain matches (aligns with) the visible From domain.
Example: A company publishes a DMARC policy of p=reject, so spoofed emails claiming to be from its domain are rejected, and it receives daily reports of the failures.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Email security
Key Points: Builds on SPF and DKIM, does not replace them; policies: none (monitor), quarantine, reject; adds reporting and From-domain alignment; published at _dmarc.domain

Definition: DKIM lets the sending mail server add a digital signature to each message using a private key; the receiver gets the matching public key from the sender's DNS and verifies that the message came from that domain and the signed parts were not altered.
Example: A receiving server checks the DKIM signature on an invoice email and finds it valid, confirming it was signed by the vendor's domain and not changed in transit.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Email security
Key Points: Signature in the email header, public key in DNS (selector._domainkey); proves domain origin and integrity of signed content; does not encrypt the message; vs SPF, which checks the sending server's IP

Definition: SPF is a DNS TXT record listing which mail servers or IP addresses are allowed to send email for a domain. Receivers check whether the sending server is on the list and can treat mail from other servers as suspicious.
Example: Spam claiming to be from the company is sent from an IP not in the company's SPF record, so receiving servers fail the SPF check.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Email security
Key Points: Checks the sending server IP against an authorized list published as a DNS TXT record; checks the envelope sender domain, not the visible From address (DMARC alignment covers that); forwarding can break SPF; "-all" means hard fail, "~all" soft fail

Definition: An email gateway (secure email gateway) is a system that all inbound and outbound mail passes through, filtering spam, phishing and malware, checking SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and often applying DLP and encryption policies.
Example: The email gateway strips a malicious macro attachment and quarantines a phishing message before it reaches the user's inbox.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security > Email security
Key Points: Can be on premises or cloud based; filters in both directions; enforces SPF/DKIM/DMARC results; may sandbox attachments and rewrite links

Definition: File integrity monitoring watches important files, such as system files, configuration files and application binaries, for unauthorized changes, usually by comparing hashes to a known-good baseline, and alerts when something changes.
Example: FIM alerts that a web server's login page file changed outside a maintenance window, revealing an attacker's inserted credential stealer.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Detects changes using hashes compared to a baseline; examples: Tripwire, Windows System File Checker; required by some standards such as PCI DSS; legitimate changes must be expected to avoid false alerts

Definition: As an enterprise capability, data loss prevention (DLP) is configured with policies that find sensitive data on endpoints, in network traffic, in email and in cloud services, and then block, encrypt, quarantine or alert when it would leave the organization improperly.
Example: A DLP policy blocks copying files labeled Confidential to USB drives and encrypts outbound emails containing credit card numbers.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Modify policies for the data types the business holds (card numbers, health data, labels); endpoint, network, email and cloud DLP; actions: block, alert, encrypt, quarantine; 4.4 covers DLP as a monitoring tool

Definition: NAC decides whether a device may join the network, and which part of it, by checking identity and posture (for example patch level, antivirus status, encryption) before granting access. Noncompliant devices can be blocked or sent to a remediation network.
Example: A visitor's laptop without current antivirus is placed on a quarantine VLAN until it is updated, while compliant company laptops get full access.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Uses 802.1X for identity plus posture assessment; persistent agent, dissolvable agent or agentless checks; noncompliant goes to quarantine or remediation VLAN; controls access before and after connection

Definition: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) records detailed activity on endpoints, detects threats with behavior analysis rather than only signatures, and lets responders investigate and act, for example isolating a host or rolling back changes. Extended detection and response (XDR) correlates data from endpoints plus network, cloud, email and identity sources for a broader view.
Example: EDR detects ransomware-like file encryption behavior on a laptop, kills the process, isolates the device and shows the attack timeline.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: EDR = endpoints only, behavior-based, investigation and automated response; XDR = many sources (endpoint, network, cloud, email); both go beyond signature antivirus

Definition: User behavior analytics builds a baseline of normal activity for each user, such as login times, locations, systems used and data volumes, and flags significant deviations that could indicate compromised accounts or insider threats. When it also covers devices and other entities it is called UEBA.
Example: UBA flags an accountant who normally works 9 to 5 locally but is suddenly downloading large amounts of engineering data at 2 a.m. from a new country.
Category: 4.5 Enhancing enterprise security
Key Points: Baseline of normal, then alert on anomalies; good at finding compromised credentials and insider threats; often uses machine learning; UEBA adds entities such as devices

items.front: SY0-701 4.6: Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management
items.back:
Definition: Objective 4.6 covers managing who can get in and what they can do: creating and removing accounts, verifying identities, single sign-on and federation, access control models, multifactor authentication, password policy and privileged access management.
Example: A scenario describes a contractor who still has VPN access a month after leaving and asks which IAM process failed (de-provisioning).
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management
Key Points: Scenario objective: pick the right control for the situation; Know the access control models apart (MAC, DAC, RBAC, rule-based, ABAC); Know SAML vs OAuth vs LDAP and federation vs SSO; MFA factors include somewhere you are

Definition: Provisioning creates an account and grants the access a person needs when they join or change roles. De-provisioning disables or removes the account and its access when they leave or no longer need it.
Example: HR marks an employee as terminated and the identity system disables their directory account, email and VPN access the same afternoon.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Provisioning/de-provisioning user accounts
Key Points: Grant only what the role needs at provisioning; De-provisioning promptly on departure prevents orphaned accounts; Disable first, delete later, so data and audit trails are kept; Often automated from the HR system

Definition: How rights are granted to users and groups, and the security effects of those choices. Excess or accumulated permissions widen the damage a compromised or careless account can do.
Example: An employee who moved from finance to marketing still has finance share access because old rights were never removed: privilege creep.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Permission assignments and implications
Key Points: Assign permissions to groups or roles, not individuals; Watch for privilege creep after role changes; Periodic access reviews catch excess rights; Over-permissioned accounts raise impact of compromise

Definition: Verifying that a person really is who they claim to be before issuing them an identity or credentials, for example by checking government ID or confirming known personal details.
Example: A bank asks a new online customer to photograph their passport and take a live selfie before opening the account.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Identity proofing
Key Points: Happens before credentials are issued; Differs from authentication, which checks a credential each login; NIST SP 800-63A defines identity assurance levels for proofing; Also used for account recovery

Definition: A trust relationship between separate organizations or domains that lets users authenticate with their home identity provider and access another party's services without a separate account there.
Example: Employees use their company login to access a partner's supplier portal, because the partner trusts the company's identity provider.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Federation
Key Points: Federation crosses organizational or domain boundaries; SSO is one login for many apps, usually within one organization; Built on standards like SAML, OAuth and OpenID Connect; 'Sign in with Google' on a third-party site is federation

Definition: Authenticating once and then accessing many applications or systems without logging in again. Protocols that support it include LDAP-backed directories, Kerberos, OAuth and SAML.
Example: A user signs in to the company portal in the morning and opens email, HR and the ticketing system without further password prompts.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Single sign-on (SSO)
Key Points: One authentication, many resources; Convenient but a stolen SSO credential opens everything, so pair it with MFA; Listed protocols: LDAP, OAuth, SAML; Federation extends SSO-like access across organizations

Definition: A protocol for reading and updating a directory of users, groups and devices, such as Active Directory. Applications query or bind to the directory to look up and verify identities.
Example: A web app checks a user's credentials and group membership against the company's Active Directory over LDAP.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Single sign-on (SSO) > LDAP
Key Points: LDAP uses TCP 389; LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) uses 636; Directory protocol, organized as a tree with distinguished names; Unlike SAML and OAuth it is not web-token based; Plain LDAP binds can send credentials in cleartext

Definition: An authorization framework that lets a user grant an application limited access to their resources on another service using access tokens, without sharing their password. It handles authorization, not authentication by itself.
Example: A photo printing site asks permission to read your cloud photo album; you approve and it receives a token limited to that album.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Single sign-on (SSO) > OAuth
Key Points: OAuth is about authorization (delegated access via tokens); OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of OAuth 2.0; Common for web and mobile apps and APIs; Contrast SAML (XML assertions, authn and authz, enterprise web SSO)

Definition: An XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP), commonly used for browser-based enterprise SSO and federation.
Example: An employee opens a cloud HR app, is redirected to the corporate IdP to log in, and returns with a signed SAML assertion that logs them in.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Single sign-on (SSO) > SAML
Key Points: XML assertions passed from IdP to SP; Provides authentication and authorization; Built for web browsers, not designed for native mobile apps; OAuth uses tokens for delegated authorization, LDAP queries a directory; The OASIS standard name is Security Assertion Markup Language (singular); the outline writes Assertions

Definition: The ability of different identity systems, vendors and platforms to work together, usually by supporting common standards so identities and access decisions can be shared.
Example: A company chooses a cloud app that supports SAML and SCIM so it works with their existing identity provider instead of needing separate accounts.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Interoperability
Key Points: Achieved through open standards (SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect, LDAP); Required for federation and SSO across vendors; Check protocol support before buying a service; Poor interoperability leads to duplicate, unmanaged accounts

Definition: Confirming a claim with evidence. In SY0-701 identity management it means verifying a user's identity claims with extra details, such as a passport or driver's license, an in-person meeting or questions drawn from credit history. Study material also uses it for access attestation (managers periodically certify each user's access is still needed) and device attestation (a TPM proves a device and its boot state are trusted).
Example: Before a new remote employee's account is activated, they show their passport on a video call and answer questions about past addresses from their credit report.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Attestation
Key Points: Identity attestation: extra evidence (ID documents, in-person check, credit-history questions) that the person is who they claim; Works alongside identity proofing when an account is created; Access attestation: periodic review or recertification of who has access; Device attestation: a TPM-signed report proves the hardware and boot state

Definition: The rules and models that decide what an authenticated subject may do with a resource. Listed models and constraints: mandatory, discretionary, role-based, rule-based, attribute-based, time-of-day restrictions and least privilege.
Example: A hospital uses roles for nurses and doctors, adds a rule that blocks logins outside shifts, and grants each role only the records it needs.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls
Key Points: MAC: labels set by administrators; DAC: owner decides; RBAC: job role; Rule-based: admin rules applied to all; ABAC: many attributes; Time-of-day and least privilege restrict any model

Definition: An access control model where the operating system enforces access using security labels on data (such as Secret) and clearances on users. Only administrators set labels; users cannot change or share access.
Example: A government system lets an analyst with Secret clearance open Secret and Confidential files but not Top Secret ones.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Mandatory
Key Points: Labels and clearance levels; Users cannot override or delegate; Most strict, common in military and government; Look for 'classification' or 'clearance' in the question

Definition: An access control model where the owner of a resource decides who can access it and with what rights.
Example: A user who created a file share grants read access to two colleagues and full control to their manager.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Discretionary
Key Points: Owner sets permissions; Flexible but weak central control; Typical of Windows NTFS and Unix file permissions; Look for 'owner' or 'creator' in the question
