Definition: An access control model where permissions are assigned to roles that match job functions, and users get access by being placed in a role.
Example: Every new help desk technician is added to the Help Desk group and automatically gets password reset rights and ticket system access.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Role-based
Key Points: Access follows job function; Usually implemented with groups; Simplifies onboarding and role changes; Do not confuse with rule-based, which uses admin-defined conditions for everyone

Definition: An access control model where an administrator defines rules or conditions that are applied to all access attempts, regardless of who the user is.
Example: A firewall ACL allows traffic to the web server only on TCP 443, or a lab PC denies all logins after 6 p.m.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Rule-based
Key Points: System-wide rules set by admins, not per role; Firewall ACLs are the classic example; Sometimes also abbreviated RBAC, so read the full name; Not role-based (job function) and not ABAC (many combined attributes)

Definition: An access control model that decides access by evaluating attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, such as department, data sensitivity, device, location and time.
Example: A policy allows access to a customer file only if the user is in Sales, on a managed device, inside the country and during business hours.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Attribute-based
Key Points: Combines many attributes in one policy; Most granular and context-aware model; Look for several conditions evaluated together; Rule-based uses simple fixed rules, RBAC uses only the role

Definition: Limiting when an account or resource can be used, such as allowing logins only during working hours or shifts.
Example: Training lab accounts can log in only between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on weekdays; a 2 a.m. login attempt is blocked.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Time-of-day restrictions
Key Points: Reduces window for misuse of stolen credentials; Can be applied within any access model; A form of rule or attribute condition; Off-hours login attempts are also a useful alert

Definition: Granting users, services and processes only the minimum rights they need to do their job, and only for as long as they need them.
Example: A web application's service account can read and write its own database tables but cannot create users or access other databases.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Access controls > Least privilege
Key Points: Limits the impact of a compromised account; Remove rights when no longer needed (fights privilege creep); Admins use a normal account for daily work; Just-in-time permissions put least privilege into practice

Definition: Authentication that requires two or more different factor types, such as something you know plus something you have. Two items from the same factor type do not count as MFA.
Example: A user enters their password and then approves a code from an authenticator app on their phone.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication
Key Points: Factors must be different types: password plus PIN is still one factor; Factors: know, have, are, somewhere you are; Implementations: biometrics, hard or soft tokens, security keys; Defeats most password-only attacks

Definition: The concrete technologies used to deliver an MFA factor. The objectives list biometrics, hardware and software authentication tokens, and security keys.
Example: A company issues FIDO2 security keys to administrators and an authenticator app to everyone else.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Implementations
Key Points: Biometrics deliver something you are; Tokens and security keys deliver something you have; Security keys resist phishing best; Choose by cost, usability and risk

Definition: Authentication based on a measured physical or behavioral trait, such as a fingerprint, face, iris, voice or typing pattern.
Example: A laptop unlocks with a fingerprint reader after the user enters a PIN.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Implementations > Biometrics
Key Points: Delivers the something you are factor; False acceptance rate (FAR) vs false rejection rate (FRR), crossover error rate (CER) compares systems; A biometric cannot be changed if stolen; Often stored as a template, not an image

Definition: Tokens that generate one-time passcodes. A hard token is a dedicated physical device; a soft token is an app on a phone or computer. Codes are usually time-based (TOTP) or counter-based (HOTP).
Example: A user reads a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds from an authenticator app and types it after their password.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Implementations > Hard/soft authentication tokens
Key Points: Both are something you have; Hard token: key fob device; soft token: authenticator app; TOTP changes with time, HOTP with each use; SMS codes are weaker (SIM swapping)

Definition: Small physical devices, usually USB or NFC, that perform cryptographic authentication with standards such as FIDO2 or U2F. The private key never leaves the device.
Example: An administrator taps a USB security key when signing in to the cloud console; a fake phishing site cannot use the response.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Implementations > Security keys
Key Points: Something you have; Phishing-resistant because each credential is bound to the real site's domain; Uses public key cryptography, no code to type; Lost keys need a backup key or recovery process

Definition: The categories of evidence used to prove identity. SY0-701 lists something you know, something you have, something you are and somewhere you are.
Example: Password (know) plus phone app (have) plus login allowed only from the office network (somewhere you are).
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Factors
Key Points: MFA needs two or more different categories; Somewhere you are counts as a factor on SY0-701; Something you do (behavior) is sometimes discussed but is not on this list; Two passwords are still single-factor

Definition: A secret the user remembers, such as a password, PIN, passphrase or security question answer.
Example: Entering a PIN at an ATM after inserting the bank card.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Factors > Something you know
Key Points: Passwords, PINs, patterns, security questions; Weakest alone: can be guessed, phished or reused; A PIN is know, the card is have

Definition: A physical or digital item in the user's possession, such as a smart card, hardware token, security key or phone with an authenticator app.
Example: Inserting a smart card into a reader to log in to a workstation.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Factors > Something you have
Key Points: Smart cards, tokens, security keys, phones; Can be lost or stolen, so pair with another factor; An OTP from an app proves possession of the phone

Definition: A biometric characteristic of the user's body, such as fingerprint, face, iris, retina or voice.
Example: Unlocking a phone with facial recognition.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Factors > Something you are
Key Points: Biometrics; Cannot be changed if compromised; Accuracy measured with FAR, FRR and CER; Not the same as somewhere you are (location)

Definition: A factor based on the user's location, determined by IP address, GPS or network, used to allow, deny or require extra checks for an authentication.
Example: A login from the office network is allowed, but the same account logging in from another country is blocked.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Multifactor authentication > Factors > Somewhere you are
Key Points: Counts as an authentication factor on SY0-701; Uses IP geolocation, GPS or the connected network; Usually supports other factors rather than standing alone; Basis for geofencing and impossible travel alerts

Definition: The objective's password topics: best practices for password policy (length, complexity, reuse, expiration, age), password managers, and passwordless authentication.
Example: A policy requires 14-character passphrases, blocks reuse of the last 24 passwords and encourages a company password manager.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts
Key Points: Length is the strongest single control; Expiration is maximum age, age is minimum age; Password managers enable unique passwords; Passwordless removes the shared secret entirely

Definition: Policy settings that make passwords harder to guess or reuse: minimum length, complexity requirements, preventing reuse, expiration and minimum age.
Example: A domain password policy sets minimum length 12, remembers 10 previous passwords and has a minimum age of 1 day.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices
Key Points: Exam settings: length, complexity, reuse, expiration, age; Current NIST SP 800-63B guidance favors length and breached-password checks over forced complexity and routine expiration; Still know each setting for the exam

Definition: The minimum number of characters a password must have. Each added character greatly increases the number of possible passwords, so length is the strongest defense against brute force.
Example: Raising the minimum from 8 to 14 characters so users choose passphrases like a short sentence.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices > Length
Key Points: Longer beats more complex; Passphrases make long passwords memorable; Brute force time grows exponentially with length

Definition: A requirement that passwords mix character types, such as uppercase, lowercase, numbers and symbols, to enlarge the character set an attacker must try.
Example: A policy rejects 'summertime' but accepts 'Summer!time7'.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices > Complexity
Key Points: Expands character set; Users fall into predictable patterns (Capital first, ! at the end); Length usually adds more strength than complexity; Distinct from complexity as an automation consideration

Definition: Preventing users from using the same password again, enforced by a password history, and discouraging the same password across different sites.
Example: The system remembers the last 12 passwords and rejects a change back to any of them.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices > Reuse
Key Points: Enforced with password history; Reuse across sites enables credential stuffing; Minimum age stops users cycling through history to get back to an old password

Definition: The maximum time a password can be used before the user must change it, also called maximum password age.
Example: Passwords expire every 90 days and users are prompted to set a new one.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices > Expiration
Key Points: Expiration equals maximum age: forces a change; Age (minimum age) limits how soon a change is allowed; NIST SP 800-63B now advises changing only on evidence of compromise

Definition: The minimum password age: how long a user must keep a new password before changing it again. It stops users from changing repeatedly to cycle past the history and reuse an old password.
Example: Minimum age is 1 day, so a user cannot change their password 12 times in an afternoon to get back to their favorite one.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password best practices > Age
Key Points: Minimum age works with password history to prevent reuse; Not the same as expiration (maximum age); Classic exam trap: 'users keep reusing old passwords despite history' points to minimum age

Definition: Applications that generate, store and fill strong unique passwords in an encrypted vault protected by one master password or other strong authentication.
Example: An employee uses the company password manager to create a random 24-character password for each vendor site.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Password managers
Key Points: Make unique, long passwords practical; Stop reuse across sites; Protect the vault with a strong master password and MFA; A user tool; PAM password vaulting is the enterprise version for privileged accounts

Definition: Authentication without a typed password, using methods such as biometrics, security keys, passkeys or a push approval on a trusted device.
Example: A user signs in to a laptop with Windows Hello face recognition and to websites with a passkey on their phone.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Password concepts > Passwordless
Key Points: Removes passwords that can be phished, guessed or reused; Often based on FIDO2 and public key cryptography; Can still be multifactor (device plus biometric or PIN); Requires a recovery plan for lost devices

Definition: Tools that secure, control and monitor accounts with elevated rights, such as administrators and service accounts. Listed features: just-in-time permissions, password vaulting and ephemeral credentials.
Example: Admins request domain admin rights through the PAM tool, which checks out a vaulted password for one hour and records the session.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Privileged access management tools
Key Points: Protects the most valuable accounts; Features: JIT, vaulting, ephemeral credentials, session recording; Enforces least privilege for admins; Gives an audit trail of privileged actions

Definition: Granting elevated permissions only when they are requested and approved, for a limited time, then removing them automatically.
Example: A database admin requests admin rights to apply a patch; access is approved for two hours and then revoked.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Privileged access management tools > Just-in-time permissions
Key Points: No standing admin rights; Time-limited and usually approved; Shrinks the window an attacker can use; Contrast ephemeral credentials, which are temporary accounts or secrets

Definition: Storing privileged account passwords in a secure, access-controlled vault where they are checked out when needed, often rotated after use, and every access is logged.
Example: No one knows the root password of the production servers; admins check it out from the vault, and it is changed automatically afterward.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Privileged access management tools > Password vaulting
Key Points: Central, encrypted, audited storage; Check-in and check-out with automatic rotation; Removes shared passwords in spreadsheets; Enterprise privileged counterpart of a password manager

Definition: Temporary credentials created for a single session or task that expire automatically after a short time and cannot be reused.
Example: A cloud automation job receives access keys valid for 15 minutes; after the job they are useless.
Category: 4.6 Identity and access management > Privileged access management tools > Ephemeral credentials
Key Points: Short-lived, created on demand; Nothing long-term to steal; Common in cloud (temporary tokens) and PAM; JIT grants rights to an account, ephemeral creates a throwaway credential

items.front: SY0-701 4.7: Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations
items.back:
Definition: Objective 4.7 covers why security teams automate repetitive tasks with scripts and orchestrate them across tools: the use cases, the benefits and the considerations or risks that come with automation.
Example: A question asks which benefit an organization gains by scripting account creation from HR records (efficiency, enforcing baselines, reaction time).
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration
Key Points: Automation: one task done by script; orchestration: many automated tasks coordinated across systems; Know use cases, benefits and other considerations lists; Risks: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, supportability

items.front: Use cases of automation and scripting (security operations)
items.back:
Definition: Common security tasks worth automating: user and resource provisioning, guard rails, security groups, ticket creation, escalation, enabling or disabling services and access, continuous integration and testing, and integrations through APIs.
Example: A script creates a ticket, adds the new hire to the right security groups and builds their virtual desktop from a template.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases of automation and scripting
Key Points: Best for repetitive, rule-based, high-volume tasks; Scripts and APIs connect tools; Reduce human error and delay

Definition: Automatically creating, changing and removing user accounts and their access based on a trusted source such as the HR system.
Example: When HR enters a new hire, a workflow creates the directory account, mailbox and group memberships before day one.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > User provisioning
Key Points: Consistent access for each role; Fast, reliable de-provisioning at exit; Removes manual errors and forgotten accounts

Definition: Automatically creating and removing infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage, containers and network settings, often from templates or infrastructure as code.
Example: A developer requests a test server and a script builds a hardened VM from the approved image in minutes, then deletes it after the project.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Resource provisioning
Key Points: Every build matches the secure template; Decommissioning stops unused, unpatched resources; Often done with infrastructure as code

Definition: Automated checks and limits that keep actions within safe, approved boundaries, blocking or correcting changes that would break policy.
Example: A cloud policy automatically blocks anyone from making a storage bucket public and reverts the change if it happens.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Guard rails
Key Points: Prevent mistakes before they happen; Enforce policy without a manual review every time; Examples: blocking public storage, denying unapproved regions or open ports

Definition: Automatically assigning and removing users or resources from security groups that control access, including cloud security groups that act as virtual firewalls.
Example: A script moves an employee from the Sales group to the Marketing group when HR records a transfer, removing old access at the same time.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Security groups
Key Points: Group membership drives access, so automate it; Prevents privilege creep on role changes; Cloud security groups filter traffic to instances

Definition: Automatically opening tickets in the help desk or incident system when an event occurs, filled with the relevant details.
Example: A SIEM alert for repeated failed logins automatically opens a ticket with the source IP, account and log excerpts.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Ticket creation
Key Points: No alert is lost or forgotten; Tickets carry consistent details; Starts the tracking and audit trail at once

Definition: Automatically routing an issue to a higher tier, a specialist or management when it meets set conditions such as severity or time unresolved.
Example: A critical malware alert that is not acknowledged within 15 minutes pages the on-call incident responder.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Escalation
Key Points: Right people notified quickly; Based on severity and time rules; Prevents important alerts sitting in a queue

items.front: Enabling and disabling services and access (automation use case)
items.back:
Definition: Automatically turning services, ports or account access on or off in response to events, schedules or policy.
Example: When an endpoint tool detects ransomware behavior, automation disables the user's account and isolates the host from the network.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Enabling/disabling services and access
Key Points: Fast containment response; Can enforce schedules (access only when needed); Often triggered by SOAR playbooks

items.front: Continuous integration and testing (automation use case)
items.back:
Definition: Automatically building and testing code each time developers commit changes, including security tests such as static analysis and dependency scanning.
Example: Every code commit triggers a pipeline that runs unit tests and a vulnerability scan; the build fails if a critical flaw is found.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Continuous integration and testing
Key Points: Problems found early, when cheaper to fix; Security checks run every time, not occasionally; Part of a DevSecOps pipeline

items.front: Integrations and application programming interfaces (APIs) (automation use case)
items.back:
Definition: Using APIs to connect different security and IT tools so they share data and trigger actions in each other without manual steps.
Example: A SOAR platform calls the firewall's API to block an IP address that the threat intelligence feed flagged.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Use cases > Integrations and APIs
Key Points: APIs are the glue of orchestration; Let tools from different vendors work together; Protect API keys and limit their permissions

items.front: Benefits of security automation and orchestration
items.back:
Definition: The gains from automating security work: efficiency and time saving, enforcing baselines, standard infrastructure configurations, scaling securely, employee retention, faster reaction time and acting as a workforce multiplier.
Example: After automating patch deployment and account changes, a small team handles twice the systems with fewer errors.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits
Key Points: Speed and consistency are the core gains; Fewer human errors; Staff freed for higher-value work; Weigh against the other considerations (cost, complexity, debt)

Definition: Automation finishes repetitive tasks faster and with less effort than people doing them by hand.
Example: Account setup that took a technician 30 minutes now runs in under a minute.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Efficiency/time saving
Key Points: Less manual work per task; Frees staff for analysis; Fewer mistakes from repetition

Definition: Automation checks systems against a security baseline and applies or restores the approved settings, keeping configurations from drifting.
Example: A configuration tool runs nightly and resets any server whose firewall settings have changed from the hardened baseline.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Enforcing baselines
Key Points: Detects and fixes configuration drift; Applies the same security settings everywhere; Supports compliance evidence

Definition: Building systems from the same templates or code so every server, network device or cloud resource is configured identically.
Example: All web servers are deployed from one infrastructure-as-code template, so none is missing the logging agent.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Standard infrastructure configurations
Key Points: Identical, predictable builds; Easier troubleshooting and auditing; Baselines keep them that way afterward

items.front: Scaling in a secure manner (automation benefit)
items.back:
Definition: Automation lets an organization add many systems or users quickly while each one still receives the correct security settings.
Example: During a sales peak, auto-scaling adds 50 web servers, each built from the hardened image and joined to monitoring.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Scaling in a secure manner
Key Points: Growth without skipping security steps; Every new instance gets the same controls; Manual processes break down at scale

Definition: Automating tedious, repetitive work reduces burnout and lets staff do more interesting work, so skilled people are more likely to stay.
Example: Analysts no longer spend their days closing duplicate alerts by hand and instead work on threat hunting.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Employee retention
Key Points: Less boring repetitive work; Reduces burnout and turnover; Keeps skilled staff on valuable tasks

Definition: Automated detection and response acts in seconds, much faster than a person who must notice, decide and act.
Example: A playbook isolates an infected laptop seconds after the alert, before the malware spreads.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Reaction time
Key Points: Response at machine speed, any hour; Limits damage and spread; Key value of SOAR playbooks

Definition: Automation lets a fixed number of staff accomplish the work of a much larger team.
Example: A three-person SOC monitors thousands of endpoints because enrichment and triage are automated.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Benefits > Workforce multiplier
Key Points: Same team, more output; Helps with security staff shortages; Different from efficiency per task: it is about team capacity

Definition: The drawbacks and risks to weigh before automating: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt and ongoing supportability.
Example: A team weighs whether a homegrown script that only one engineer understands is worth the maintenance burden.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations
Key Points: Automation is not free or risk-free; Plan for maintenance and failure; These are the 'cons' list on the exam

Definition: Automated workflows and integrations can become complicated to build, understand, troubleshoot and change, which can itself introduce errors.
Example: A chain of scripts across five tools fails silently and nobody can tell where the break is.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations > Complexity
Key Points: More moving parts, harder troubleshooting; Needs documentation and testing; Distinct from complexity as a password best practice

Definition: Automation requires spending on tools, licenses, development time and training before it pays back.
Example: A SOAR platform license and integration project cost more in the first year than the hours it saved.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations > Cost
Key Points: Upfront and ongoing costs; Compare to the time and risk saved; Includes staff time to build and maintain

Definition: When many processes depend on one automation system or script, its failure can stop all of them at once.
Example: The orchestration server goes down and no new accounts, tickets or firewall changes are processed until it is fixed.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations > Single point of failure
Key Points: Central automation can halt everything if it fails; Plan redundancy and manual fallback procedures; Also a risk if one person alone understands it

Definition: The future cost of quick fixes, shortcuts or poorly designed scripts that must later be reworked, patched or replaced.
Example: Hard-coded paths and credentials in old scripts break after a server migration and need a full rewrite.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations > Technical debt
Key Points: Shortcuts now, extra work later; Grows when scripts are not maintained; Can create security risks such as hard-coded secrets

Definition: Automation must be maintained over time as systems, APIs and staff change, and someone must be able to support and update it.
Example: A vendor changes its API and the integration stops working; the original author has left and there is no documentation.
Category: 4.7 Automation and orchestration > Other considerations > Ongoing supportability
Key Points: Plan who maintains each script; Document and version-control automation; Updates are needed when tools change

items.front: SY0-701 4.8: Explain appropriate incident response activities
items.back:
Definition: Objective 4.8 covers the incident response process from preparation to lessons learned, training and testing the plan, root cause analysis, threat hunting and digital forensics activities.
Example: A question asks what an analyst should do right after isolating an infected server (eradication: remove the malware).
Category: 4.8 Incident response
Key Points: Memorize the process order: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned; Tabletop is discussion, simulation is hands-on; Legal hold preserves, chain of custody documents handling

Definition: The ordered phases CompTIA lists for handling an incident: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
Example: A phishing compromise is spotted, investigated, the account is locked, the malware removed, the user's laptop restored and the team then meets to improve email filtering.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process
Key Points: Order matters: contain before eradicate, eradicate before recover; The older NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 grouped detection with analysis and containment with eradication and recovery (Rev. 3, April 2025, now follows the CSF 2.0 functions); The exam uses CompTIA's seven-phase list; Lessons learned feed back into preparation

Definition: The phase before any incident: writing the plan, forming and training the team, setting up communication methods and getting tools, contact lists and baselines ready.
Example: The security team builds a jump kit with forensic laptops and write blockers and keeps an up-to-date call list.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Preparation
Key Points: First phase; happens before an incident; Includes IR plan, roles, tools, training, communication plan; Lessons learned feed improvements back here

Definition: Recognizing that an incident may be happening, from alerts, logs, monitoring tools or user reports.
Example: The SIEM raises an alert for a workstation contacting a known malicious domain.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Detection
Key Points: Sources: SIEM, IDS/IPS, EDR, users, third parties; Many events, few true incidents; Comes before analysis confirms and scopes it

Definition: Investigating detected events to confirm whether an incident is real, and determining its scope, type, impact and priority.
Example: An analyst correlates firewall and endpoint logs to confirm the alert is real malware and finds two more infected hosts.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Analysis
Key Points: Separates true incidents from false positives; Determines scope and severity to prioritize; Indicators of compromise guide the investigation

Definition: Limiting the spread and damage of an incident, for example by isolating systems, disabling accounts or blocking traffic, while preserving evidence.
Example: The infected hosts are moved to an isolated VLAN so they cannot reach other systems.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Containment
Key Points: Stop the spread first; Comes before eradication; Isolation or segmentation, account lockout, blocking IPs; Sandboxing a sample is also a containment technique

Definition: Removing the cause of the incident from the environment: deleting malware, closing exploited vulnerabilities, removing attacker accounts and backdoors.
Example: Technicians wipe the infected drives, patch the exploited VPN flaw and delete the rogue admin account.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Eradication
Key Points: Containment stops spread, eradication removes the threat; Fix the vulnerability so it cannot recur; Comes before recovery

Definition: Restoring affected systems to normal operation, such as rebuilding or restoring from clean backups, and monitoring to confirm the threat is gone.
Example: Servers are rebuilt from the golden image, data is restored from last night's backup and extra monitoring watches for reinfection.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Recovery
Key Points: Return to normal operations; Restore from known-good backups and images; Verify and monitor before declaring done

Definition: The final phase: a post-incident review of what happened, what worked and what to improve, done soon after the incident while details are fresh.
Example: A week after the breach, the team meets and decides to add MFA to the VPN and update the IR plan's contact list.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Process > Lessons learned
Key Points: Last phase; also called post-incident activity; Hold it soon after the incident; Improvements go back into preparation

Definition: Teaching incident response team members and other staff their roles, procedures and tools so they can act correctly during a real incident.
Example: New SOC analysts complete training on the IR plan, evidence handling and escalation contacts before joining the on-call rotation.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Training
Key Points: Covers responders, management and general staff; Part of preparation; Differs from testing, which checks the plan works

Definition: Exercising the incident response plan to find gaps before a real incident. The objectives list tabletop exercises and simulations.
Example: Twice a year the organization runs one discussion-based exercise and one hands-on simulation of a ransomware attack.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Testing
Key Points: Validates the plan and the team's readiness; Tabletop: talk through it; Simulation: perform it; Results feed plan updates

Definition: A discussion-based exercise where key people walk through a hypothetical incident scenario step by step and talk about how they would respond, without touching real systems.
Example: Executives and IT sit in a conference room while a facilitator describes a ransomware outbreak and asks each person what they would do next.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Testing > Tabletop exercise
Key Points: Talk only, no systems affected; Low cost, low disruption; Good for checking roles and communication; Contrast simulation, which acts out the scenario

Definition: A hands-on exercise that mimics a real incident so responders carry out actual response steps with systems and tools, often in a test environment.
Example: The security team sends a fake phishing campaign and responders must detect, report and contain it as if it were real.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Testing > Simulation
Key Points: Hands-on, more realistic than a tabletop; Tests tools and technical procedures; Costs more and needs planning to avoid disrupting production

Definition: Determining the underlying reason an incident happened, not just its symptoms, so the real problem can be fixed and the incident does not recur.
Example: The malware came from a phishing email, but the root cause was that the mail gateway did not scan attachments of that file type.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Root cause analysis
Key Points: Find the cause, not the symptom; Methods include the five whys and cause-and-effect diagrams; Often done during or after eradication and in lessons learned

Definition: Proactively searching networks and systems for signs of threats that existing tools have not detected, often starting from a hypothesis or threat intelligence.
Example: After reading a report on a new attacker technique, an analyst searches endpoint logs for that behavior and finds a dormant backdoor.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Threat hunting
Key Points: Proactive, assumes a breach may already exist; Driven by hypotheses and threat intelligence; Differs from responding to alerts (reactive detection)

Definition: Collecting, preserving, analyzing and reporting digital evidence in a way that keeps it reliable and legally defensible. Listed activities: legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, reporting, preservation and e-discovery.
Example: After an insider data theft, investigators image the employee's laptop, hash the image and document every person who handles it.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics
Key Points: Evidence must stay unchanged and accounted for; Collect in order of volatility; Legal hold preserves data, chain of custody records handling; Work on copies, not originals

Definition: A formal instruction, usually from legal counsel, to preserve all data related to a case or expected lawsuit and suspend normal deletion or retention policies.
Example: Legal tells IT to stop auto-deleting a former manager's mailbox because the company expects a wrongful termination lawsuit.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > Legal hold
Key Points: Preserve, do not delete: overrides retention schedules; Triggered by litigation or expected litigation; Chain of custody is different: it documents who handled evidence

Definition: Documentation that records every person who collected, handled, transferred or stored a piece of evidence, with dates and times, proving it was not tampered with.
Example: A hard drive's evidence form shows it went from the responder to the evidence locker to the forensic lab, signed at each step.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > Chain of custody
Key Points: Who, when, where, why for every handling; Gaps can make evidence inadmissible; Hashes help prove integrity; Legal hold preserves data, chain of custody tracks it

Definition: Collecting evidence from systems, such as disk images, memory captures and logs, in a sound way and in order of volatility, from most to least volatile.
Example: A responder captures RAM from a running server first, then takes a bit-for-bit disk image using a write blocker.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > Acquisition
Key Points: Order of volatility: CPU registers and cache, then memory, then temporary files, then disk, then remote logs, then archives; Bit-for-bit images, hashed; Use write blockers

Definition: Documenting the forensic investigation and its findings: what was collected, how it was analyzed, the timeline and conclusions, written for its audience such as management or a court.
Example: The investigator writes a report with the timeline of the intrusion, the methods used and hashes proving the evidence was unaltered.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > Reporting
Key Points: Facts, methods, timeline, conclusions; Must be repeatable and defensible; Different from automated reports used as a data source in 4.9

Definition: Protecting evidence so it stays unchanged and available, for example by working on verified copies, using write blockers, hashing and storing originals securely.
Example: The original drive is sealed in an evidence bag in a locked locker, and analysts work only on a hashed image.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > Preservation
Key Points: Keep evidence intact and unaltered; Hash originals and copies to prove integrity; Analyze copies, store originals securely

Definition: The legal process of identifying, collecting and producing electronically stored information, such as email and documents, for a lawsuit or investigation.
Example: In a contract dispute, the company searches and hands over all email between two managers about the deal for a date range.
Category: 4.8 Incident response > Digital forensics > E-discovery
Key Points: Legal process of finding and handing over electronic data; Follows a legal hold that kept the data; Focuses on producing data, not on analyzing an attack

items.front: SY0-701 4.9: Given a scenario, use data sources to support an investigation
items.back:
Definition: Objective 4.9 covers choosing the right evidence for an investigation: the kinds of log data (firewall, application, endpoint, OS security, IDS/IPS, network, metadata) and other data sources (vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards, packet captures).
Example: A question asks which source shows the actual contents of a suspicious data transfer (packet capture).
Category: 4.9 Data sources for investigations
Key Points: Match the question to the source that holds that evidence; Logs show events, packet captures show full content; Metadata is data about data; A SIEM gathers many of these sources together

Definition: Records of events written by devices, systems and applications. Listed types: firewall, application, endpoint, OS-specific security, IPS/IDS and network logs, plus metadata.
Example: An analyst lines up firewall, VPN and Windows security logs to build a timeline of an attacker's login and movement.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data
Key Points: Logs record events with timestamps; Correlating several logs builds the timeline; Time synchronization (NTP) is essential; Usually collected in a SIEM

Definition: Records of traffic a firewall allowed or blocked, typically with source and destination IP addresses, ports, protocol, action and time.
Example: Firewall logs show an internal host making outbound connections to an unknown IP on port 4444 every few minutes.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > Firewall logs
Key Points: Shows who talked to whom, on which port, allowed or denied; Good for spotting scans and command-and-control traffic; Next-generation firewalls may log application and user too

Definition: Events recorded by a specific application, such as logins, errors, transactions and changes within that application.
Example: A web application's log shows hundreds of failed logins for different usernames from one IP address.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > Application logs
Key Points: Specific to one app (web server, database, custom software); Show actions inside the application; Format varies by vendor

Definition: Logs from user devices and servers, such as from endpoint protection or EDR agents, recording processes, file changes, logins and security detections on that host.
Example: EDR logs show a Word document launching PowerShell, which then downloaded a file to the user's temp folder.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > Endpoint logs
Key Points: Host-level detail: processes, files, users; Often from antivirus or EDR agents; Shows what happened on the device itself

Definition: Security events logged by the operating system itself, such as logons, privilege use, account changes and policy changes, for example the Windows Security event log or Linux authentication logs.
Example: The Windows Security log shows repeated failed logon events followed by a successful one for an admin account.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > OS-specific security logs
Key Points: Windows: Event Viewer Security log; Linux: auth or secure logs, journald; Track logons, account and permission changes; Format depends on the OS

items.front: Intrusion prevention system / intrusion detection system (IPS/IDS) logs
items.back:
Definition: Records of traffic that matched attack signatures or anomalies, showing what was detected and, for an IPS, whether it was blocked.
Example: IPS logs show a SQL injection attempt against the web server from an external IP, which was dropped.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > IPS/IDS logs
Key Points: Name the attack or signature matched; IDS only alerts, IPS can also block; Can include false positives that need analysis

Definition: Logs from network infrastructure such as switches, routers, wireless controllers, DNS, DHCP and VPN servers, recording connections, changes and device events.
Example: DHCP and switch logs show which device had a suspicious IP address at the time of the attack and which switch port it used.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > Network logs
Key Points: Infrastructure events: routing, interfaces, VPN, DHCP, DNS; Help locate a device and trace its path; Flow data (NetFlow) summarizes traffic without contents

Definition: Data that describes other data, such as email headers, file creation dates and authors, photo location tags, or connection details without content.
Example: An email header shows the message really came from an overseas mail server, not the CEO's account it claimed.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Log data > Metadata
Key Points: Data about data, not the content itself; Examples: email headers, file properties, photo EXIF data, mobile call records; Useful when content is encrypted or unavailable

Definition: Other information used in investigations besides logs: vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards and packet captures.
Example: An analyst uses the dashboard to spot a spike, a packet capture to see the traffic and the last vulnerability scan to see which flaw was exploited.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Data sources
Key Points: Pick the source that answers the question asked; Scans show weaknesses, captures show traffic content; Reports and dashboards summarize many sources

Definition: Scan results listing systems, open ports, missing patches and known vulnerabilities, which help investigators see how an attacker may have gotten in.
Example: An investigation into a compromised server finds the last scan had flagged its unpatched remote access service as critical.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Data sources > Vulnerability scans
Key Points: Show weaknesses, not what an attacker actually did; Help explain the likely entry point; Compare scans before and after an incident

Definition: Reports generated on a schedule or by trigger from tools such as a SIEM or vulnerability scanner, summarizing events, trends and findings.
Example: A daily SIEM report lists the top blocked IPs and accounts with the most failed logins, highlighting an ongoing password spray.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Data sources > Automated reports
Key Points: Created by tools, not written by hand; Summarize large volumes of data; Different from forensic reporting written by investigators

Definition: Real-time visual displays, often in a SIEM, that summarize key security information so analysts can spot trends and anomalies at a glance.
Example: A SOC dashboard shows outbound traffic suddenly tripling, prompting an investigation into data exfiltration.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Data sources > Dashboards
Key Points: Visual, near real-time summary; Good for spotting anomalies quickly; A starting point: details come from the underlying logs

Definition: Recordings of the actual network packets, including headers and payloads, collected with tools such as Wireshark or tcpdump.
Example: A packet capture shows an unencrypted file being sent to an external FTP server, revealing exactly what data left.
Category: 4.9 Data sources > Data sources > Packet captures
Key Points: Full content of traffic, the most detailed network evidence; Large storage needs; Encrypted traffic hides payloads; Logs and flow data show only that a connection happened

items.front: SY0-701 Domain 5.0: Security Program Management and Oversight (20%)
items.back:
Definition: The domain covering how a security program is governed, how risk is managed, how vendors are assessed, how compliance is proven, how audits and penetration tests work, and how users are trained. It is 20% of the SY0-701 exam.
Example: A CISO writes policies, keeps a risk register, signs an SLA with a cloud provider, reports compliance to a regulator, hires a pen test firm, and runs phishing simulations: all Domain 5 work.
Category: 5.0 Security Program Management and Oversight
Key Points: Six objectives: 5.1 governance, 5.2 risk management, 5.3 third-party risk, 5.4 compliance, 5.5 audits and assessments, 5.6 security awareness; Heavy on definitions and look-alikes (RTO vs RPO, MOU vs MOA, controller vs processor); Expect SLE/ALE math

items.front: SY0-701 5.1: Summarize elements of effective security governance
items.back:
Definition: Security governance is the framework of documents, structures and roles that directs and controls security: guidelines, policies, standards and procedures, external considerations, monitoring and revision, governance structures, and data roles.
Example: A company board approves an information security policy, a committee sets password standards, and IT writes the onboarding procedure that follows them.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Know the document hierarchy: policy (why, mandatory) > standard (what, mandatory, specific) > procedure (how, step by step), with guidelines optional; Know data roles: owner, controller, processor, custodian/steward; External drivers: regulatory, legal, industry, local to global

Definition: Recommended practices and advice that help people meet policies and standards. Guidelines are optional and flexible, not mandatory.
Example: A guideline suggests using a passphrase of four random words, while the password standard only requires 14 characters minimum.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Guidelines = recommended, not required; Standards and policies are mandatory, guidelines are not; Trap: a document saying "should" is a guideline, "must" is a policy or standard

Definition: High-level, management-approved statements of what the organization requires and why. Policies are mandatory and broad; standards and procedures put them into practice.
Example: An information security policy states that all company data must be protected according to its classification.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Policies set intent and direction, not technical detail; Approved by senior management; Listed policy types: AUP, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management

Definition: A policy defining what users may and may not do with the organization's systems, networks and data. Users typically sign or acknowledge it, which gives a basis for discipline if it is violated.
Example: An AUP forbids using company laptops for cryptocurrency mining and personal file sharing; an employee caught doing so is disciplined under it.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: AUP = rules of behavior for users; Usually acknowledged at onboarding; Supports legal and HR action after misuse

Definition: The core policies that state how the organization protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of its information, including roles, data classification and the authority of the security team.
Example: The information security policy names the CISO as responsible for the program and requires all data to be classified as public, internal or confidential.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: Top of the policy set; other policies and standards flow from it; Defines responsibilities and authority; Big picture, not technical settings

Definition: A policy that sets how the organization keeps critical business functions running during and after a disruption, including alternate processes when technology is unavailable.
Example: During a payment system outage, the business continuity policy lets stores take manual card imprints so sales continue.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: Business continuity = keep the business operating; Disaster recovery = restore IT systems; BCP is broader and includes non-technical workarounds

Definition: A policy that sets how IT systems and data are restored after a major disruption such as a natural disaster, fire or large cyberattack, often by switching to a recovery site.
Example: After a flood destroys the data center, the disaster recovery plan moves operations to a warm site and restores from offsite backups.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: DR is a subset of business continuity focused on technology recovery; Tied to RTO and RPO from the BIA; Tested with tabletop exercises and failover tests

Definition: A policy that defines how the organization prepares for, detects, contains, eradicates and recovers from security incidents, and who is on the response team.
Example: The incident response policy requires suspected ransomware to be reported to the security team within 15 minutes and names who may isolate systems.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: Policy level: who, authority, reporting duties; Detailed steps live in procedures and playbooks; Phases (4.8): preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned

Definition: A policy that requires security to be built into every stage of software development, from requirements and design through coding, testing, deployment and maintenance.
Example: The SDLC policy requires code review and a static analysis scan before any code reaches production.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: SDLC = Software Development Life Cycle in the acronym list; Security from the start costs less than fixing later; Covers testing, environments (dev, test, staging, production) and secure coding

Definition: A policy requiring that changes to systems are requested, reviewed, approved, tested and documented before they are made, to avoid outages and security gaps.
Example: The change management policy says no firewall rule may be changed without approval from the change advisory board.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Policies
Key Points: Policy = the requirement that changes are controlled; Procedure = the actual steps to submit and implement a change; Links to 1.3 change management processes

Definition: Mandatory, specific requirements that make policies measurable, such as exact settings, technologies or levels. Standards can be internal or come from bodies such as NIST or ISO.
Example: A standard requires AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher for data in transit.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Standards = mandatory and specific; More detailed than policies, less step by step than procedures; Listed standards: password, access control, physical security, encryption

Definition: A standard defining password requirements, such as minimum length, complexity, reuse limits, storage (hashing) and when MFA is required.
Example: The password standard requires at least 14 characters, blocks known breached passwords, and requires hashing with salt.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Standards
Key Points: Specific numbers live in the standard, not the policy; Modern guidance favors length and breached password checks over forced frequent changes; Pairs with password management training (5.6)

Definition: A standard defining how access is granted, reviewed and removed, which access control model is used, and requirements such as least privilege and periodic access reviews.
Example: The access control standard requires role-based access, quarterly access reviews and removal of access within 24 hours of termination.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Standards
Key Points: Covers models (RBAC, MAC, DAC, ABAC, rule-based); Least privilege and separation of duties; Access reviews catch privilege creep

Definition: A standard defining required physical protections for facilities and equipment, such as badge access, visitor logs, cameras, locks and secure areas.
Example: The physical security standard requires badge plus PIN for the server room and visitor escorts at all times.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Standards
Key Points: Physical controls protect the people, buildings and hardware; Examples: bollards, access control vestibules, guards, cameras; Do not confuse with physical penetration testing (5.5)

Definition: A standard defining which encryption algorithms, key lengths, protocols and key management practices are approved for data at rest, in transit and in use.
Example: The encryption standard approves AES-256 and TLS 1.3, bans DES and SSL, and requires keys to be stored in an HSM.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Standards
Key Points: Names approved and banned algorithms; Covers key management and rotation; Helps meet regulations that require encryption

Definition: Detailed, step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task in line with policies and standards, so it is done the same way every time.
Example: A procedure lists the exact steps to create a new user account, assign groups and enable MFA.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Procedures = how; Most detailed governance document; Listed procedures: change management, onboarding/offboarding, playbooks

Definition: The step-by-step process for making a change: submit a request, assess impact and risk, get approval, test, schedule a maintenance window, implement, have a backout plan, and document.
Example: An admin submits a change ticket to patch a database server, the CAB approves it for Saturday 2 a.m., and a rollback plan is attached.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Procedures
Key Points: Procedure = the operational steps; the policy only requires change control; Key parts: approval, impact analysis, testing, backout plan, maintenance window, documentation

Definition: Procedures for bringing a person into the organization (accounts, equipment, AUP and training) and for removing them (disable accounts, collect devices and badges, revoke access) when they leave.
Example: When an employee is terminated, offboarding disables the account immediately, collects the laptop and badge, and transfers their files to the manager.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Procedures
Key Points: Offboarding failures leave orphaned accounts that attackers can use; Onboarding includes signing the AUP and NDA and initial training; Timely deprovisioning is the main exam point

Definition: Documented, step-by-step responses to a specific type of event or incident, so responders act quickly and consistently. They are often automated in a SOAR platform.
Example: A phishing playbook says: pull the email from all mailboxes, block the sender domain, reset credentials of users who clicked, and notify the users.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Procedures
Key Points: Playbook = procedure for one specific scenario; Used in incident response and automated with SOAR; A runbook is similar and often more technical or automated

Definition: Outside factors that shape security governance: regulations, laws, industry requirements, and rules at the local or regional, national and global level.
Example: A hospital in California must follow HIPAA (national), state privacy law (regional) and, for EU patients, GDPR (global).
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Six listed: regulatory, legal, industry, local/regional, national, global; Laws and regulations are mandatory; industry standards may be contractual; Scope depends on where data subjects and operations are

Definition: Requirements set by government agencies or regulators that an organization must follow, with penalties for non-compliance.
Example: A US healthcare provider must protect patient records under HIPAA; a public company must keep financial controls under SOX.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: Regulations come from government bodies and are enforceable; Examples: HIPAA, SOX, GDPR; Do not confuse with industry standards like PCI DSS, which is enforced by card brands through contracts

Definition: Legal factors that affect security, such as laws, contracts, liability, e-discovery and legal holds, and breach notification duties.
Example: A legal hold requires the company to preserve all emails related to a lawsuit, overriding the normal deletion schedule.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: Includes contracts and liability, not only statutes; Legal hold overrides data retention schedules; Breach notification laws set deadlines to inform people

Definition: Requirements and best practices that come from a specific industry rather than from government, often enforced through contracts or certification.
Example: Any merchant that stores or processes payment card data must meet PCI DSS, required by the card brands.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law; Industry frameworks can also be voluntary best practice; Different sectors (finance, healthcare, energy) have their own expectations

Definition: Rules that apply in a specific city, state, province or region and add to national requirements.
Example: A company with California customers must follow the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) even though there is no equivalent federal law.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: State and provincial laws can be stricter than national ones; Example: CCPA in California; Organizations must track rules everywhere they operate or have customers

Definition: Laws and regulations that apply across an entire country.
Example: Every US healthcare provider follows HIPAA regardless of the state it is in.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: Apply countrywide; Examples: HIPAA and SOX in the US; Can conflict with or overlap local and global requirements

Definition: Requirements that reach across borders, applying to organizations based on whose data they handle or where they do business, not only where they are located.
Example: A US online store selling to customers in France must comply with GDPR for those customers' data.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > External considerations
Key Points: GDPR is the classic global example (applies to data of people in the EU); Multinationals must reconcile different countries' rules; Data sovereignty and cross-border transfer rules matter

Definition: Governance documents are regularly reviewed, checked for effectiveness and updated when laws, technology, threats or the business change, or after an incident.
Example: After a breach shows the remote access policy did not cover personal devices, the policy is revised and re-approved.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Governance is a continuous cycle, not a one-time document; Triggers: scheduled review, new regulation, incident, audit finding, business change; Version control and re-acknowledgement by users

Definition: The bodies and models through which security decisions are made and overseen: boards, committees, government entities, and centralized or decentralized models.
Example: A board of directors sets risk appetite, a security steering committee sets priorities, and business units run their own controls in a decentralized model.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Four listed: boards, committees, government entities, centralized/decentralized; Boards provide top-level oversight, committees focus on specific topics; Centralized = consistent, decentralized = flexible

Definition: A board of directors or similar body that provides top-level oversight of the organization, including approving strategy and risk appetite and holding executives accountable for security.
Example: The board reviews quarterly cyber risk reports from the CISO and approves the security budget.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Types of governance structures
Key Points: Highest oversight level; Sets direction and risk appetite, does not run daily operations; Often delegates to committees such as an audit committee

Definition: Groups of people, often from several departments, that oversee a specific area such as security, risk, audit or change, and make recommendations or decisions.
Example: A security steering committee with IT, legal, HR and finance meets monthly to approve new security policies.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Types of governance structures
Key Points: Bring cross-functional input; Examples: security steering committee, audit committee, change advisory board; Usually report to the board or executives

Definition: Public sector bodies that govern security either for themselves (agencies with their own structures) or for others by setting and enforcing laws, regulations and frameworks.
Example: A national agency publishes required controls that all federal contractors must follow.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Types of governance structures
Key Points: Government entities have public accountability and often strict, formal structures; They also act as regulators for private organizations; Example: NIST publishes frameworks used by US agencies

Definition: Centralized governance puts security decisions in one central group for consistency and control. Decentralized governance spreads decisions to business units or regions for flexibility and speed.
Example: A bank uses centralized governance so every branch follows identical controls; a conglomerate lets each subsidiary set its own security program (decentralized).
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Types of governance structures
Key Points: Centralized: consistent, easier to enforce, can be slow and a bottleneck; Decentralized: flexible and local, risk of inconsistency and gaps; Many organizations use a hybrid

items.front: Roles and responsibilities for systems and data
items.back:
Definition: The defined roles that decide about, process and look after data and systems: owners, controllers, processors and custodians/stewards.
Example: The VP of Sales owns customer data, the company is the GDPR controller, a cloud payroll firm is a processor, and IT admins are custodians who run the backups.
Category: 5.1 Security governance
Key Points: Owner = accountable and classifies; Controller = decides why and how personal data is processed; Processor = processes on the controller's behalf; Custodian/steward = handles day-to-day care

Definition: The person, usually a senior manager, who is ultimately accountable for a data set or system. The owner classifies the data, decides who may access it, and approves how it is protected.
Example: The head of HR is the data owner for employee records and approves who in the company may view salaries.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Roles and responsibilities for systems and data
Key Points: Accountable, not hands-on; Sets classification and access rules; Delegates daily work to custodians; Trap: the owner is not the IT admin

Definition: The entity that decides the purposes and means of processing personal data (the why and how). Under GDPR the controller carries primary legal responsibility.
Example: An online retailer decides to collect customer addresses for shipping, so it is the controller of that data.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Roles and responsibilities for systems and data
Key Points: Controller decides; processor acts on instructions; Controller remains responsible even when it outsources processing; GDPR term

Definition: An entity that processes personal data on behalf of a controller and only according to the controller's instructions.
Example: A payroll service company processes employee salary data for its client company, which remains the controller.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Roles and responsibilities for systems and data
Key Points: Processor does not decide purposes; Often a third party (cloud, payroll, marketing service); Has its own GDPR obligations, such as security and breach notification to the controller

Definition: Custodians are the people who handle the day-to-day protection of data, such as applying access controls, backups and patching. Data stewards focus on data quality, labeling, metadata and proper use, often making sure owner decisions are followed.
Example: A database administrator (custodian) applies the access rights the owner approved and runs nightly backups.
Category: 5.1 Security governance > Roles and responsibilities for systems and data
Key Points: Custodian = hands-on technical care; Steward = data quality and correct handling; Both act for the owner and do not set policy

items.front: SY0-701 5.2: Explain elements of the risk management process
items.back:
Definition: Risk management identifies risks, assesses and analyzes them, records them in a register, compares them to appetite and tolerance, chooses a strategy (transfer, accept, avoid, mitigate), reports on them, and uses a business impact analysis to set recovery targets.
Example: A company lists ransomware as a risk, calculates an ALE of $50,000, buys cyber insurance (transfer) and adds EDR (mitigate), then reports to the board.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Know SLE = AV x EF and ALE = SLE x ARO; Know the four strategies and exemption vs exception; Know RTO vs RPO and MTTR vs MTBF; Appetite vs tolerance vs threshold

Definition: The first step of risk management: finding and listing the threats, vulnerabilities and assets that could lead to harm.
Example: A workshop with IT and business leaders lists risks such as ransomware, insider data theft, a key vendor failing, and floods at the data center.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Comes before assessment and analysis; Sources: vulnerability scans, threat intelligence, audits, interviews, past incidents; Output feeds the risk register

Definition: The process of evaluating identified risks to determine their likelihood and impact. On the exam it is described by how often it is done: ad hoc, recurring, one-time or continuous.
Example: The security team assesses each identified risk annually and whenever a major new system is added.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Four frequencies: ad hoc, recurring, one-time, continuous; Assessment results feed risk analysis and the register; NIST SP 800-30 is the US guide for risk assessments

Definition: A risk assessment done as needed, in response to a specific event or question, rather than on a schedule.
Example: After news of a new zero-day in the company's VPN product, the team runs an ad hoc assessment of its exposure.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk assessment
Key Points: Triggered by an event, not a calendar; Unplanned; Compare: recurring = scheduled, one-time = single project, continuous = always running

Definition: A risk assessment repeated at regular, planned intervals, such as quarterly or annually.
Example: The organization reassesses all its top risks every year before budget planning, as required by its compliance program.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk assessment
Key Points: Scheduled and repeated; Often required by regulation or policy; Different from continuous, which is ongoing and often automated

Definition: A risk assessment done once for a specific purpose, such as a new project, merger or system purchase.
Example: Before acquiring a smaller company, the security team performs a one-time assessment of its network and data practices.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk assessment
Key Points: Single event tied to a project or decision; Not repeated on a schedule; Compare with ad hoc, which reacts to an unexpected event

Definition: Ongoing, usually automated assessment of risk in near real time, using monitoring, scanning and metrics.
Example: A platform continuously scans cloud resources and raises the risk score immediately when a storage bucket becomes public.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk assessment
Key Points: Always running, often tool-driven; Supports continuous monitoring and KRIs; Catches changes between scheduled assessments

Definition: Working out how big each risk is, either qualitatively (ratings such as high, medium, low) or quantitatively (money and numbers such as SLE, ALE and ARO), based on likelihood and impact.
Example: The team calculates that a database breach has an ALE of $40,000 and rates insider fraud as medium likelihood and high impact.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Qualitative = categories and judgment; quantitative = monetary values; Formulas: SLE = asset value x EF, ALE = SLE x ARO; Risk = likelihood x impact

Definition: Risk analysis that uses descriptive categories or scores, such as low, medium and high, often shown in a heat map, rather than exact monetary values.
Example: A risk matrix rates phishing as high likelihood and medium impact, placing it in the orange zone.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Subjective but quick and easy to communicate; Uses likelihood and impact ratings; Trap: anything with dollar figures is quantitative

Definition: Risk analysis that assigns numeric and monetary values to risk using measures such as asset value, exposure factor, SLE, ARO and ALE.
Example: Asset value $100,000, EF 50% gives SLE $50,000; with ARO 0.2 the ALE is $10,000 per year.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Objective numbers support cost-benefit decisions; A control is worth it if it costs less per year than the ALE reduction it brings; Needs reliable data, which can be hard to get

Definition: The expected monetary loss from one occurrence of a risk event. SLE = asset value (AV) x exposure factor (EF).
Example: A $200,000 server room loses 25% of its value in a fire: SLE = $200,000 x 0.25 = $50,000.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: SLE = AV x EF; Loss per single event, not per year; Then ALE = SLE x ARO

Definition: The expected monetary loss from a risk over one year. ALE = SLE x ARO.
Example: SLE $50,000 and the event happens once every 5 years (ARO 0.2): ALE = $50,000 x 0.2 = $10,000 per year.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: ALE = SLE x ARO = AV x EF x ARO; Used to justify control spending: spend less per year than the loss avoided; Trap: do not multiply ALE by ARO again

Definition: How many times a risk event is expected to happen in one year. Once every 10 years is 0.1; four times a year is 4.
Example: Floods hit the site once every 20 years, so the ARO is 1/20 = 0.05.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Frequency per year, can be below 1; Once every N years = 1/N; Used in ALE = SLE x ARO

Definition: A measurable, numeric chance that a risk event will happen, usually based on statistics or historical data, expressed as a percentage or decimal.
Example: Historical data shows a 10% chance per year that a major vendor outage will occur.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Probability = numeric, statistical (quantitative); Likelihood = rating such as high, medium, low (qualitative); Both describe how likely a risk is to happen

Definition: How likely a risk event is to occur, usually expressed as a qualitative rating such as rare, possible or almost certain.
Example: The team rates the likelihood of a phishing attack succeeding as high because staff training is overdue.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Often qualitative, used in risk matrices; Combined with impact to rank risks; Compare with probability, which is numeric

Definition: The percentage of an asset's value that would be lost in one occurrence of a risk event, from 0% to 100% (0 to 1).
Example: A flood would destroy 40% of the warehouse inventory value, so the EF is 0.4.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: EF is a percentage of the asset value; SLE = AV x EF; Total loss = EF of 100%

Definition: The size of the consequence if a risk event happens, such as financial loss, downtime, safety harm, legal penalties or reputational damage.
Example: A breach of customer card data would have high impact: fines, card replacement costs and lost customers.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk analysis
Key Points: Risk = likelihood x impact; Impact can be quantitative (dollars) or qualitative (high, medium, low); Includes life and safety, property, finance and reputation

Definition: A central document or tool that lists identified risks with details such as description, likelihood, impact, score, owner, key risk indicators, threshold, chosen strategy and status.
Example: A risk register row: "Ransomware, likelihood high, impact high, owner IT director, strategy mitigate with EDR and offline backups, status in progress."
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Also called a risk log; Living document updated over time; Listed parts: key risk indicators, risk owners, risk threshold

Definition: Metrics that give early warning that a risk is rising or close to its threshold, so action can be taken before an incident.
Example: A KRI tracks the number of unpatched critical vulnerabilities; when it rises above 20, the risk is escalated.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk register
Key Points: KRIs are forward-looking warning signs; Compare with KPIs, which measure performance; Each KRI should have a threshold that triggers action

Definition: The person accountable for managing a specific risk, including making sure the chosen response is carried out and monitored.
Example: The head of finance is the risk owner for payment fraud and must approve and track the controls.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk register
Key Points: Every risk in the register needs a named owner; Usually a manager with authority and budget; Accountability, not necessarily hands-on work

Definition: The defined level of risk or KRI value at which a risk is no longer acceptable and must be escalated or acted on.
Example: If expected yearly loss from a risk goes above $25,000, the threshold is crossed and it goes to the steering committee.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk register
Key Points: A trigger point for action; Set based on appetite and tolerance; Trap: appetite is the overall attitude, the threshold is the specific trigger line

Definition: The amount of deviation from the risk appetite an organization can accept for a specific risk or objective; the practical limit of risk it can handle.
Example: Appetite says low risk for patient data; tolerance allows critical patches to take up to 7 days before it is unacceptable.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Tolerance = specific acceptable variation, often measurable; Appetite = broad willingness to take risk; Tolerance is usually narrower and more concrete than appetite

Definition: The overall amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or accept to achieve its goals, usually set by leadership. The exam lists three postures: expansionary, conservative and neutral.
Example: A startup chasing growth has a high risk appetite; a bank holding savings deposits has a low one.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Set at the top (board, executives); Appetite = willingness, tolerance = acceptable deviation, threshold = trigger point; Three types: expansionary, conservative, neutral

Definition: A posture willing to accept higher risk in exchange for growth, innovation or new opportunities.
Example: A tech company launches a new cloud product quickly, accepting some security risk to beat competitors to market.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk appetite
Key Points: Higher risk taking for higher reward; Common in startups and growth phases; Opposite of conservative

Definition: A posture that avoids risk and prefers safety and stability, even at the cost of slower growth.
Example: A hospital refuses to adopt a new unproven medical app until it is fully tested and certified.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk appetite
Key Points: Low willingness to take risk; Common in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare and government; Favors avoid and mitigate strategies

Definition: A balanced posture that weighs risk and reward evenly, taking risks only when the expected benefit justifies them.
