Example: A retailer approves a new payment option only after a cost-benefit analysis shows the added revenue outweighs the added fraud risk.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk appetite
Key Points: Balanced between expansionary and conservative; Decisions driven by cost-benefit analysis; Neither seeks nor strongly avoids risk

Definition: The four ways to respond to a risk: transfer it to someone else, accept it, avoid it by stopping the activity, or mitigate it with controls.
Example: For ransomware a company buys cyber insurance (transfer), adds backups and EDR (mitigate) and accepts the small remaining residual risk (accept).
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Transfer, accept, avoid, mitigate; Acceptance includes exemption and exception; Residual risk = what is left after controls; Strategies are often combined

Definition: Shifting the financial impact of a risk to another party, most often through insurance or by outsourcing under a contract.
Example: A company buys cybersecurity insurance to cover breach response costs.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies
Key Points: Also called sharing; Insurance is the classic example; Trap: accountability and reputational damage are not transferred, only the financial burden

Definition: Choosing to take no further action on a risk because it is within appetite or because the cost of controls is higher than the expected loss. The exam lists two forms: exemption and exception.
Example: A small office accepts the risk of a two-hour internet outage because a backup line would cost more than the lost sales.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies
Key Points: Used when the cost of controls exceeds the ALE; Must be documented and approved by the risk owner; Accepting is a decision, ignoring a risk is not

Definition: A formal approval that releases a system, group or situation from having to meet a specific requirement, so the requirement does not apply to it.
Example: A legacy lab system that cannot run the required endpoint agent is formally exempted from the EDR standard, with the risk accepted by its owner.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies > Accept
Key Points: Exemption = the rule does not apply to this case; Exception = the rule applies but a temporary deviation is allowed; Both must be documented, approved and reviewed; Scope decides it, not duration alone

Definition: An approved, usually temporary deviation from a policy or standard that still applies, often with compensating controls and an end date.
Example: A server is allowed to miss the 30-day patch requirement for 60 days while a vendor certifies the patch, with extra network isolation in place.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies > Accept
Key Points: Temporary and time-limited, with a review or expiry date; Often requires compensating controls; Compare exemption, which removes the requirement for that case

Definition: Eliminating a risk by not doing, or by stopping, the activity that creates it.
Example: A company drops a planned feature that would let customers upload files, because hosting user files is too risky; the risk never exists because the activity never starts.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies
Key Points: Stop or never start the risky activity; Removes the risk but also its benefits; Trap: paying another party to carry the risk (insurance, outsourcing) is transfer, stopping the activity is avoid

Definition: Reducing the likelihood or impact of a risk by applying controls, leaving some residual risk.
Example: Installing a firewall, enabling MFA and patching reduce the risk of an external breach.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Risk management strategies
Key Points: Also called reduction; Controls such as firewalls, MFA and patching are the classic mitigation; Residual risk remains and is then accepted or transferred

Definition: Communicating the organization's risks, their status, trends and treatment to stakeholders such as executives, the board and regulators, in a form they can act on.
Example: The CISO gives the board a quarterly report showing the top 10 risks, KRI trends, and which mitigations are behind schedule.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: Audience-appropriate: executives want business impact, technical teams want detail; Often built from the risk register; Supports decisions and compliance

Definition: An analysis that identifies critical business functions and the impact of losing them over time, and sets recovery targets such as RTO and RPO, using reliability measures such as MTTR and MTBF.
Example: The BIA finds online ordering loses $20,000 per hour when down, so it gets an RTO of 2 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes.
Category: 5.2 Risk management
Key Points: BIA drives business continuity and DR planning; Identifies critical functions, dependencies and impact; Key metrics: RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF

Definition: The maximum acceptable amount of time a system or process can be down before it must be restored and running again after a disruption.
Example: The RTO for the email system is 4 hours: it must be back online within 4 hours of an outage.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Business impact analysis
Key Points: RTO = time to get back up (downtime limit); RPO = how much data you can lose (measured back in time); Shorter RTO needs faster recovery options such as hot sites

Definition: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time: how far back the last good copy of data may be when restoring.
Example: An RPO of 1 hour means backups or replication must happen at least every hour, so no more than 1 hour of transactions is lost.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Business impact analysis
Key Points: RPO drives backup frequency; RPO looks backward (data lost), RTO looks forward (time to restore); Trap: RPO is not about how long recovery takes

Definition: The average time it takes to repair a failed component or system and return it to service. Objective 5.2 says mean time to repair; the SY0-701 acronym list expands MTTR as mean time to recover.
Example: Over a year, a router failed 3 times and repairs took 2, 3 and 4 hours, so MTTR = 3 hours.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Business impact analysis
Key Points: Lower MTTR is better; MTTR = time to fix, MTBF = time between failures; MTTR should fit within the RTO

Definition: The average time a repairable system operates between one failure and the next, a measure of reliability.
Example: A disk array ran 9,000 hours in total and failed 3 times, so MTBF = 3,000 hours.
Category: 5.2 Risk management > Business impact analysis
Key Points: Higher MTBF is better (more reliable); For repairable items; MTTF (mean time to failure) is for items replaced, not repaired; Compare MTTR = average repair time

items.front: SY0-701 5.3: Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management
items.back:
Definition: Third-party risk management assesses, selects, contracts with and monitors vendors and partners, because their weaknesses become yours. It covers vendor assessment, vendor selection, agreement types, monitoring, questionnaires and rules of engagement.
Example: Before hiring a cloud payroll provider, a company reviews its SOC 2 report, signs an MSA, SLA and NDA, and sends a yearly security questionnaire.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Know agreement types: SLA, MOA, MOU, MSA, WO/SOW, NDA, BPA; Right-to-audit clause and independent assessments give assurance; Supply chain attacks make vendor risk an exam favorite

Definition: Evaluating a vendor's security posture and risk before and during the relationship, using pen tests, right-to-audit clauses, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.
Example: A bank reviews a software vendor's ISO 27001 certificate, audit reports and pen test results before allowing it to connect to the network.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Five methods: ask for their own audit results (evidence of internal audits), bring in outsiders (independent assessments, penetration testing), keep the right to check them yourself (right-to-audit clause), and look past them to their suppliers (supply chain analysis); Assessment is ongoing, not one-time; Higher-risk vendors get deeper assessment

Definition: Testing a vendor's systems or the products and services it provides by simulating real attacks, either by the customer with permission or by reviewing the vendor's own pen test results.
Example: Before integration, a company gets permission and scope from a SaaS vendor and hires testers to attack the vendor's API.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor assessment
Key Points: Requires explicit written permission and rules of engagement from the vendor; Often the vendor shares a third-party pen test summary instead; Different from 5.5 pen testing types (known, unknown environment)

Definition: A contract clause that gives the customer the right to audit the vendor's security controls, records or facilities, or to have a third party do so.
Example: After a vendor breach, the customer uses its right-to-audit clause to inspect the vendor's access logs and controls.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor assessment
Key Points: Must be negotiated into the contract up front; Gives direct verification rather than trusting the vendor's word; Often allows a third-party auditor to act for the customer

Definition: Documentation showing that the vendor regularly audits itself, such as internal audit reports, findings and remediation status.
Example: A customer asks a vendor for its latest internal audit report and proof that last year's findings were fixed.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor assessment
Key Points: Shows the vendor checks itself; Less independent than an external audit; Look for findings and how they were remediated

Definition: Reviews of a vendor by an impartial outside party, such as SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certification or third-party audits, giving more trustworthy assurance than the vendor's own claims.
Example: A cloud provider shares its SOC 2 Type II report, prepared by an independent audit firm, with prospective customers.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor assessment
Key Points: Independent = no conflict of interest; More credible than self-reporting; Examples: SOC 2 Type II (controls over a period), ISO 27001 certificate

Definition: Examining the vendor's own suppliers and components (hardware, software, services) to find risks that come in through the supply chain.
Example: A company checks where its network switches are manufactured and reviews the software bill of materials (SBOM) of a vendor's product for vulnerable libraries.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor assessment
Key Points: Your vendor's vendors are also your risk; SBOMs help reveal software components; Supply chain attacks insert malicious code or hardware upstream

Definition: Choosing vendors with security in mind, including due diligence on their background and security and checking for conflicts of interest.
Example: A hospital compares three EHR vendors on security certifications, breach history, financial stability and data handling before choosing one.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Two listed parts: due diligence and conflict of interest; Security requirements should be part of the selection criteria; Decisions should be documented

Definition: Investigating a potential vendor before signing, including its security practices, financial health, reputation, legal history and compliance, to confirm it can be trusted.
Example: Before outsourcing, the company checks the vendor's breach history, financial statements, references and certifications.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor selection
Key Points: Done before the contract; Shows the organization acted responsibly; Compare due care (5.4), the ongoing actions taken to protect

Definition: A situation where a person involved in selecting a vendor has a personal or financial interest that could bias the decision.
Example: The IT manager choosing a managed service provider owns shares in one of the bidders and must disclose it and step aside.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Vendor selection
Key Points: Conflicts must be disclosed and managed; Can lead to choosing an unsuitable or insecure vendor; Also applies to auditors, who must be independent

Definition: The documents that set out relationships with vendors and partners: SLA (service levels), MOA and MOU (cooperation, MOA more formal), MSA (general terms), WO/SOW (specific work), NDA (confidentiality) and BPA (business partnership).
Example: A company signs an MSA with a consulting firm, then a SOW for each project, an NDA covering secrets, and an SLA defining support response times.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: MSA = umbrella terms, SOW = specific project under it; MOU = informal intent, MOA = more formal, defined responsibilities; SLA = measurable service levels and penalties; NDA = confidentiality, BPA = partner relationship

Definition: A contract that defines the minimum level of service a provider must deliver, with measurable metrics such as uptime, response time and resolution time, and penalties if they are missed.
Example: An SLA promises 99.9% uptime and a 4-hour response to critical tickets, with service credits if either is missed.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: Measurable performance terms; Common with ISPs, cloud and managed service providers; Trap: the SLA is about service levels, not confidentiality (NDA) or project scope (SOW)

Definition: A document in which two or more parties agree to cooperate toward a shared goal, setting out each party's responsibilities. It is more formal and specific than an MOU and can be binding, but is less detailed than a full contract.
Example: Two universities sign an MOA stating which one provides the servers and which one manages the shared research data.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: MOA is more formal than an MOU, with defined responsibilities and conditions; MOU is a statement of intent, usually not legally binding; Neither is a full commercial contract like an MSA

Definition: An informal document stating that parties intend to work together and describing their shared understanding. It is usually not legally binding.
Example: Two government agencies sign an MOU saying they intend to share threat intelligence.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: Least formal agreement: a letter of intent; Usually not legally enforceable; Often precedes a more formal MOA or contract

Definition: A contract that sets the general terms of a long-term relationship (payment, liability, confidentiality, dispute handling), so future work can be added through work orders or statements of work without renegotiating.
Example: A company signs an MSA with a security consulting firm, then issues a separate SOW for each pen test.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: Umbrella contract for many future projects; Specific work is defined in WOs or SOWs under it; Saves renegotiating terms each time

Definition: A document defining a specific job: scope, deliverables, timeline, location and cost. It usually falls under an MSA.
Example: A SOW states the pen test will cover 3 web applications, run from March 1 to 15, and deliver a final report for $20,000.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: Specific and project-level; MSA = general terms, SOW = this job; Clear scope prevents disputes and scope creep

Definition: A legal contract that requires parties to keep shared confidential information secret and limits how it may be used.
Example: A pen testing firm signs an NDA before receiving network diagrams and test results.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: Protects confidentiality; Can be one-way (unilateral) or mutual; Common with employees, contractors and vendors

Definition: An agreement between business partners describing how they will work together: responsibilities, sharing of profits and losses, decision making, and how shared data and systems are handled.
Example: Two companies that jointly sell a product sign a BPA defining profit split, who handles customer data, and who secures the shared portal.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk > Agreement types
Key Points: For an ongoing partnership, not a simple service purchase; Defines ownership, responsibilities and financial terms; Can include security obligations for shared data

Definition: Ongoing oversight of vendors after the contract is signed, checking performance against the SLA, security posture, compliance and any incidents or changes.
Example: Each quarter the company reviews its cloud vendor's uptime reports, new SOC reports and any breach news.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Third-party risk does not end at signing; Includes SLA tracking, reassessments and watching for breaches or financial trouble; Frequency based on vendor risk

Definition: Standard sets of security questions sent to vendors to learn how they protect data and systems, used during selection and periodically afterward.
Example: A vendor completes a 200-question security questionnaire covering encryption, access control, incident response and background checks.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Cheap and scalable way to assess many vendors; Answers are self-reported, so verify high-risk vendors with audits or evidence; Often repeated yearly

Definition: A document that defines the boundaries of an engagement such as a pen test or vendor assessment: scope, allowed techniques, timing, contacts, data handling and how to stop or report problems.
Example: Rules of engagement allow testing of the web servers only, between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., with no denial-of-service attacks, and name an emergency contact.
Category: 5.3 Third-party risk
Key Points: Defines what is in and out of scope and what testers may do; Needed before any testing; Protects both parties legally and operationally

items.front: SY0-701 5.4: Summarize elements of effective security compliance
items.back:
Definition: Security compliance means meeting the laws, regulations, standards and contracts that apply to the organization, and proving it. It covers compliance reporting, consequences of non-compliance, compliance monitoring and privacy.
Example: A retailer reports PCI DSS compliance yearly, monitors controls with automated tools, has staff acknowledge policies, and honors GDPR erasure requests.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance
Key Points: Consequences: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts; Due diligence vs due care; Privacy roles: data subject, controller, processor

Definition: Documenting and communicating the organization's compliance status, either internally to management and the board or externally to regulators, auditors and customers.
Example: The compliance officer gives the board a monthly status report and submits an annual compliance filing to the regulator.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance
Key Points: Two types: internal and external; Accurate records support audits and defense; False reporting can bring its own penalties

Definition: Compliance reports produced for people inside the organization, such as executives, the board or the audit committee, to track status and fix gaps.
Example: A monthly dashboard shows the CISO which departments have not finished required security training.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance reporting
Key Points: Audience inside the organization; Used to find and fix gaps before external review; Often prepared by a compliance team or officer

Definition: Compliance reports sent to outside parties such as regulators, government agencies, auditors, business partners or customers.
Example: A bank files required reports with its financial regulator, and a payment processor submits its PCI DSS attestation to card brands.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance reporting
Key Points: Audience outside the organization; Often mandatory with deadlines and formats; Includes breach notifications required by law

Definition: The penalties and harm that follow failing to comply: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license and contractual impacts.
Example: A company that ignores GDPR faces a large fine, bad press, and customers ending contracts.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance
Key Points: Five listed: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts; Can be financial, legal, operational and reputational; Often several happen together

Definition: Monetary penalties imposed by regulators or courts for failing to follow a law or regulation.
Example: Under GDPR, the most serious violations can be fined up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Consequences of non-compliance
Key Points: Direct financial penalty; Amount often based on severity and size of the organization; Distinct from sanctions, which can be non-monetary

Definition: Penalties or restrictions imposed by a government or authority, such as limits on operations, trade or processing, or orders to stop an activity.
Example: A regulator orders a company to stop processing personal data until it fixes its controls.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Consequences of non-compliance
Key Points: Can be restrictions rather than money; Imposed by governments or regulators; May limit doing business in a country or sector

Definition: Loss of trust from customers, partners and the public after non-compliance or a breach becomes known, leading to lost business.
Example: After news of a privacy violation, customers move to a competitor and the stock price falls.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Consequences of non-compliance
Key Points: Hard to measure and slow to recover; Cannot be transferred by insurance; Often costs more than the fine itself

Definition: Revocation or suspension of a license, permit or certification needed to operate or provide certain services.
Example: A bank loses its operating license, or a merchant loses the ability to accept payment cards after repeated PCI DSS failures.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Consequences of non-compliance
Key Points: Can stop the business from operating in that area; Applies to regulated industries such as banking, healthcare and payments; Among the most severe consequences

Definition: Effects on contracts when an organization fails to meet compliance terms: penalties, breach of contract claims, lost contracts or the other party ending the agreement.
Example: A cloud provider fails the security requirements in its contract, so a major customer ends the contract and claims damages.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Consequences of non-compliance
Key Points: Contracts often require compliance with standards (PCI DSS, SOC 2); Breach of contract can bring penalties or termination; Separate from government penalties

Definition: Ongoing checking that the organization stays compliant, using due diligence and due care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external monitoring, and automation.
Example: Automated tools check every server daily against the hardening standard, and employees reacknowledge policies yearly.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance
Key Points: Compliance is continuous, not a once-a-year event; Four listed: due diligence/care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external, automation; Evidence collection supports audits

Definition: Due diligence is investigating and understanding risks and requirements (doing your homework). Due care is acting on that knowledge by implementing and maintaining reasonable protections (doing the right thing).
Example: Due diligence: researching which privacy laws apply. Due care: then actually encrypting data and training staff to meet them.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance monitoring
Key Points: Diligence = investigate and know; care = act and maintain; Together they show a prudent person standard and reduce liability; Trap: both are needed, knowing without acting is negligence

Definition: Attestation is a formal statement, by management or an auditor, that controls or compliance are in place. Acknowledgement is people confirming that they have read, understood and will follow policies or requirements.
Example: Employees acknowledge the AUP each year, and the CEO signs an attestation that financial controls are effective.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance monitoring
Key Points: Acknowledgement creates accountability for individuals; Attestation affirms compliance status, often signed and legally significant; See also attestation as an audit type in 5.5

Definition: Internal monitoring is done by the organization itself (compliance team, internal audit). External monitoring is done by outside parties such as regulators, auditors or customers.
Example: The internal compliance team reviews controls monthly, and an external auditor tests them once a year.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance monitoring
Key Points: Internal = ongoing and self-run; External = independent and more credible; Both together give full coverage

Definition: Using tools to check compliance continuously and collect evidence automatically, such as configuration scanners, SIEM rules and compliance dashboards.
Example: A cloud security tool automatically flags any storage bucket made public and records the finding for the auditors.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Compliance monitoring
Key Points: Faster, more consistent and less error-prone than manual checks; Enables continuous compliance; Automated evidence makes audits easier

Definition: The protection of personal data and the rights of individuals over it, governed by laws at many levels and by roles such as data subject, controller and processor.
Example: A company maps where customer personal data is stored, sets retention periods, and builds a process to delete data on request.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance
Key Points: Covers who the data is about (the data subject) and their right to be forgotten; who decides and who handles it (controller vs processor) and who owns it; what you hold and how long (data inventory and retention); and the legal implications; GDPR is the main reference law; Privacy is about personal data rights, security is about protecting all data

Definition: Privacy laws create legal obligations and liability, and they differ by place: local or regional, national and global. Organizations must follow all that apply to the data they handle.
Example: A US company with customers in California and the EU must follow CCPA and GDPR, as well as any federal sector laws.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: Three levels listed: local/regional, national, global; Violations bring fines, lawsuits and notification duties; Applicability depends on where the data subjects are

Definition: Privacy laws that apply only in a state, province or region.
Example: The California Consumer Privacy Act gives California residents the right to know about and delete personal information businesses hold about them.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy > Legal implications
Key Points: Example: CCPA (California); State breach notification laws differ in deadlines; Can be stricter than national law

Definition: Privacy laws that apply across a whole country.
Example: HIPAA protects health information across the entire United States; Canada's PIPEDA covers private sector personal data nationally.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy > Legal implications
Key Points: Countrywide scope; Examples: HIPAA (US health data), PIPEDA (Canada); May be sector-specific in the US

Definition: Privacy laws that reach beyond a country's borders, applying to any organization that handles data of people in that jurisdiction, wherever the organization is located.
Example: GDPR applies to a US website that tracks visitors in Germany.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy > Legal implications
Key Points: GDPR is the main example; Applies based on the location of data subjects; Affects cross-border data transfers

Definition: The identified or identifiable living person that personal data is about.
Example: A customer whose name, email and purchase history a store holds is the data subject of that data.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: GDPR term; Has rights such as access, correction and erasure; The data subject is the person, not the organization

Definition: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and is primarily responsible for compliance. The processor handles the data on the controller's behalf and only on its instructions.
Example: A hospital (controller) uses a cloud billing company (processor) to send patient invoices.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: Controller = decides purposes and means; processor = follows instructions; Controller stays accountable even when using a processor; A contract (data processing agreement) binds the processor

Definition: Who has rights and accountability over data. In privacy terms, the organization holds and is accountable for personal data, but the data subject keeps rights over data about them; inside the organization a data owner is accountable for it.
Example: A marketing company holds a customer list but must delete a person's data on request, because that person has rights over it.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: Holding data does not mean unlimited rights over it; Data owner role assigns internal accountability; Ownership issues come up with vendors and cloud contracts

Definition: A data inventory records what data the organization holds, where it is, what type it is and who is responsible. Retention rules define how long each type is kept before it is securely disposed of.
Example: The inventory shows customer records in three databases; policy keeps them for 7 years after the last purchase, then deletes them.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: You cannot protect or delete data you do not know you have; Keep data only as long as needed or legally required; Legal holds override normal retention

Definition: A data subject's right to have their personal data erased when it is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn, subject to exceptions. In GDPR it is the right to erasure (Article 17).
Example: A former customer asks an online store to delete their account and data, and the store must do so unless it has a legal reason to keep it.
Category: 5.4 Security compliance > Privacy
Key Points: GDPR right to erasure, Article 17; Not absolute: legal obligations and some other grounds can override it; Requires knowing where all copies are (data inventory)

items.front: SY0-701 5.5: Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments
items.back:
Definition: Audits and assessments check whether controls exist and work. They include attestation, internal audits, external audits and assessments, and penetration testing with its environments and reconnaissance types.
Example: An audit committee oversees internal audits, a regulator examines the bank, an independent firm issues a SOC 2 report, and a red team runs an unknown-environment pen test.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments
Key Points: Internal vs external; Pen test teams: offensive (red), defensive (blue), integrated (purple); Environments: known, partially known, unknown; Recon: passive vs active

Definition: A formal, written statement from an auditor or other qualified party giving an opinion that certain information or controls are accurate and effective.
Example: An independent auditor issues a SOC 2 Type II report attesting that a cloud provider's controls operated effectively over 12 months.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments
Key Points: An attestation is the auditor's formal opinion; Gives customers and regulators assurance; Compare 5.4 attestation and acknowledgement, which includes users confirming policies

Definition: Audits and assessments performed by the organization's own staff to check compliance and control effectiveness, including compliance checks, audit committee oversight and self-assessments.
Example: The internal audit team tests whether access reviews really happen every quarter.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments
Key Points: Three listed: compliance, audit committee, self-assessments; Cheaper and more frequent but less independent than external; Prepares for external audits

Definition: An internal audit that checks whether the organization is following the laws, regulations, standards and its own policies that apply to it.
Example: The internal compliance team checks that all systems handling card data meet PCI DSS requirements before the external assessment.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Internal
Key Points: Focus is adherence to requirements; Run by internal staff; Finds gaps before regulators or external auditors do

Definition: A subcommittee of the board of directors that oversees the audit process, financial reporting and internal controls, and receives audit findings.
Example: The internal audit team reports findings directly to the audit committee rather than to the IT department being audited.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Internal
Key Points: Board-level oversight of audits; Helps keep auditors independent of management; Reviews audit plans and results

Definition: Reviews where a team or department evaluates its own controls and compliance, often using a checklist or framework.
Example: Each department completes a yearly security checklist rating its own controls against the company standards.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Internal
Key Points: Low cost and quick; Least independent, so results can be biased; Good for preparation and awareness

Definition: Audits and assessments performed by parties outside the organization, such as regulators, examiners, assessors or independent auditors, giving independent assurance.
Example: A regulator examines a bank, and an independent firm audits a SaaS company for SOC 2.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments
Key Points: Four listed: regulatory, examinations, assessment, independent third-party audit; More independent and credible than internal; Often required by law, contracts or customers

Definition: An audit carried out by, or required by, a government regulator to check compliance with laws and regulations in its area.
Example: A health regulator audits a hospital's protection of patient records under HIPAA.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > External
Key Points: Mandatory, with possible penalties; Done by or for a regulator; Scope set by the regulation

Definition: Formal reviews, usually by regulators or their examiners, that inspect an organization's records, operations and controls in detail.
Example: Banking examiners spend two weeks on site reviewing a bank's cybersecurity program and records.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > External
Key Points: Formal and detailed inspection; Common in banking and finance; Results can require corrective action

Definition: An evaluation by an outside party of security posture or risk, measuring controls against a framework, often less formal than an audit and focused on improvement.
Example: A consulting firm assesses the company's security program against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and recommends improvements.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > External
Key Points: Assessment = evaluate and recommend; audit = verify against requirements with formal findings; Can be done by consultants or assessors

Definition: An audit by an outside firm with no stake in the outcome, giving an objective opinion on the organization's controls.
Example: A certified audit firm audits a payroll provider and issues a SOC 2 report its customers can trust.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > External
Key Points: Independence gives credibility; Common for SOC 2, ISO 27001 certification and PCI DSS; Customers often require it from vendors

Definition: Authorized simulated attacks that try to exploit vulnerabilities to show what a real attacker could do. Types include physical, offensive, defensive and integrated tests, in known, partially known or unknown environments, with passive or active reconnaissance.
Example: A hired team gets written permission, scans the network, exploits a weak web app and reports how it reached the database.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments
Key Points: Pen test exploits; a vulnerability scan only finds; Needs written authorization and rules of engagement; Know team types and environment types

Definition: A test of physical security controls by trying to get into buildings or secure areas, for example by tailgating, picking locks, cloning badges or posing as a worker.
Example: A tester dressed as a delivery driver tailgates into the office and plugs a device into a network port.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Tests locks, guards, badges, cameras and staff behavior; Often combined with social engineering; Needs careful authorization letters

Definition: Testing from the attacker's side: a red team actively attacks systems to find and exploit weaknesses.
Example: The red team tries for weeks to gain domain admin access without being detected.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Offensive = red team = attack; Defensive = blue team = defend; Integrated = purple team = both working together

Definition: The defending side of a test: a blue team detects, responds to and blocks simulated attacks, measuring how well defenses and monitoring work.
Example: During the exercise, the blue team spots the red team's lateral movement in the SIEM and isolates the host.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Blue team = defenders, the SOC; Tests detection and response, not just prevention; Pairs with red team in exercises

Definition: Offensive and defensive teams working together and sharing findings in real time, so defenses improve during the test.
Example: The red team runs each attack technique while the blue team watches and tunes detection rules immediately.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Purple team = red + blue cooperating; Goal is improvement, not winning; Faster feedback than separate red and blue exercises

Definition: A test where the testers get full information about the target in advance, such as network diagrams, source code and credentials. Formerly called white box.
Example: Testers receive the application's source code and architecture documents to review it thoroughly.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Known = full knowledge (white box); Most thorough and efficient coverage; Does not simulate an outside attacker's starting point

Definition: A test where the testers get some information, such as IP ranges or a normal user account, but not full details. Formerly called gray box.
Example: Testers get a standard employee login and must find out how far they can escalate privileges.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Partially known = some knowledge (gray box); Simulates an insider or an attacker who did some research; Balance of realism and efficiency

Definition: A test where the testers get no prior information and start like an outside attacker. Formerly called black box.
Example: Testers get only the company name and must discover its domains, IPs and systems themselves.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: Unknown = no knowledge (black box); Most realistic outsider simulation; Takes longer and may miss areas

Definition: The information-gathering phase of a pen test, done before attacking, to learn about the target. It can be passive or active.
Example: Testers search public records and DNS, then scan the discovered IP range for open ports.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing
Key Points: First phase of a test; Passive = no direct contact with target; Active = interacts with target and can be detected

Definition: Gathering information without directly interacting with the target's systems, using public sources (OSINT) such as websites, social media, DNS records and search engines.
Example: A tester collects employee names from a professional networking site and email formats from the company website.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing > Reconnaissance
Key Points: No packets sent to target systems, so hard to detect; Uses OSINT; Trap: a port scan is active, not passive

Definition: Gathering information by directly interacting with the target's systems, such as port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing and vulnerability scans.
Example: A tester runs Nmap against the company's public IP addresses to find open ports and services.
Category: 5.5 Audits and assessments > Penetration testing > Reconnaissance
Key Points: Touches target systems, so it can be logged and detected; More detailed than passive; Must be within the rules of engagement

items.front: SY0-701 5.6: Given a scenario, implement security awareness practices
items.back:
Definition: Security awareness turns users into a line of defense: phishing campaigns, recognizing anomalous behavior, user guidance and training on many topics, reporting and monitoring of results, and the development and execution of the program.
Example: A company runs monthly phishing simulations, trains staff on remote work and removable media, and tracks click rates from an initial baseline over time.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Scenario objective: pick the right training or response; Anomalous behavior: risky, unexpected, unintentional; Reporting: initial vs recurring; Program: development then execution

Definition: Awareness work focused on phishing: running simulated phishing campaigns, teaching users to recognize phishing attempts, and handling suspicious messages users report.
Example: Staff receive a fake package delivery email; those who click get short training, and those who report it are thanked.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Three listed: campaigns, recognizing a phishing attempt, responding to reported suspicious messages; Goal: fewer clicks, more reports; Phishing is one of the most common initial attack vectors

Definition: Authorized simulated phishing emails sent to employees to test and train them, measuring who clicks, enters credentials or reports.
Example: IT sends a fake password reset email to all staff; 12% click, and they get immediate training.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Phishing
Key Points: Simulated and authorized, not real attacks; Track click rate and report rate over time; Training should be educational, not punishing

Definition: Knowing the warning signs of phishing: urgency or threats, unexpected attachments or links, mismatched or look-alike sender domains, requests for credentials or payment, poor spelling, and links that point somewhere other than shown.
Example: A user notices an email from "micros0ft-support.com" demanding a password reset within one hour and does not click.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Phishing
Key Points: Check sender domain and hover over links; Urgency and unusual requests are red flags; Verify through a separate known channel

Definition: The process the security team follows when users report suspicious emails: analyze the message, remove copies from other mailboxes, block senders and links, reset affected credentials, and give feedback to the reporter.
Example: After three users report the same email, the SOC pulls it from all mailboxes and blocks the malicious URL.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Phishing
Key Points: Make reporting easy (a report button); Respond quickly and thank reporters to encourage reporting; Feed findings into phishing playbooks

Definition: Training people to notice and report behavior that differs from normal, whether risky, unexpected or unintentional, by coworkers, accounts or systems.
Example: An employee notices a colleague copying large amounts of files to a USB drive late at night and reports it.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Three types: risky, unexpected, unintentional; Users see things tools may miss; Report, do not investigate yourself

Definition: Actions that knowingly or carelessly increase risk, such as disabling security software, sharing passwords, installing unapproved software or bypassing controls.
Example: A user turns off the antivirus because it slows down a game they installed on a work laptop.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Anomalous behavior recognition
Key Points: Deliberate or careless choices that raise risk; May violate the AUP; Different from unintentional mistakes

Definition: Activity that is out of the ordinary for a user or system, such as logins at odd hours or from unusual places, sudden access to new data, or a system acting strangely.
Example: An accountant's account logs in at 3 a.m. from another country and starts browsing engineering files.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Anomalous behavior recognition
Key Points: Deviation from the normal baseline; Can signal a compromised account or insider threat; Should be reported and investigated

Definition: Honest mistakes that create risk without bad intent, such as sending data to the wrong recipient, misconfiguring a share, or mistyping a website address.
Example: An employee accidentally emails a spreadsheet of customer data to the wrong external address.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Anomalous behavior recognition
Key Points: No malicious intent, but still a risk; Training and controls such as DLP reduce it; Encourage reporting without fear of punishment

Definition: Teaching users the security knowledge and habits they need, covering policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid or remote work.
Example: New hires get training on the handbook, password managers, phishing and secure home Wi-Fi before receiving system access.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Eight listed topics; Should be role-based and repeated, not one-time; Measured through reporting and monitoring

Definition: Training users on the organization's security policies and employee handbook so they know the rules and where to find them, often with a signed acknowledgement.
Example: During onboarding, employees review the handbook's security section and sign that they understand the AUP.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Users cannot follow rules they do not know; Acknowledgement creates accountability; Update training when policies change

Definition: Training users to stay alert to their surroundings and to security risks around them, such as shoulder surfing, tailgating, unknown people in secure areas, and suspicious devices.
Example: An employee notices someone without a badge following them through a secure door and stops to ask for ID.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Be aware of people and physical surroundings, not just screens; Counters tailgating and shoulder surfing; Report suspicious activity

Definition: Training users to understand that threats can come from people inside the organization, malicious or careless, and to recognize and report warning signs.
Example: Staff learn that an unhappy coworker suddenly downloading customer lists before resigning is a warning sign to report.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Insiders already have access, which makes them dangerous; Signs: unusual access, data hoarding, disgruntlement; Pairs with least privilege and monitoring

Definition: Training users to create strong, unique passwords or passphrases, use a password manager, never share or reuse passwords, and use MFA.
Example: Users are taught to store unique passwords in the company password manager instead of a sticky note.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Unique password per site prevents credential stuffing; Password managers and MFA; Never share credentials, even with IT

Definition: Training users not to plug in unknown USB drives, cables or chargers, because they can carry malware or act as malicious devices, and to follow rules for approved media.
Example: An employee finds a USB drive labeled "Salaries" in the parking lot and hands it to IT instead of plugging it in.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Baiting with dropped USB drives is a common attack; Malicious cables can act as keyboards or exfiltrate data; Use only approved, encrypted media

Definition: Training users to recognize manipulation tactics such as pretexting, impersonation, phishing, vishing, smishing, tailgating and urgency, and to verify requests before acting.
Example: A caller claiming to be the CEO asks for an urgent wire transfer; the employee calls the CEO back on a known number to verify.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Attackers exploit trust, authority and urgency; Verify through a separate trusted channel; Covers email, phone, text and in-person attacks

Definition: Training users to protect sensitive information in daily activity, such as not posting work details online, keeping a clean desk, and not discussing confidential matters in public.
Example: An employee avoids posting a photo of their desk because the monitor shows internal project names and a login screen.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: OPSEC = do not leak information through normal behavior; Social media posts can help attackers; Clean desk and screen locking

Definition: Training users on working securely outside the office: using the VPN, securing home Wi-Fi, avoiding public networks, protecting devices and screens from others, and keeping work and personal use separate.
Example: A remote worker connects through the company VPN and uses a privacy screen when working in a coffee shop.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
Key Points: Home and public networks are less trusted; Use VPN, updates and strong Wi-Fi security; Watch for shoulder surfing and family use of work devices

Definition: Measuring and reporting how well the awareness program works, through initial (baseline) and recurring measurements such as phishing click rates, report rates and training completion.
Example: The program reports a 30% click rate at launch and 8% after a year of training.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Two listed: initial and recurring; Metrics prove effectiveness and guide changes; Track both failures (clicks) and good behavior (reports)

Definition: The first measurement taken when an awareness program starts, setting a baseline to compare future results against.
Example: Before any training, a phishing simulation shows 30% of staff click, which becomes the baseline.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Reporting and monitoring
Key Points: Baseline = starting point; Needed to show improvement later; Compare recurring = ongoing measurement

Definition: Regular, ongoing measurement and reporting of awareness results over time, such as monthly phishing metrics and training completion rates.
Example: Each month the security team reports phishing click and report rates to management to track trends.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness > Reporting and monitoring
Key Points: Shows trends and whether training works; Finds departments or users needing more help; Compare initial = one baseline measurement

Definition: Creating the awareness program: assessing needs, setting goals, identifying audiences and roles, choosing topics and formats, and building the content.
Example: The team surveys staff, sees remote work risks are high, and builds short monthly videos and a phishing program aimed at each department.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Development = plan and build; Tailor content to roles and risks; Set measurable goals before launch

Definition: Delivering the awareness program: rolling out training, running campaigns, scheduling sessions, tracking participation and adjusting based on results.
Example: Training launches company-wide in January, phishing simulations run monthly, and managers get completion reports.
Category: 5.6 Security awareness
Key Points: Execution = deliver and run; Track completion and results; Feeds back into development to improve the program
